The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Grace, a nurse who objects to abortion on grounds of conscience, works on a ward where a woman develops a severe haemorrhage during a medical termination. The registrar asks Grace to help immediately because no other nurse is free. What should Grace do?
o: Decline and fetch a colleague from the next ward to assist instead
Help after recording her objection in the patient's notes first
Help with the emergency, as the objection does not apply when life is at risk
Help with observations and leave the treatment itself to the registrar
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Section 4(2) Abortion Act 1967 (as summarised in NMC conscientious objection guidance) removes the right to object where treatment is necessary to save the life or prevent grave permanent injury to the pregnant woman. Code 15 also requires help in an emergency.

n.0: The statutory right to object does not extend to treatment necessary to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.
n.1: Delaying emergency care to complete documentation puts the woman at risk; the objection does not apply in this situation.
n.3: Limiting her role on conscience grounds is not available in an emergency where her help is needed to save life.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, has capacity and wants to return home after a fall. In a meeting her son says firmly that she must go to a care home and answers every question put to her. What is the most appropriate next step for the nurse?
o: Refer for a best interests meeting to settle the disagreement
Ask the son to put his concerns in writing for the discharge team
Speak with Mrs Lewis privately to explore her own views and wishes
Arrange a care home placement as her son holds strong views
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC proficiency P1.9 requires decisions based on people's needs and preferences, recognising and addressing factors that may unduly influence them. Speaking with her alone lets her express her wishes freely (Code 2.3, 2.4, 4.1).

n.0: Best interests decisions apply when a person lacks capacity (MCA s4); Mrs Lewis has capacity, so the decision is hers.
n.1: This may record his concerns but leaves the undue influence unaddressed and does not establish what Mrs Lewis wants.
n.3: The son's views do not replace the decision of a person with capacity; Code 1.3 and P1.9 require decisions based on her needs and preferences.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A journalist telephones a medical ward asking how a well-known footballer admitted that morning is doing. The admission has already been reported on local news. The nurse who answers is the most senior person on the ward. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Confirm that he is a patient but share no clinical details
Decline to comment and refer the caller to the communications team
Give a brief general update, as the admission is already public
Ask the patient's consultant to call the journalist back later
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 21.6: cooperate with the media only when appropriate, always protecting the confidentiality and dignity of people receiving care. Code 5.1 respects privacy; trust communications teams handle media enquiries with the patient's consent.

n.0: Confirming that someone is a patient is itself a disclosure of confidential information (Code 5).
n.2: Media reports do not remove the duty of confidentiality (Code 5.1); no information should be shared without consent and agreed process.
n.3: Passing the request to a clinician bypasses the trust's media process; media contact goes through the communications team.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Leanne, a staff nurse, is asked by the nurse in charge to remove a patient's chest drain because the doctors are busy. Leanne has read about the procedure but has never been trained or assessed in it. What should Leanne do first?
o: Watch an online video of the procedure and then remove the drain
Remove the drain with the nurse in charge talking her through it
Remove the drain and record that she did so on the instruction given
Explain she is untrained and ask a competent practitioner to do it
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 13.3: ask for help from a suitably qualified professional for any procedure beyond your competence; 13.5: complete training first; 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Safe evidence-based practice in procedures (P1.20) depends on this.

n.0: Self-directed viewing is not training or assessment; Code 13.5 requires the necessary training before a new role or procedure.
n.1: Verbal guidance from someone not supervising hands-on does not make her competent; she would be practising beyond her competence (Code 13.3).
n.2: Being instructed does not transfer accountability; each registrant is accountable for working within competence (Code 13).

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Joanne is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and is preparing to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she show over the three-year period?
o: 900 hours, including 450 for each registration
675 hours, as half of the second registration counts
1,350 hours, including 450 for each registration
450 hours across both registrations combined
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC revalidation, practice hours (page updated 26/05/2021): 450 hours for one registration, 900 hours for nurse and midwife (450 each), 1,350 for triple registration.

n.1: There is no pro rata reduction; each registration needs its own 450 hours.
n.2: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as nurse, midwife and nursing associate.
n.3: 450 hours is the figure for a single registration; dual nurse and midwife registration requires 900.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ama is due to revalidate next month. Her CPD log shows 35 hours: 18 hours at a study day and team workshops, and 17 hours reading journal articles on her own. What is the position on her CPD requirement?
o: She needs five more hours of any type of CPD
She needs two more hours of participatory learning
She needs fifteen more hours of participatory learning
She meets it, as she has 35 hours in total
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC revalidation CPD requirement (updated 08/09/2021): 35 hours of CPD in three years, of which at least 20 must include participatory learning. 20 - 18 = 2 participatory hours still needed.

n.0: Her total of 35 is already met; the shortfall is in participatory hours, not overall hours.
n.2: She needs 20 participatory hours in total; with 18 already logged, the gap is two hours.
n.3: The total is met, but at least 20 of the 35 hours must be participatory; she has 18.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is planning CPD for revalidation. Which activity would count as participatory learning under the NMC requirements?
o: Completing a self-directed e-learning module on sepsis
A live online workshop discussing cases with other nurses
Watching a recorded conference lecture on wound care
Reading a systematic review and writing summary notes
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC CPD guidance: participatory learning means activity involving interaction with one or more other professionals, in a physical or virtual environment; you do not have to be in the same room.

n.0: E-learning completed alone involves no interaction with other professionals, so it is non-participatory.
n.2: A recording watched alone has no interaction; participatory learning needs engagement with others.
n.3: Independent reading is valuable CPD but does not involve interaction with another professional.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A patient's family sends Hannah a thank-you card that names their mother and praises Hannah's care during her last days. Hannah wants to use it as practice-related feedback for revalidation. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Place a copy of the card in her revalidation portfolio
Ask her line manager to countersign the card before use
Note the content of the feedback without identifying details
Exclude it, as feedback must be formal and in writing
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC revalidation: five pieces of practice-related feedback from any source, written or verbal, formal or informal. Keep a note of the content and how it improved practice, without recording anything that could identify another person.

n.0: The card names the patient; NMC guidance says not to record information that may identify another person.
n.1: Feedback does not need countersigning; the key requirement is to remove identifying information.
n.3: Feedback can be written or verbal, formal or informal, from patients, families or colleagues.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Kwame is a practice nurse whose line manager, a non-registered practice manager, will act as his revalidation confirmer. He has written his five reflective accounts. How should he complete his reflective discussion?
o: Hold it with the practice manager during the confirmation meeting
Hold it with an NMC registrant before the confirmation meeting
Submit his five accounts to the NMC in place of a discussion
Hold it with a GP partner as part of his annual appraisal
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC reflective discussion guidance: hold the discussion with another registered nurse, midwife or nursing associate, face to face, about your five reflective accounts. If the confirmer is not an NMC registrant, the reflective discussion must take place before the confirmation discussion.

n.0: The reflective discussion must be with an NMC registrant; a non-registrant confirmer cannot hold it.
n.2: The written accounts and the reflective discussion are separate requirements; one cannot replace the other.
n.3: A GP is registered with the GMC, not the NMC; the discussion partner must be a nurse, midwife or nursing associate.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Marta works as an NHS ward nurse and plans to start offering cosmetic injections at a private clinic at weekends. Her NHS employer's indemnity covers her NHS work. What does the Code require before she starts the private work?
o: Confirmation from the clinic that her NHS indemnity extends to it
An appropriate indemnity arrangement that covers the private practice
Written approval of the private work from her NHS ward manager
A note of the private work in her next revalidation application
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 12.1: make sure you have an appropriate indemnity arrangement in place relevant to your scope of practice. Professional indemnity is also a revalidation declaration.

n.0: Her NHS indemnity covers NHS work; the clinic cannot extend it, so she needs separate appropriate cover.
n.2: Employer approval may be needed under her contract, but the Code requirement is indemnity cover relevant to her scope of practice.
n.3: Recording it later does not meet Code 12.1, which requires cover to be in place before she practises.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ravi took a career break and has practised 300 hours as a registered nurse in the three years since he last renewed. His renewal date is in four months. Which option will allow him to renew his registration?
o: Complete an approved return to practice programme before renewal
Ask his confirmer to sign off his study time as practice hours
Make up the shortfall by completing 150 extra CPD hours
Revalidate now and complete supervised practice hours afterwards
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC practice hours guidance: if you have not practised the required 450 hours, you must successfully complete an approved return to practice programme or a Test of Competence before your renewal application date.

n.1: Practice hours are hours relying on registered nurse skills and knowledge; a confirmer cannot convert study into practice.
n.2: CPD hours are a separate requirement and cannot substitute for practice hours.
n.3: Practice hours must be met by the application date, or a return to practice programme or Test of Competence completed first.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A student nurse asks Eleni to explain the difference between the two duties of candour that apply in English hospitals. Which statement is correct?
o: The statutory duty applies to doctors; the professional duty applies to nurses
The statutory duty applies to individual nurses; the professional duty applies to NHS trusts
Both duties apply to individual nurses and are enforced by the CQC
Statutory duty binds registered providers; professional duty binds individual registrants
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 places the statutory duty on registered providers (regulated by CQC). The professional duty (Code 14, NMC/GMC guidance refreshed December 2024) applies to individual registrants.

n.0: The professional duty applies to all regulated professionals including doctors; the statutory duty binds organisations.
n.1: This reverses the two duties; reg 20 binds registered providers and the Code binds individual registrants.
n.2: The CQC regulates the statutory duty on providers; the NMC oversees the professional duty on nurses.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: At 08:00 nurse Ollie gives Mrs Brown, 72, her 10:00 dose of paracetamol 1 g in error, two hours early. She is alert and well, and the next dose has not yet been given. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her, apologise, inform the prescriber and report it as an incident
Tell her and apologise, then retime later doses without reporting
Inform the prescriber and record the error in the medicines chart
Report it as an incident and tell her if harm develops later
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 14.1-14.3: put the situation right, explain fully and promptly and apologise, then document and escalate. The NMC/GMC duty of candour guidance (Dec 2024) also covers reporting incidents and near misses.

n.1: Adjusting doses is right, but Code 14.3 also requires the event to be documented and escalated.
n.2: This omits explaining and apologising to Mrs Brown, which the professional duty requires.
n.3: Code 14 applies when an incident had the potential for harm; candour does not wait for harm to occur.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Under regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations, an apology must be given as part of the duty of candour. Which statement to a patient best meets the regulation's definition of an apology?
o: "Errors like this are rare and are usually harmless."
"The trust accepts legal liability for the error."
"I am very sorry that this happened to you."
"An investigation will decide who was responsible."
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Reg 20(7): 'apology' means an expression of sorrow or regret in respect of a notifiable safety incident. Code 14.2 requires the nurse to apologise to the person affected.

n.0: This minimises the incident and does not express sorrow or regret.
n.1: An admission of liability is not what the regulation means by an apology; it means an expression of sorrow or regret.
n.3: This explains process but contains no expression of sorrow or regret.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Following a fall caused by a missed risk assessment, Mrs Doyle, 80, develops anxiety and disturbed sleep. The hospital is deciding whether this is prolonged psychological harm under the statutory duty of candour. Which threshold applies?
o: Psychological harm lasting at least 14 days in total over the admission
Psychological harm lasting at least 3 months after discharge
Psychological harm lasting, or likely to last, 28 continuous days or more
Psychological harm needing a referral to mental health services
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Reg 20(7): prolonged psychological harm means psychological harm which a service user has experienced, or is likely to experience, for a continuous period of at least 28 days.

n.0: The regulation uses 28 continuous days, not 14 days.
n.1: The threshold is 28 continuous days, not three months.
n.3: Referral is not the legal test; the test is duration of at least 28 continuous days.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A patient's family was told in person, with an apology, about a notifiable safety incident on the day it was identified. Under regulation 20, what must the provider do next?
o: Follow it with a written notification and keep a copy
Arrange a further meeting within 28 days to repeat the apology
Report the incident to the NMC for each nurse involved
Wait for the investigation to finish before any further contact
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Reg 20(3)-(4): notification must be given in person, include an apology and be followed by a written notification; the provider must keep a copy and written records.

n.1: Reg 20 requires a written notification after the in-person one; a repeat meeting is not the specified step.
n.2: Reg 20 is about notifying the relevant person; NMC referral relates to fitness to practise concerns, not candour steps.
n.3: The written notification follows the in-person notification and gives what is known so far; it does not wait for the investigation to finish.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Sam, 34, died after an incident on a surgical ward that the trust accepts is a notifiable safety incident. Under regulation 20, who should the trust notify about the incident?
o: Sam's GP, who will discuss the incident with the family
The CQC, which notifies families on the trust's behalf
A person lawfully acting on Sam's behalf, such as next of kin
The coroner, who will then decide whether to inform the family
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Reg 20(7): the relevant person is the service user or, on their death, a person lawfully acting on their behalf (also if under 16 and not competent, or 16 or over and lacking capacity).

n.0: The GP is not the relevant person; reg 20 notification goes to the person acting on Sam's behalf.
n.1: The CQC regulates compliance but does not notify relevant persons for providers.
n.3: Coroner referral is a separate duty; reg 20 requires the relevant person to be notified.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Nurse Adebayo nearly gives insulin to the wrong patient but notices at the bedside check, so no dose is given. A colleague says there is no need to report it because nothing happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss it at the next team meeting without making a report
Make a note in her own reflective log for revalidation
Tell the patient about the near miss and make no further record
Report the near miss through the local incident reporting system
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: The NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (refreshed December 2024) covers openness within organisations, including reporting adverse incidents and near misses. Code 19.1 requires action to reduce the likelihood of mistakes and near misses.

n.0: Discussion helps learning, but candour guidance expects near misses to be reported formally so the system can learn.
n.1: Personal reflection is useful but does not replace organisational reporting of the near miss.
n.2: Telling the patient is not enough; the near miss must still be documented and reported (Code 14.3, 19.1).

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Laura, a staff nurse, has worried for several weeks that the night skill mix on her ward is unsafe, with frequent missed observations. She has not yet raised it with anyone. According to NMC guidance, who should she raise it with first?
o: The NMC, so that it can investigate the ward's safety
The trust chief executive, as the person accountable for staffing
The Care Quality Commission, as the regulator for the ward
Her line manager, verbally or in writing, keeping a record
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: stage 1 line manager (verbally or in writing, keep a record); stage 2 designated person; stage 3 higher level; stage 4 regulator or helpline. Code 16.1.

n.0: The NMC regulates individual professionals; this is a system concern for the line manager first.
n.1: A higher level in the organisation is stage 3, after the line manager and designated person.
n.2: Going to a regulator is stage 4 of the NMC guidance, used if internal routes fail or are unsuitable.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Jade believes her ward manager is altering staffing records to hide unfilled shifts. She does not feel able to raise this with the manager herself. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Raise it with the manager's own staff at the next team meeting
Raise it with the designated person named in the trust's policy
Post her concerns on a professional social media group
Wait until she has more evidence before telling anyone
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: if you cannot raise the concern with your line manager, stage 2 is the designated person in your organisation (for example a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian). Code 16.1.

n.0: Discussing it with peers does not escalate it to someone able to act.
n.2: Public posting bypasses proper channels and risks confidentiality; NMC guidance uses internal and regulatory routes.
n.3: Code standard 16 requires her to act without delay; she does not need proof to raise a concern.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Kofi raised a patient safety concern with his manager and then with the trust's director of nursing. Three months later nothing has changed and patients remain at risk. Under NMC guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record his concerns in his reflective accounts for revalidation
Raise the concern again with his manager in writing
Contact a national newspaper to make the risk public
Raise the concern with a regulator such as the CQC
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance stage 4: if internal routes have not worked, raise the concern with a regulator or helpline, for example the CQC in England. Code 16.1.

n.0: Reflection does not escalate the risk to anyone able to act.
n.1: He has already used the internal stages without result; repeating stage 1 delays action.
n.2: Media disclosure is not a stage in NMC guidance and may lose legal protection.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ellie qualified six weeks ago. At the start of a night shift she is told she will be the only registered nurse for 28 patients on an unfamiliar ward, and has never taken charge. What should she do first?
o: Accept the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Raise her concerns at once with the person in charge and record it
Leave the ward and return to her own ward for safety
Accept the shift and phone her own ward manager at home
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 and NMC Raising concerns guidance support escalation and keeping a record.

n.0: Delaying until the morning leaves patients at risk; Code 16.2 requires her to raise concerns immediately.
n.2: Leaving abandons patients; she must raise the concern so safe cover is arranged.
n.3: Her absent manager cannot change tonight's staffing; the site lead or person in charge must be told now.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A healthcare assistant tells Nurse Ade that she has seen poor care but wants to raise it anonymously because she fears losing her job. What advice reflects NMC raising concerns guidance?
o: Giving her name aids investigation and gives her better legal protection
Anonymous concerns cannot be investigated, so she must give her name
She should wait until she has written evidence before raising anything formally
She should tell the patient's family so they can raise it instead
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance recommends giving your name because the concern is easier to investigate and you get the best legal protection; concerns can be raised confidentially within limits.

n.1: NMC guidance allows confidential raising, though naming oneself is recommended; anonymous concerns can still be looked at.
n.2: No proof is needed to raise a concern; waiting delays action on a possible risk.
n.3: Passing the duty to relatives is not an NMC route and does not protect patients promptly.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: At 22:00 two registered nurses phone in sick on a 30-bed ward with three acutely unwell patients. The nurse in charge has one registered nurse and two healthcare assistants. What is the priority action?
o: Escalate to the site manager now and request extra staff
Ask the healthcare assistants to give the evening medicines
Complete an incident report at the end of the shift
Reallocate patients and report the shortfall at the morning huddle
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P6.2: understand the relationship between safe staffing, skill mix, safety and quality and escalate concerns. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt escalation of risks; an incident report follows.

n.1: Delegating medicines beyond competence adds risk (Code 11.1) and does not solve the staffing gap.
n.2: Reporting is needed but does not resolve the immediate risk; escalation comes first.
n.3: Waiting until morning leaves an unsafe skill mix all night; it needs escalating now.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Nadia, a ward manager, learns that a staff nurse who raised a concern about a doctor's practice is now being left out of break rotas and ignored by some colleagues. What does the Code require Nadia to do?
o: Act to protect the nurse from detriment or victimisation
Wait for the concern to be investigated before taking any action
Advise the nurse to request a transfer to another ward
Report the nurse's colleagues to the NMC straight away
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 16.5-16.6: do not obstruct, intimidate or victimise anyone raising a concern, and protect anyone you have management responsibility for from harm, detriment, victimisation or unwarranted treatment after a concern is raised.

n.1: The victimisation is happening now; Code 16.6 requires her to act to protect the nurse.
n.2: Moving the nurse penalises the person who raised the concern; Code 16.6 requires protection from detriment.
n.3: Local management action comes first; referral may follow if misconduct is serious, but protection is the duty now.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ben is unsure whether his worry about a care home's practice is a whistleblowing matter and wants free, confidential, independent advice before acting. Which source does NMC guidance suggest?
o: Protect, the independent whistleblowing charity
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
NHS Resolution, the NHS litigation authority
Healthwatch, the local patient voice organisation
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance lists Protect (independent whistleblowing charity), professional bodies and trade unions as sources of advice.

n.1: The Ombudsman handles unresolved complaints about services; it does not advise staff on whistleblowing.
n.2: NHS Resolution handles clinical negligence claims, not staff advice on raising concerns.
n.3: Healthwatch gathers public views on services rather than giving staff whistleblowing advice.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mia, a nurse on a children's surgical ward, receives a social media friend request from the mother of a child currently in her care. The mother says she wants to thank Mia personally. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the request and remove her once the child is discharged
Politely decline the request and keep contact within the ward
Accept the request as the mother made the first contact
Accept the request and restrict what the mother can view
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 20.6: maintain clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including former patients, their families and carers. NMC social media guidance: do not use social networks to build or pursue relationships with patients or service users.

n.0: A relationship with a family member of a current or former patient blurs boundaries (Code 20.6).
n.2: Who initiates the contact does not change the professional boundary set out in Code 20.6.
n.3: Privacy settings do not remove the boundary issue; NMC guidance says not to use social media to build relationships with people in your care or their families.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: On discharge, several patients offer gifts to the ward team. According to the Code, which gift would it be acceptable to accept, subject to local policy?
o: A £50 gift voucher for the nurse who cared for her
A £100 cheque for the nurse's personal use
A designer handbag for the nurse in charge
A box of chocolates for the whole team to share
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality, as accepting them could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment.

n.0: A voucher of this value is not trivial; Code 21.1 says refuse all but the most trivial gifts.
n.1: Money for personal use is not a trivial gift and may be seen as an inducement.
n.2: An expensive gift could be seen as seeking preferential treatment and breaches Code 21.1.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Callum, a district nurse, mentions that his car has broken down. The son of a patient he visits offers to lend him £500 to repair it until payday. What should Callum do?
o: Accept the loan and declare it to his manager
Decline the loan and keep the relationship professional
Accept the loan and repay it in full on payday
Accept a smaller amount as a gift in place of a loan
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 21.2: never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them. Code 21.3 requires honesty and integrity in financial dealings.

n.0: Declaring it does not make it acceptable; loans from people close to patients are prohibited by Code 21.2.
n.2: Code 21.2 says never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them, even if repaid.
n.3: A cash gift of this kind is not trivial and breaches Code 21.1.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Two weeks after discharge from an acute mental health unit, a former patient messages Sam, his named nurse, asking to meet for coffee to say thank you. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Meet in a public place as the patient has been discharged
Accept if the patient's care coordinator agrees to it
Decline the invitation and keep contact professional
Meet once with a colleague present to say goodbye
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 20.5-20.6: do not take advantage of vulnerability; stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past.

n.0: Code 20.6 boundaries extend to people who have been in your care in the past.
n.1: Another professional's agreement does not change the boundary set by Code 20.6.
n.3: A social meeting, even accompanied, blurs the professional relationship with a former patient.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: At a retirement celebration on the ward, a nurse takes a team photograph. A patient sitting in a bay is visible in the background. The nurse wants to post it on her public social media account. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Post the photograph after blurring the patient's face
Post the photograph with no names or ward details
Post the photograph using strict privacy settings
Post a version without the patient, who has not consented
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC social media guidance: do not post pictures of patients and people receiving care without their consent, regardless of whether you believe they could be identified. Code 5.1 and 20.10.

n.0: NMC guidance requires consent before posting images of patients, whether or not you believe they could be identified.
n.1: Removing names does not remove the need for the patient's consent to the image being shared.
n.2: Privacy settings do not replace consent and content can still be shared onward.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A staff nurse uses a public social media profile that states she is a registered nurse at the local hospital. Which post would most clearly breach the Code?
o: Sharing the NHS flu vaccination campaign with her followers
Celebrating her own nursing graduation with a family photo
Posting a link to an NMC consultation on the Code
Urging followers, as a nurse, to vote for a political party
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 21.5: never use your status as a registered professional to promote causes that are not related to health. Code 20.7 also cautions against expressing personal political beliefs inappropriately.

n.0: Promoting a public health message is related to health and supports Code 3.1.
n.1: A personal photo with no patient information does not breach the Code.
n.2: Sharing professional regulatory information is not a breach.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Leah sees that a colleague has posted a joke on a public social media page about 'the difficult patient in bed 4', with enough detail for others on the ward to identify the patient. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Message the colleague privately and take no further action
Report the post to the social media platform as offensive
Raise it with her manager through the trust's concern channels
Reply publicly to the post telling the colleague to delete it
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NMC social media guidance: concerns about colleagues' inappropriate use of social media should be raised through the proper channels in line with Raising concerns guidance. Code 5.1, 16.1, 20.10.

n.0: A private word may be reasonable first, but identifiable patient information online is a confidentiality breach that needs escalating.
n.1: Platform reporting may remove the post but does not address the professional concern locally.
n.3: Engaging publicly spreads the content further; NMC guidance points to raising concerns through proper channels.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: The husband of a woman on a medical ward has started texting Rhys, her nurse, on his personal mobile, asking for updates late at night. Rhys gave him the number to arrange a visit. What should Rhys do?
o: Block the number without explaining his reasons to the husband
Reply with brief updates as the husband is her next of kin
Explain the boundary, give the ward number and tell the nurse in charge
Reply to messages during his shifts and switch off his phone at home
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P1.13: develop, manage and maintain appropriate relationships with people, their families and carers. Code 20.6 boundaries; Code 5 confidentiality; Code 8.2 keep colleagues informed.

n.0: Blocking without explanation damages the therapeutic relationship and leaves the husband without a proper contact route.
n.1: Next of kin status does not authorise sharing without her consent, and personal phone contact blurs boundaries.
n.3: Continuing private messaging keeps an unprofessional channel open and risks confidentiality.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: During equality training, a healthcare assistant asks which personal characteristic is protected under section 4 of the Equality Act 2010. Which of these is a protected characteristic?
o: Pregnancy and maternity
Body weight or size
Socioeconomic background
Caring responsibilities
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Equality Act 2010 s4 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

n.1: Weight is not a protected characteristic, although a related condition may amount to a disability.
n.2: Socioeconomic background is not one of the nine protected characteristics in s4.
n.3: Being a carer is not itself a listed characteristic in s4.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Josh, 24, is autistic and finds busy waiting rooms overwhelming, so he has missed two outpatient appointments. Under section 20 of the Equality Act 2010, what is the clinic's duty?
o: Make adjustments if he provides a formal diagnosis letter
Offer him the same appointment process as other patients
Discharge him back to his GP after two missed appointments
Take reasonable steps to avoid his substantial disadvantage
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Equality Act 2010 s20: duty to make reasonable adjustments where a provision, criterion or practice puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage. Proficiency P1.14 and P3.7.

n.0: The duty is to take reasonable steps; insisting on paperwork first delays an adjustment such as a quiet room or first appointment.
n.1: Treating him identically is what causes the disadvantage; s20 requires adjustments.
n.2: Discharging without adjustment ignores the disadvantage caused by his disability and the s20 duty.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mr Hughes, 70, tells Ama, a Black staff nurse, that he does not want 'someone like her' looking after him. Ama is upset. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse in charge?
o: Reassign Ama quietly to avoid any further conflict
Challenge the remark, support Ama and report the incident
Ask Ama to carry on and to disregard the remark
Tell Mr Hughes he must leave the ward for his behaviour
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 3.4: challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour; Code 20.2: treat people fairly without discrimination, bullying or harassment. Proficiency P1.4: understand and challenge discriminatory behaviour; report through local policy.

n.0: Reassigning without challenge colludes with the discrimination; Code 3.4 and 20.2 require it to be challenged.
n.2: This leaves the racist behaviour unchallenged and fails to support the colleague.
n.3: Withdrawing care is disproportionate; the behaviour should be challenged while care continues safely.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: At handover a colleague describes Mrs Evans, 91, who is medically fit for discharge but waiting for a care package, as 'just another bed-blocker'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Challenge the language and refocus on her needs
Laugh it off to keep handover moving quickly
Report the colleague to the NMC after the shift
Raise it at the colleague's appraisal in a few months
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 1.1 and 1.3: treat people with respect and avoid assumptions; Code 3.4: challenge poor practice and discriminatory attitudes. Age is a protected characteristic (Equality Act 2010 s4).

n.1: Letting it pass condones an ageist label; Code 3.4 requires discriminatory attitudes to be challenged.
n.2: A first remark is best challenged directly and locally; NMC referral is for serious fitness to practise concerns.
n.3: Waiting months misses the chance to challenge it now and protect Mrs Evans's dignity.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Rosa reviews feedback and notices she spends less time explaining care to patients who speak English with a strong accent, assuming they will not understand. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Offer these patients an interpreter in place of her explanation
Ask colleagues to explain care to these patients for her
Continue as before, as shorter explanations reduce confusion
Recognise this as possible unconscious bias and reflect on it
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Annexe A 1.7: be aware of your own unconscious bias in communication. Code 1.3 avoid assumptions; Code 9.2 reflect on feedback to improve practice.

n.0: An accent does not mean an interpreter is needed; offering one by default is another assumption.
n.1: Passing the task on avoids addressing her own bias and its effect on communication.
n.2: This keeps an assumption that denies patients information; Code 1.3 says avoid assumptions.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Fatima, 45, is admitted for an elective procedure. She asks that only female staff provide her intimate personal care because of her religious beliefs. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree to her request if her religion is recorded on the notes
Arrange female staff for her personal care where possible
Explain that personal care will be given by whoever is on duty that shift
Ask her to bring a female relative to give her personal care
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P1.14: provide non-discriminatory, person-centred, sensitive care reflecting people's values, beliefs and culture. Code 1.3 and 2.4; religion or belief is a protected characteristic (Equality Act s4).

n.0: Respecting a preference does not depend on paperwork; it should be accommodated where possible now.
n.2: This disregards her beliefs; P1.14 requires care that reflects people's values, beliefs and culture.
n.3: This shifts care onto family and may not be safe or what she wants.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: An NHS trust plans to move all outpatient bookings to an online-only app. A senior nurse on the project group is asked what the public sector equality duty requires. Which answer is correct?
o: Obtain written consent from disabled patients before making the change
Have due regard to the effect on people with protected characteristics
Seek approval for the change from the CQC before launch
Ensure that every patient has a smartphone before the change
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Equality Act 2010 s149: public authorities must have due regard to the need to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations between people with and without protected characteristics.

n.0: Section 149 does not require individual consent; it requires due regard when making decisions.
n.2: The CQC does not approve booking systems; s149 places the due regard duty on the trust itself.
n.3: The duty is to have due regard to equality aims, not to supply equipment to every patient.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Daniel, 38, is admitted unconscious after a cycling accident. His husband, Mark, arrives, but Daniel's parents ask staff not to let Mark visit or receive information. Daniel's record names Mark as next of kin. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the parents and Mark to agree a single visitor between them
Follow the parents' request as they are blood relatives
Support Mark's role as next of kin and involve him as Daniel wishes
Restrict both parties' visiting until Daniel can decide
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 1.3 and 20.2: avoid assumptions and treat people fairly without discrimination; sexual orientation and marriage are protected characteristics (Equality Act s4). P1.14 person-centred care based on the person's wishes.

n.0: This hands the decision to the family dispute rather than following Daniel's recorded wishes.
n.1: Blood relationship gives no priority; Daniel's recorded wishes and his marriage must be respected without discrimination.
n.3: Excluding his recorded next of kin is unfair to Mark and not based on Daniel's wishes.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: At the start of a late shift, Nurse Kim notices that her colleague smells strongly of alcohol, is slurring words and is about to start the medicines round. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Report her to the NMC and let her continue the shift
Offer to do the medicines round with her as a second checker
Stop her giving medicines and tell the nurse in charge now
Speak to her privately at the end of the shift about support
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but never at the expense of patient or public safety. Code standard 16 act without delay on risks to safety (16.1 raise and escalate concerns); P1.5.

n.0: Allowing her to continue exposes patients to harm; local escalation and removal from duties come first.
n.1: Supervising her still allows an impaired nurse to give medicines; patient safety must come first.
n.3: Support matters, but waiting leaves patients at immediate risk (Code 8.7).

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ellie has worked 60 hours a week for a month to cover vacancies. She has twice nearly given the wrong dose and feels exhausted. Her manager asks her to do another extra shift. What should Ellie do?
o: Accept the shift and ask colleagues to double-check her work
Decline the shift and tell her manager about the near misses
Accept the shift and rest fully on her next day off
Decline the shift and keep the near misses to herself
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need for your role. Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code. Proficiency P1.5.

n.0: Working while exhausted keeps patients at risk; she must address her fitness for practice (Code 20.9).
n.2: Planning rest later does not address the current risk she has recognised.
n.3: Declining helps, but Code 16.3 requires her to tell someone in authority about problems affecting safe practice.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation, Lucy, a staff nurse, is tearful in the clean utility room. She is due to start the next medicines round in ten minutes. What is the most appropriate response from her colleague?
o: Tell her to go home and let the nurse in charge know later
Reassure her that she will get used to deaths over time
Advise her to take a few minutes and then start the round on time
Offer support, ask how she feels and help arrange cover if needed
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems without compromising safety. Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risk.

n.0: Sending her home without discussion or escalation leaves the ward uncovered and her unsupported.
n.1: This dismisses her distress and offers no practical support.
n.2: This overlooks whether she is safe to give medicines right now.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ben, a theatre nurse, has developed persistent back pain that is making patient transfers difficult. He has not told anyone. Which action best reflects his professional responsibility for his own health?
o: Wait until his annual appraisal to mention the problem
Seek occupational health advice and discuss adjustments
Take regular painkillers and keep doing transfers as before
Avoid transfers by swapping tasks with colleagues informally
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role. Proficiency P1.6: take responsibility for a healthy lifestyle to maintain fitness for practice; Code 19.4 personal precautions.

n.0: Waiting delays support; Code 20.9 requires maintaining the health needed for the role now.
n.2: Masking symptoms risks harm to himself and patients and does not address fitness for his role.
n.3: Informal swaps hide the problem and may leave the team short of safe handlers.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A student nurse asks Priti why she called the outreach team for a patient whose NEWS2 is 4, when the escalation chart only requires a ward review. Priti had noticed new subtle confusion. Which response best shows sound professional judgement?
o: Explain that her clinical concern justified the escalation
Explain that students should not question escalation decisions
Explain that the score required outreach review at that level
Explain that she prefers to escalate every patient to be safe
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P1.10: demonstrate resilience and emotional intelligence and explain the rationale for judgements and decisions. NEWS2 (RCP 2017): clinical concern can prompt escalation beyond the aggregate score; new confusion scores 3.

n.1: This shuts down learning; Code 9.4 requires her to support students' learning.
n.2: Under NEWS2 (RCP 2017) an aggregate of 4 calls for a ward-based response, urgent review by the ward medical team if one parameter scores 3, not outreach; her call rested on clinical concern.
n.3: Blanket escalation is not a reasoned judgement; P1.10 requires the rationale to be explained.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: After the unexpected death of a young patient, several members of the ward team seem shaken. The ward manager wants to support the team's resilience. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Offer the team extra shifts to keep them occupied
Ask each nurse to write a statement about what went wrong
Encourage the team to move on and focus on the next shift
Hold a supportive debrief and signpost wellbeing services
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P6.11: accept and manage uncertainty and develop resilience in self and others. Code 8.7 support colleagues; Code 25.2 support staff you are responsible for.

n.0: More shifts may increase fatigue and do not address distress.
n.1: Statements may be needed for review, but they do not address the team's wellbeing.
n.2: This dismisses the emotional impact and misses the chance to support resilience.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Over two months, Zara has noticed her usually cheerful colleague has become withdrawn, irritable with patients and has had several short-term absences. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Speak to her privately, voice concern and signpost support
Avoid raising it in case it causes her more stress
Suggest she takes annual leave to recover from stress
Report her absence pattern to the ward manager at once
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to health. Code 8.7 support colleagues; escalate if patient safety becomes affected.

n.1: Avoiding the issue fails to support a colleague showing signs of vulnerability (P1.5).
n.2: Advising leave without understanding the problem may not meet her needs.
n.3: Raising it with the manager may follow, but a supportive conversation is the appropriate first step when there is no immediate safety risk.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Your close colleague, going through a divorce, asks you not to mention that she has given several time-critical medicines over an hour late this week. She promises it will stop. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree to keep it confidential if she promises to improve
Offer support but explain you must tell the nurse in charge
Give her time-critical medicines for her so the delays stop
Report her to the NMC without speaking to anyone locally
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but this must never compromise patient safety. Code 16.1: raise and escalate safety concerns; 19.1 reduce harm.

n.0: Code 8.7 says support must not compromise patient safety; late time-critical medicines need escalating.
n.2: Covering for her hides the problem and leaves the risk unmanaged.
n.3: Local escalation and support should come first; referral is not the immediate proportionate step.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A ward team wants the strongest evidence on whether a new dressing reduces infection in surgical wounds. Which type of study gives the highest level of evidence for this question?
o: An expert consensus opinion paper from specialists
A single large randomised controlled trial
A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
A large prospective cohort study of patients
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Oxford CEBM levels of evidence (therapy): level 1a is a systematic review of randomised controlled trials; expert opinion is level 5. Code 6.1 requires evidence-based information.

n.0: Expert opinion is the lowest level in evidence hierarchies such as the Oxford CEBM levels.
n.1: A well-designed RCT is strong evidence but ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
n.3: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs for treatment effects.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A ward manager wants to check whether patients' falls risk assessments are completed within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires, by reviewing 50 sets of notes. How should this project be classified?
o: Research, which needs NHS research ethics committee review
Health surveillance, which tracks outbreaks and health threats
Service evaluation, which judges a service without a standard
Clinical audit, which measures practice against a set standard
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (October 2022): clinical audit answers 'Does this service reach a predetermined standard?', uses care already in use and does not require REC review.

n.0: It tests no hypothesis and seeks no generalisable knowledge; it compares practice with an existing standard.
n.1: Surveillance monitors threats to population health, not compliance with a ward policy.
n.2: Service evaluation does not measure against a predetermined standard; this project does.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A district nursing team wants to find out how patients rate their new evening visiting service, with no benchmark to compare against, by asking current patients to complete a short questionnaire. What type of project is this?
o: Qualitative research study
Clinical audit
Randomised controlled trial
Service evaluation
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): service evaluation asks 'What standard does this service achieve?', measures the current service without reference to a standard and does not need REC review.

n.0: It aims to judge the current service, not to generate generalisable knowledge.
n.1: Audit compares practice with a predetermined standard; here there is no standard.
n.2: There is no allocation to interventions or randomisation.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mr Green, 66, has venous leg ulcers. NICE guidance supports compression therapy, but after a full explanation he declines it because he previously found it painful. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Discharge him from the clinic as he has declined treatment
Ask the GP to prescribe stronger analgesia and apply it anyway
Apply the compression, as NICE guidance must be followed
Explore his concerns, discuss alternatives and record his choice
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: NICE guidance ('Your responsibility' statement, as in NG253) is not mandatory; professionals take it fully into account alongside individual needs and preferences. Code 2.5 and 4.2; P1.8 critical evidence-informed decisions.

n.0: Declining one option does not end care; alternatives and support should be explored.
n.1: Applying compression he has refused would breach his right to refuse (Code 2.5).
n.2: NICE guidance is not mandatory; it must be applied alongside the person's needs and preferences.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A company representative gives a ward manager a single-site study of 20 patients, funded by the company, with no control group, reporting that its new catheter reduces infections. The manager wants to switch at once. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Switch now, as published evidence shows a clear benefit
Appraise the study's limits and seek stronger evidence first
Reject the product, as industry-funded studies are invalid
Switch now and audit infection rates after six months
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Proficiency P1.7-P1.8: critically analyse research findings and think critically when applying evidence. Code 6.1 information must be evidence-based; small uncontrolled studies sit low in evidence hierarchies.

n.0: A small, uncontrolled, industry-funded study has a high risk of bias and does not justify a change alone.
n.2: Funding source raises the risk of bias but does not automatically invalidate a study; appraisal is needed.
n.3: Auditing after a change does not replace appraising whether the evidence supports the change.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A nurse researcher wants to understand what living with a new stoma is like for young adults, in their own words. Which research approach is most suitable?
o: A qualitative design using in-depth interviews
A randomised controlled trial of stoma care products
A retrospective audit of stoma complication rates
A cross-sectional survey using closed questions
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022) recognises qualitative research approaches; interviews explore meaning and experience. Proficiency P1.7: understand research methods to critically analyse findings.

n.1: An RCT compares interventions; it does not explore lived experience.
n.2: An audit measures practice against a standard, not personal experience.
n.3: Closed questions limit responses and do not capture experience in people's own words.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mrs Shah, 58, asks a practice nurse whether a herbal supplement she has bought online will help her blood pressure alongside her prescribed amlodipine. The nurse is unsure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her that nurses cannot discuss non-prescribed products
Check a reliable source or the pharmacist before advising her
Advise her that herbal products are natural and safe to take
Advise her to stop the amlodipine while she tries the supplement
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 6.1: information or advice must be evidence-based, including about health products; Code 18.3: check compatibility with other treatment, including over-the-counter medicines; Code 13.3 seek help when unsure.

n.0: Code 18.3 expects compatibility with other treatments, including over-the-counter products, to be checked.
n.2: This is not evidence-based and ignores possible interactions (Code 6.1, 18.3).
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review could be harmful and is outside the nurse's evidence base.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: At 07:00 Nurse Joe realises he did not record that Mrs Ali, 79, had an unwitnessed fall at 02:30, though he assessed her at the time. What is the correct way to document this?
o: Ask the day nurse to record the fall at her first check
Write the entry and time it 02:30 so the record is in order
Add the fall to the handover sheet in place of the notes
Write a 07:00 entry stating it relates to the fall at 02:30
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.1: complete records at the time or as soon as possible after an event, recording if notes are written some time after the event. Code 10.3 no falsification.

n.0: She did not witness the event; Code 10.4 requires entries to be attributed to the person who made them.
n.1: Back-timing misrepresents when the note was written; Code 10.1 requires late entries to be recorded as such.
n.2: Handover sheets are not the formal record; the fall must be documented in the patient's notes.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Nurse Sara notices she has written the wrong blood pressure value in a patient's paper observation chart. What is the correct way to correct the entry?
o: Write the right value over the top of the wrong one
Cover the entry with correction fluid and rewrite it neatly
Tear out the page and copy the chart onto a new sheet
Strike through once, keep it legible, then sign, date and time
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.3-10.4: complete records accurately without falsification, attribute entries and date and time them. Annexe A 1.8: write accurate, clear, legible records.

n.0: Overwriting makes both values illegible and unattributed.
n.1: Obscuring the original entry could be seen as falsification and makes the change untraceable (Code 10.3).
n.2: Removing pages destroys part of the record and breaches Code 10.3.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Which entry in a patient's nursing notes best meets the Code's requirements for record keeping?
o: Pt fell again, prob drunk as usual. Dr aware, all fine, will watch. JL
Afternoon: patient found on floor but appears OK. Will monitor. Nurse
14:30 Patient on floor, probably slipped on wet floor, unhurt and settled
14:30 Found on floor by bed. Alert, uninjured. Dr Khan informed. J Lee, RN
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.4: attribute entries to yourself, clearly written, dated and timed, without unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation; Code 10.2 record steps taken.

n.0: This includes speculation and judgemental language and lacks a time (Code 10.4).
n.1: No exact time, vague content and not attributed to a named person.
n.2: The cause is speculation, it is not attributed and no escalation is recorded.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Agency nurse Paul's electronic record login has expired. A permanent colleague offers him her smartcard so he can document his care until IT resets his access. What should Paul do?
o: Use her card and add his own name at the start of each entry
Use her card and ask her to check his entries afterwards
Wait until his access returns and write all entries then
Decline and use the approved paper back-up until access returns
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.4: attribute entries to yourself; Code 10.5: keep records secure. Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely; P1.15 digital skills for safe practice.

n.0: Entries would still be attributed to her login, breaching Code 10.4 and information security.
n.1: Her checking does not correct the false attribution of entries to her.
n.2: Delaying documentation risks missing information; Code 10.1 requires timely records.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Reviewing the night's charts, Nurse Hana sees that a healthcare assistant recorded hourly observations for a patient who was off the ward in theatre for three of those hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Mention it informally to the healthcare assistant next week
Amend the entries herself so the chart is accurate
Leave it, as the patient has now returned safely
Escalate it to the nurse in charge straight away
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.3: complete records without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to these requirements. Code 16.1 escalate concerns.

n.0: Falsified observations are a safety concern; Code 10.3 requires immediate action.
n.1: Altering another person's entries is itself inappropriate; the concern must be escalated.
n.2: The patient's safety now does not remove the falsification; it must be acted upon.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Over 24 hours, Mr Ito, 74, receives 1,000 mL IV fluid and drinks 650 mL. His output is 1,500 mL urine and 600 mL vomit. He is drowsy with a dry mouth. What is the fluid balance and the best action?
o: Minus 450 mL; continue current fluids and recheck tomorrow
Minus 1,100 mL; restrict oral fluids as he is vomiting
Minus 450 mL; report the deficit and signs of dehydration
Plus 450 mL; continue current fluids and recheck tomorrow
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Input 1,000 + 650 = 1,650 mL; output 1,500 + 600 = 2,100 mL; balance = 1,650 - 2,100 = -450 mL. P1.15 numeracy for safe practice; Code 13.1 recognise deterioration and 13.2 refer in a timely way.

n.0: The figure is right, but drowsiness and a dry mouth with a negative balance need prompt escalation.
n.1: 1,650 - 2,100 = -450 mL; restricting fluids would worsen dehydration.
n.3: Input 1,650 mL minus output 2,100 mL gives minus 450 mL, not plus.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Ruth is running late at the end of a shift and plans to email herself her patients' details so she can finish the care plans at home on her personal laptop. What should she do?
o: Print the details and complete the plans at home that night
Email the details to herself and delete them afterwards
Finish the care plans on the trust system before leaving
Email the details to herself with the names removed
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.5: take all steps to make sure records are kept securely; Caldicott principle 6 comply with the law; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality principle. Annexe A 1.10 share digital information safely.

n.0: Taking paper records home risks loss and breaches confidentiality (Code 5, 10.5).
n.1: Sending patient data to personal email breaches secure storage requirements, even if later deleted.
n.3: Pseudonymised clinical details on a personal device remain a security risk and are not trust records (Code 10.5).

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which abbreviation practice best supports safe record keeping when documenting medicines and care in the notes. Which approach should she follow?
o: Write terms in full unless the trust approves the abbreviation
Use abbreviations for drug names to save time in busy shifts
Use the abbreviations she learned during her training abroad
Use any abbreviation that colleagues on the ward understand
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 10.4: records must be clearly written and not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. Annexe A 1.8 accurate, clear, legible records.

n.1: Abbreviating drug names risks medication errors and breaches Code 10.4.
n.2: Abbreviations vary between countries and may not be understood here.
n.3: Local shorthand may be misread by others; Code 10.4 says no unnecessary abbreviations.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse on a surgical ward, is reading the Code during her preceptorship. She wants to know which of the four themes contains the standard on keeping clear and accurate records. Which theme is it?
o: Promote professionalism and trust
Prioritise people
Practise effectively
Preserve safety
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: The Code (NMC 2015, updated 2018) has four themes: Prioritise people (1-5), Practise effectively (6-12), Preserve safety (13-19) and Promote professionalism and trust (20-25). Standard 10, keep clear and accurate records, sits under Practise effectively.

n.0: Promote professionalism and trust covers standards 20-25 (reputation, registration, investigations, complaints, leadership), not record keeping.
n.1: Prioritise people covers standards 1-5 (dignity, preferences, needs, best interests, confidentiality); records sit under standard 10.
n.3: Preserve safety covers standards 13-19 (competence, candour, emergencies, raising concerns, medicines, harm reduction); records are standard 10.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Daniel is a registered nurse on a gynaecology ward. He holds a religious objection to abortion and is allocated to help prepare a patient for a surgical termination of pregnancy this afternoon. Under the Code, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell the nurse in charge at the end of the shift that he objects to this work
Tell colleagues, manager and patient, and arrange a qualified colleague to cover
Take part in today's procedure and register his objection with the NMC afterwards
Explain his religious reasons to the patient so that she understands his decision
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care about a conscientious objection and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over responsibility for that person's care. Section 4(1) Abortion Act 1967 gives the statutory right to refuse to participate.

n.0: Telling one person after the event leaves the patient's care unplanned; Code 4.4 requires colleagues, manager and patient to be told and cover arranged.
n.2: The NMC does not hold a register of objections; Code 4.4 requires him to declare the objection and hand over care in advance.
n.3: Code 20.7 says not to express personal beliefs to people in an inappropriate way; he must tell her he objects, not argue his beliefs.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: A healthcare assistant asks Sofia, a staff nurse, what the Code means by 'the fundamentals of care' that every registrant must deliver effectively (standard 1.2). Which aspect of care does the Code name as one of the fundamentals?
o: Discharge planning with the wider team
Medicines reconciliation on admission
Wound assessment and dressing selection
Bladder and bowel care
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: The note to Code 1.2 says the fundamentals of care include, but are not limited to, nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and keeping people in clean and hygienic conditions.

n.0: Discharge planning relates to coordinating care, not to the fundamentals listed in the note to standard 1.2.
n.1: Medicines reconciliation is important but it falls under standard 18 on medicines, not the Code's definition of fundamentals of care.
n.2: Wound care is a clinical procedure; the Code's fundamentals are nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and hygiene.

The Code & Professional Accountability.q: Mr Okafor, 68, is recovering from a hip replacement and has capacity. After the nurse explains why his evening enoxaparin injection is prescribed and the risk of a blood clot, he says clearly that he does not want it tonight. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Respect his decision, document the refusal and inform the prescriber
Carry out a formal mental capacity assessment before accepting the refusal
Record the omission code on the chart and review at tomorrow's dose
Ask his daughter to visit and persuade him to accept the injection
The Code & Professional Accountability.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment; Code 4.1 balances best interests with that right. Informing the prescriber allows the VTE plan to be reviewed (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.1: Capacity is presumed (MCA 2005 s1(2)) and nothing suggests he lacks it; refusing advice is not itself evidence of incapacity.
n.2: Recording the code is part of the answer, but the prescriber must be told so the VTE risk can be reviewed now.
n.3: Recruiting family to pressure him undermines his autonomy; Code 2.5 requires the nurse to respect and support his right to refuse.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Novak, 48, starts telling the nurse about his worries about returning to work after a heart attack, then stops mid-sentence and looks down. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Use a gentle prompt such as "Go on" and wait
Change the subject to his discharge medicines
Summarise what he has said and close the conversation
Reassure him that everything will be fine at work
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.2: use prompts and positive verbal and non-verbal reinforcement. Minimal prompts and silence encourage the person to continue (Annexe A 1.1 active listening).

n.1: Moving on closes the conversation just as he is opening up.
n.2: Summarising can help, but closing now prevents him finishing his thought.
n.3: This is false reassurance that dismisses his concern.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: The evening before major surgery, Mrs Reid, 67, asks the nurse quietly, "Am I going to die tomorrow?" Which response is most appropriate?
o: "You'll need to ask the surgeon that question."
"Everyone feels like that the night before."
"Don't worry, the surgeons do this every day."
"What is worrying you most about tomorrow?"
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.5: use caring conversation techniques. Exploring the person's concern before giving information responds compassionately to distress (Code 2.6).

n.0: Redirecting her without exploring her fear misses the chance to support her now.
n.1: Generalising her feelings minimises her individual concern.
n.2: This is false reassurance that closes down her concern.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Owusu, 81, says he 'came over funny' before his fall at home. The nurse needs to understand what happened. Which response best clarifies his account?
o: "So you fainted, then. How long were you unconscious?"
"What did 'came over funny' feel like for you?"
"Lots of older people feel funny. Let's move on."
"Did you trip on something on the floor?"
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.6: use clarification techniques; P1.11 communicate effectively with people at all stages of life. Code 7.4 keep misunderstanding to a minimum.

n.0: This assumes a faint and leads him to a particular answer.
n.2: This dismisses an important symptom and stops clarification.
n.3: This closed question narrows to one cause before his experience is understood.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mrs Kowalska, 74, speaks Polish and little English. She needs to consent to a planned procedure. Her 12-year-old grandson offers to interpret. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a bilingual ward housekeeper to interpret during her break
Accept the grandson's offer as he is a trusted relative
Give her the English consent form to take home overnight
Book a professional interpreter before discussing consent
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: NHS England Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; use of anyone under 16 is not acceptable except when immediate and necessary treatment is required. Code 7.2.

n.0: An untrained staff member is not a registered interpreter; reliance on unqualified interpreters is discouraged.
n.1: NHS England guidance says use of anyone under 16 is not acceptable except for immediate necessary treatment.
n.2: An English form does not meet her language needs and is not informed consent.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Haddad, 60, speaks Arabic. For a routine review he asks that his adult son interpret rather than a professional interpreter. What should the nurse do?
o: Agree straight away, as patients may choose their interpreter
Use the son and ask him to sign the record as interpreter
Confirm his choice privately via a professional interpreter
Refuse, as family members cannot act as interpreters
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): if a patient expressly wants a family member to interpret, seek informed consent in their own language independently of the family member and note it in the record.

n.0: Guidance requires informed consent obtained independently of the family member before relying on them.
n.1: The son's signature does not show the patient gave informed consent in his own language.
n.3: Patients may choose a family member if they give informed consent independently of that person.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: A hospital is reviewing how it meets the Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605). Which patient's need falls within the scope of the standard?
o: A patient whose first language is Romanian
A patient who wants a copy of their clinic letter
A Deaf patient who uses British Sign Language
A patient who prefers appointments by email
