Below the level of the bladder and not touching the floor
On the floor beside the bed to keep the tubing straight
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE CG139 (catheter care): the drainage bag is positioned below the level of the bladder to maintain flow and prevent reflux, and kept off the floor to avoid contamination, using a stand where needed.

n.0: At bladder level, drainage slows and urine can pool or reflux.
n.1: Raising the bag above the bladder allows contaminated urine to flow back towards the bladder.
n.3: A bag on the floor becomes contaminated and increases the risk of catheter-associated infection.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Kathleen, 90, lives at home with a long-term urinary catheter. Her daughter asks the community nurse to start weekly bladder washouts to stop Kathleen getting urine infections. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange weekly 0.9% sodium chloride washouts to reduce infection risk
Explain washouts do not prevent infection and support daily meatal washing
Request antibiotic prophylaxis to be given at every catheter change
Arrange to change the catheter every week to limit bacterial colonisation
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE CG139: bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection; the meatus is washed daily with soap and water. Catheters are changed when clinically necessary or per manufacturer, and antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter change is not offered routinely.

n.0: CG139 says washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection.
n.2: CG139 says do not routinely offer antibiotic prophylaxis when changing long-term catheters.
n.3: Catheters are changed according to clinical need or the manufacturer's advice, not weekly.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: While giving a subcutaneous injection to Peter, 61, who has hepatitis C, nurse Hana sustains a needlestick injury to her finger through her glove. The needle has been used. What should Hana do immediately?
o: Let it bleed without squeezing, wash with soap and running water, then report
Squeeze the wound firmly to express blood, then apply an alcohol wipe
Suck the wound, cover it with a plaster and report it after the drug round
Scrub the wound with a nail brush and chlorhexidine, then apply a dressing
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM appendix 10: allow the area to bleed but do not squeeze, do not suck, and wash with warm running water and non-antimicrobial soap. The incident is then reported urgently so that occupational health or A&E can assess the need for post-exposure management; the Sharps Regulations 2013 require all sharps injuries to be reported.

n.1: Squeezing can push contaminated material deeper into tissue; NIPCM says allow bleeding without squeezing.
n.2: Sucking the wound is specifically advised against, and reporting must be prompt so treatment is not delayed.
n.3: Scrubbing damages tissue and may increase uptake; gentle washing under running water is advised.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Pauline, 73, has an MRSA-colonised leg ulcer. The nurse removes a dressing heavily soaked with wound exudate. In an acute hospital in England, which waste stream should the used dressing go into?
o: Yellow and black striped offensive waste bag
Orange bag for infectious clinical waste
Black domestic waste bag
Purple bag for cytotoxic waste
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.9 (HTM 07-01): clinical waste that is infectious, for example from a patient known or suspected to be infected or colonised, goes in a UN-approved orange bag. Offensive (tiger) waste is for non-infectious waste containing body fluids.

n.0: Tiger bags are for offensive waste that is not infectious; this dressing is from a colonised wound.
n.2: Domestic bags are for non-healthcare general waste, not soiled dressings.
n.3: Purple is for waste contaminated with cytotoxic or cytostatic medicines.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: During the morning medication round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the drug trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. Several injections are still due. What should Lewis do with the full container?
o: Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Leave it open and start a second container beside it on the trolley
Press the contents down to make room for the remaining needles
Use it until it is completely full, then seal it before lunch
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.9: sharps containers must be disposed of when the manufacturer's fill line is reached, labelled with point of origin and dates of assembly and disposal, and use the temporary closure when not in use.

n.1: A full container left open is a sharps hazard; it should be locked and removed.
n.2: Pushing down sharps risks a needlestick injury and overfills the container.
n.3: Filling past the fill line risks protruding sharps and injury.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Blood from a dislodged cannula has spilled onto the hard floor beside the bed of Thomas, 66. Spill granules are available. The nurse has put on non-sterile gloves and an apron. What should the nurse do next?
o: Cover with paper towels and apply 70% alcohol to the towels
Apply 1,000 ppm chlorine solution and mop the area straight away
Wipe it up with paper towels and clean the area with detergent
Apply chlorine-releasing granules and leave for the contact time
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM appendix 9: for blood or high-risk body fluid spills apply chlorine-releasing granules (or towels soaked in 10,000 ppm available chlorine), follow the contact time (or 3 minutes), discard the waste as healthcare waste, then wash with detergent and dry.

n.0: Alcohol is not the NIPCM agent for blood spills.
n.1: 1,000 ppm is for urine, faeces or vomit spills; blood needs granules or 10,000 ppm, with contact time.
n.2: Detergent alone does not disinfect a blood spill, which may contain blood-borne viruses.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: A urinal has been knocked over, spilling urine across the floor of a bay. The urine contains no visible blood. The nurse wears gloves and an apron. Which approach to managing this spill is correct?
o: Sprinkle chlorine-releasing granules directly on the urine
Pour 10,000 ppm chlorine solution directly on the urine first
Soak up with paper towels, then clean with 1,000 ppm chlorine
Leave it for the domestic team to clean at the next routine round
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM appendix 9: do not use a chlorine-releasing agent directly on a urine spill (it can release chlorine gas). Soak up with disposable paper towels (a gelling agent may be used), then decontaminate with 1,000 ppm available chlorine or a combined detergent and chlorine product, then wash and dry.

n.0: Granules are for blood and high-risk body fluids; on urine they risk releasing chlorine gas.
n.1: Chlorine must not be applied directly to urine, and 10,000 ppm is the blood-spill strength.
n.3: Spills are treated immediately by trained staff, not left as a slip and infection hazard.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Ivy, 85, has confirmed norovirus and her bed linen is soiled with diarrhoea. The healthcare support worker strips the bed. How should the soiled linen be handled?
o: Roll it up and seal it in a water-soluble bag inside an impermeable bag
Shake it out over the bin, then put it in a red-tagged bag at the bedside
Rinse off the faeces in the sluice, then place it in the used linen bag
Place it on the chair while remaking the bed, then bag it as used linen
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.7: infectious linen is not sorted or rinsed but rolled together and sealed in a water-soluble (alginate) bag, then placed in an impermeable bag immediately on removal, secured and tagged before leaving the area.

n.1: Shaking linen disperses organisms into the environment.
n.2: NIPCM says used linen must not be rinsed, and linen from an infectious patient is infectious, not used, linen.
n.3: Used linen must not be placed on floors or other surfaces such as chairs.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: A communal commode has just been used by Frank, 78, who has suspected C. difficile. It must be decontaminated before use by anyone else, and there is no visible blood. Following NIPCM appendix 7, how should it be cleaned?
o: Clean with detergent, then 1,000 ppm available chlorine, rinse and dry
Clean with detergent, then 10,000 ppm available chlorine, and dry
Wipe all surfaces with 70% isopropyl alcohol wipes and dry
Clean with detergent wipes and leave it to air dry before reuse
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM appendix 7: equipment contaminated with faeces or used on a patient with known or suspected infection is cleaned with detergent then a 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or a combined product), rinsed and dried. 10,000 ppm is reserved for blood and high-risk body fluids. Equipment for an isolated patient should ideally be dedicated to them.

n.1: 10,000 ppm is for contamination with blood or high-risk body fluids, not faeces without blood.
n.2: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores and is not the appendix 7 method.
n.3: Detergent alone is for equipment not exposed to infection; this commode was used by a patient with suspected C. difficile.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: You see a colleague give an intramuscular injection to Lily, 34, then carefully recap the needle with both hands to carry it to the sharps container at the nurses' station. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she carries used sharps in a clean kidney dish to the sharps bin
Advise her to take a sharps container to the point of use and not recap
Advise her to use the one-handed scoop method when recapping needles
Suggest she removes the needle from the syringe before carrying it
Infection Prevention & Control.w: The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 and NIPCM ch 1.10: needles must not be resheathed or disassembled, sharps are discarded at the point of use by the person who generated them, and the needle and syringe go in the container as one unit.

n.0: Carrying used sharps to a distant bin still exposes staff; disposal should be at the point of use.
n.2: NIPCM does not recommend recapping by any method; the container should be at the point of use.
n.3: Needles and syringes are disposed of as one unit; removing the needle is a common cause of injury.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Rose, 70, an inpatient on a medical ward, has new dysuria and frequency. She is alert with a NEWS2 score of 1. The doctor prescribes oral nitrofurantoin. No urine sample has been sent. What should the nurse do before giving the first dose?
o: Send a sample after 48 hours if her symptoms have not improved
Obtain a urine sample first, then give the antibiotic without delay
Give the first dose now and send a sample with her next void
Withhold the antibiotic until the urine culture result is available
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.27: for patients in hospital who have suspected infections, take microbiological samples before prescribing an antimicrobial and review the prescription when results are available. Collecting the sample first takes minutes and does not delay treatment.

n.0: Delaying the sample for 48 hours loses the chance to guide treatment, contrary to NG15.
n.2: A sample taken after the antibiotic may give a false negative culture, so the prescription cannot be reviewed against reliable results.
n.3: Treatment is not delayed until culture returns; the sample is taken first and the drug given promptly.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: A GP practice nurse sees Mia, 4, who has a high fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a spreading maculopapular rash. She is unvaccinated. The GP suspects measles. Which statement about notification in England is accurate?
o: It is notified on suspicion, urgently by phone to the health protection team
It is reported online within 7 days as a routine notifiable disease
It is notified by the school nurse once two linked cases are confirmed
It is notified once laboratory confirmation of measles has been received
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, registered medical practitioners must notify UKHSA on suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Measles is listed as urgent, so it is phoned to the local health protection team within 24 hours, and all cases are reported within 3 days (UKHSA guidance).

n.1: Measles is an urgent notifiable disease, and the reporting deadline for all cases is 3 days, not 7.
n.2: The duty sits with the registered medical practitioner and applies to a single suspected case.
n.3: UKHSA states do not wait for laboratory confirmation; notification is on clinical suspicion.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: A student nurse on placement asks which of the following conditions is a notifiable disease that a doctor in England must report to UKHSA. Which is correct?
o: MRSA colonisation found on an admission screen
Uncomplicated genital chlamydia infection
Clostridioides difficile infection in a hospital inpatient
Invasive group A streptococcal disease
Infection Prevention & Control.w: The UKHSA list of notifiable diseases includes invasive group A streptococcal disease, classed as urgent. C. difficile and MRSA are monitored through separate healthcare-associated infection surveillance, and chlamydia is not on the notifiable disease list.

n.0: MRSA colonisation is managed through screening and HCAI surveillance, not notification.
n.1: Chlamydia is monitored through sexual health surveillance and is not on the notifiable disease list.
n.2: C. difficile is reported through mandatory HCAI surveillance by trusts, not as a notifiable disease by doctors.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Ahmed, 66, is on day 3 of intravenous co-amoxiclav for pneumonia. He is now afebrile, eating and drinking, and his blood culture shows a sensitive organism. His chart states 'IV for 7 days'. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
o: Ask the prescriber to review an oral switch using his results
Continue the intravenous course for the 7 days as charted
Ask for a broader-spectrum agent to prevent a relapse
Withhold the next dose as he is afebrile and improving
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.39: review intravenous antimicrobial prescriptions at 48-72 hours, including response and microbiology results, to decide whether to continue and whether to switch to oral. The nurse can prompt this stewardship review.

n.1: Continuing IV without review ignores the NG15 48-72 hour review and prolongs cannula and resistance risks.
n.2: A sensitive organism supports narrowing, not broadening, the spectrum.
n.3: Stopping a prescribed antibiotic is a prescribing decision; withholding without review risks undertreatment.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Within 24 hours, three patients in the same six-bed bay on an elderly care ward develop sudden vomiting and diarrhoea. None was admitted with these symptoms. What should the nurse in charge do first?
o: Phone UKHSA directly to notify a notifiable disease
Send stool samples and wait for results before reporting
Inform the IPC team promptly about a possible outbreak
Report it at the weekly ward governance meeting
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Two or more linked cases in the same area suggest an outbreak (P2.12, communicable disease surveillance). The IPC team should be informed promptly so that bay closure, isolation and sampling can be coordinated (NIPCM ch 2.1); the IPC team leads outbreak management and liaises with the UKHSA health protection team where needed.

n.0: Statutory notification is the registered medical practitioner's duty; the nurse in charge's first step in a ward outbreak is the IPC team, who coordinate control measures and any health protection liaison.
n.1: Samples are needed, but waiting for results before reporting delays outbreak control.
n.3: A weekly meeting delays control measures while the infection spreads.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: June, 72, has a NEWS2 score of 8 and suspected sepsis from a chest infection. Blood cultures and a lactate have been taken, and IV antibiotics are prescribed. Twenty minutes have passed since NEWS2 was calculated. The laboratory says culture results will take 48 hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Give a 250 mL fluid bolus, then wait for culture results
Give the antibiotics now, within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score
Repeat NEWS2 in 30 minutes before giving antibiotics
Wait for the Gram stain before choosing the antibiotic
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE NG253 (2025): for people at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating NEWS2. Cultures are taken first, as NG15 advises, and the prescription is reviewed when results arrive.

n.0: A fluid bolus may be indicated, but antibiotics must not wait for culture results.
n.2: NEWS2 is recalculated every 30 minutes at high risk, but treatment is not delayed to do so.
n.3: Waiting for microbiology would breach the 1-hour target for high-risk sepsis.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Victor, 81, has been taking clindamycin for 5 days for cellulitis. He now has four episodes of watery diarrhoea in 12 hours and is in a four-bed bay. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop the clindamycin and keep him in the bay with curtains drawn
Isolate him, send a stool sample and ask for an antibiotic review
Give loperamide and review his bowels at the end of the day
Send a stool sample and keep him in the bay until the result returns
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.35 highlights the risk of selecting for C. difficile with certain antibiotics. New diarrhoea on antibiotics should prompt isolation on suspicion (NIPCM ch 2.1), a stool sample and a prescriber review of the antibiotic.

n.0: Changing antibiotics is a prescriber decision, and staying in the bay exposes other patients.
n.2: Antimotility drugs are inappropriate in suspected C. difficile and delay diagnosis.
n.3: Isolation should not wait for the result, as C. difficile spreads to others in the bay.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: You are caring for Harold, 78, who is in a side room with confirmed Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea. You have just helped him to the commode and removed your gloves and apron. What is the most appropriate method of hand hygiene now?
o: Apply alcohol-based handrub, rubbing all surfaces for 20 to 30 seconds
Use a detergent hand wipe, then apply alcohol-based handrub
Rub hands with an antimicrobial surgical scrub solution until dry
Wash with liquid soap and running water, then dry with paper towels
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NHS England NIPCM (ch 1.2) says wash hands with non-antimicrobial liquid soap and water when caring for a patient with a suspected or known gastrointestinal infection, such as a spore-forming organism like C. difficile. Alcohol does not reliably act against spores, so mechanical removal by washing is needed.

n.0: Alcohol-based handrub is the routine method, but it is not effective against C. difficile spores, so NIPCM directs soap and water here.
n.1: Hand wipes followed by handrub are a fallback for when running water is unavailable; Harold's side room has running water.
n.2: Surgical scrub products are for surgical hand antisepsis before sterile procedures, not routine care of a patient with C. difficile.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse, arrives for a shift on a surgical ward wearing a long-sleeved cardigan, a wristwatch, a plain metal wedding band and short, unvarnished nails. Before giving direct care, which change does she need to make to meet standard infection control precautions?
o: Remove the cardigan, the watch and the wedding band before patient contact
Keep the cardigan on and swap the wristwatch for a fob watch
Remove the cardigan and the watch and keep the plain wedding band on
Roll the cardigan sleeves to the elbow and wear gloves over the band
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.2: before hand hygiene staff must be bare below the elbows and remove hand and wrist jewellery, with the exception of a single plain metal ring, which should be moved during hand hygiene. Short nails without products are already compliant.

n.0: A single plain metal ring is permitted under NIPCM, so the wedding band does not have to come off.
n.1: Long sleeves stop her being bare below the elbows, so keeping the cardigan on is not compliant even with a fob watch.
n.3: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene, and a pushed-up cardigan is not the bare-below-the-elbows standard.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: A nurse enters the bay of Gladys, 84, to tidy her over-bed table and move her water jug within reach. Gladys is asleep and the nurse does not touch her. The nurse then turns to leave the bed space. Which of the five moments for hand hygiene applies now?
o: After a body fluid exposure risk in the bed space
Before a clean or aseptic procedure on the ward
After touching a patient's immediate surroundings
After touching a patient during a care episode
Infection Prevention & Control.w: The five moments in NIPCM ch 1.2 are before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching a patient's immediate surroundings. Handling the over-bed table and jug is contact with the immediate surroundings, which can be contaminated.

n.0: No blood or body fluid exposure risk occurred while tidying the table.
n.1: The nurse is leaving, not about to start a clean or aseptic task.
n.3: The nurse did not touch Gladys, so the moment 'after touching a patient' does not describe this contact.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: During induction, a healthcare support worker asks Femi, a staff nurse, when the standard infection control precautions (SICPs) used on the ward should be applied. Which reply from Femi is accurate?
o: To patients having invasive procedures or with invasive devices
To patients with a known or suspected infection or colonisation
To all patients at all times, whether or not infection is known
To patients with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or an unexplained rash
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1 states SICPs are to be used by all staff, in all care settings, at all times, for all patients whether infection is known to be present or not. They reduce transmission from recognised and unrecognised sources.

n.0: Invasive procedures need aseptic technique, but SICPs apply to every patient whether or not a device is present.
n.1: Known or suspected infection triggers transmission-based precautions in addition to SICPs; SICPs themselves apply to everyone.
n.3: These symptoms flag a cross-infection risk for placement decisions, but SICPs are not limited to symptomatic patients.

Medicines Management.q: Late at night, the out-of-hours doctor phones the hospice to increase the dose of subcutaneous diamorphine for Albert, 70, who is in pain. The doctor is 40 minutes away. The nurse knows diamorphine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug. What should the nurse do?
o: Explain it cannot be a verbal order and seek a written prescription
Accept it and ask the doctor to sign the chart within 24 hours
Accept it and record the doctor's name and GMC number in the notes
Accept it with a second nurse listening on speakerphone as witness
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20 allows verbal orders in exceptional circumstances for medicines other than Schedule 2 controlled drugs. Diamorphine is Schedule 2, so a written prescription is needed; the nurse should escalate so Albert's pain is managed promptly, for example by the doctor attending or using any existing anticipatory prescription.

n.1: Later written confirmation applies to permitted verbal orders, which exclude Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: Recording the caller's details does not overcome the exclusion of Schedule 2 CDs from verbal orders.
n.3: A witness does not make a verbal order for a Schedule 2 CD acceptable.

Medicines Management.q: Martha, 58, reads the leaflet for a newly prescribed medicine and finds it describes a different condition from hers. The pharmacist confirms the medicine is licensed in the UK but has been prescribed outside the terms of its licence. Martha asks the nurse whether this is allowed. Which reply is accurate?
o: It is a dispensing error, as the leaflet does not match her condition
It is off-label use, and the prescriber should explain it to her
It is allowed once a second doctor countersigns the prescription
It is unlicensed use, so it cannot legally be given on the ward
Medicines Management.w: Off-label use means prescribing a licensed medicine outside its marketing authorisation (P4.16). It is lawful, but the prescriber takes on greater responsibility and should give the person enough information to make an informed choice. The nurse should check Martha's understanding and refer questions to the prescriber.

n.0: The pharmacist has confirmed the supply is correct; a mismatched leaflet is expected with off-label use.
n.2: Off-label prescribing does not require a second doctor's countersignature.
n.3: An unlicensed medicine has no UK licence at all; this medicine is licensed but used off-label, which is lawful.

Medicines Management.q: Before her evening dose, Shirley, 74, says her blood pressure tablets look different from the ones she had last month and asks if they are the wrong tablets. The prescription is for amlodipine 5 mg once daily. What should the nurse do?
o: Give both the old and new tablets so she gets the full effect
Check the drug and strength match and explain generics can look different
Withhold the dose until the original brand can be supplied
Report the change as a dispensing error on the incident reporting system
Medicines Management.w: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient and strength as the branded product but may differ in appearance (P4.16). The nurse confirms the label, drug and strength match the prescription before giving it, and explains this to Shirley.

n.0: Giving both would double the dose of amlodipine.
n.2: Withholding an appropriate generic omits a prescribed dose without reason.
n.3: A generic supply matching the prescription is not an error.

Medicines Management.q: In a nursing home, the GP reviews Hilda, 88, by video call and decides to reduce her bisoprolol dose from tomorrow. The GP cannot visit to amend the medication administration record (MAR). Under RPS/RCN guidance, how should the change be communicated?
o: By a message passed on by Hilda's daughter after the call
By a secure electronic message from the GP, with records updated
By the nurse amending the MAR from her notes of the call
By a text message from the GP to the nurse's personal mobile phone
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20.2: if the prescriber cannot issue a new prescription or amend the chart, the changes are communicated by an appropriately secure electronic method and the patient's records are updated.

n.0: A relayed message from a relative is not a direction from the prescriber.
n.2: Without the prescriber's written or secure electronic confirmation, the nurse would be altering a prescription.
n.3: A personal phone is not a secure, auditable route for prescribing information.

Medicines Management.q: Before giving the first dose of oral amoxicillin to Stanley, 67, the nurse notices he is wearing a red allergy wristband labelled 'penicillin'. The allergy section of his drug chart is blank and the prescriber has gone home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose with an antihistamine to cover any possible reaction
Withhold it, clarify the allergy with Stanley and contact a prescriber
Give the dose, as the drug chart has no allergy recorded
Give half the dose and observe Stanley closely for any reaction
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 requires the person administering to check allergies or previous adverse drug reactions, and to raise ambiguities with the prescriber or pharmacy without delay. Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so the dose is withheld, the reaction history clarified, the chart updated and an alternative sought.

n.0: An antihistamine would not prevent anaphylaxis and the nurse cannot add a medicine.
n.2: The wristband is a warning that must be resolved; a blank chart is an omission, not evidence of no allergy.
n.3: Altering the prescribed dose is not within the nurse's role, and any dose risks anaphylaxis.

Medicines Management.q: Hassan, 54, is prescribed 7.5 mg of an intramuscular medicine. The ampoule contains 10 mg in 2 mL. The nurse works out the volume to draw up and a colleague is available. What volume is needed, and what should happen before administration?
o: 1.5 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
2.67 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
0.75 mL, then give it straight away as the colleague is busy
3.75 mL, then record the calculation in the notes and give it
Medicines Management.w: Volume = (dose required / stock strength) x stock volume = (7.5 / 10) x 2 = 1.5 mL. RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 says any calculations needed are double checked, where practicable, by a second person.

n.1: 2.67 mL inverts the fraction (10 / 7.5 x 2); a check would catch it, but the volume is wrong.
n.2: 0.75 mL omits multiplying by the 2 mL volume, and skipping an available second check is unsafe.
n.3: 3.75 mL comes from dividing the dose by the stock volume (7.5 / 2) instead of using the formula, and no second check is made.

Medicines Management.q: At the 08:00 round, Pearl, 81, refuses her prescribed ramipril, saying it makes her dizzy. She has capacity and understands the reason for the tablet. How should the nurse record and act on this?
o: Record 'refused' with her reason and inform the prescriber
Leave the box blank and mention it at the handover
Record 'given', as the tablet was offered at the correct time
Leave the tablet on her locker and record it once she takes it
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 17: records are kept of medicines administered, withheld or declined, completed at the time or as soon as possible; the reason is recorded and the prescriber or team informed where appropriate. Dizziness may need a medication review.

n.1: A blank box is unauditable and may lead someone else to give a second dose.
n.2: Recording a refused dose as given is a false record.
n.3: She has declined it; leaving tablets unattended is unsafe and the refusal still needs recording.

Medicines Management.q: Agnes, 70, admitted for a planned hip replacement, asks to keep her own inhalers and eye drops in her bedside locker and use them herself, as she does at home. What should the nurse do?
o: Allow it once her daughter agrees to supervise her doses
Complete a self-administration risk assessment and record it
Decline, as nurses give all medicines on a hospital ward
Allow it, as they are her own supply brought in from home
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-5: organisations have a self-administration policy; a risk assessment considers risks, the person's ability and consent, decides the level of self-administration, and the outcome and the person's agreement are recorded and reassessed as necessary.

n.0: A relative's agreement does not replace the documented professional risk assessment.
n.2: RPS/RCN guidance expects patients to keep responsibility for their medicines unless a risk assessment indicates otherwise.
n.3: Ownership does not replace the risk assessment that decides whether self-administration is safe.

Medicines Management.q: Clive, 76, has moved from hospital to a nursing home. The nurse is asked to transcribe his discharge medicines onto the home's MAR chart. The insulin entry on the discharge letter reads '10U' with a smudged figure in front of it. What should the nurse do?
o: Transcribe it as 100 units, reading the smudge as a zero
Transcribe it as 10 units, as that is the most legible figure
Contact the prescriber to clarify the dose before transcribing it
Leave the insulin off the MAR until his next GP review
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 31: medicines are not transcribed where details are illegible, unclear, ambiguous or incomplete, with particular care for high-risk medicines such as insulin. The abbreviation 'U' is itself a recognised cause of insulin overdose. Clarification is sought without delay.

n.0: Reading 'U' or a smudge as a zero is the classic tenfold insulin error.
n.1: Guessing at an illegible insulin dose risks a serious error.
n.3: Omitting insulin until a routine review risks hyperglycaemia; prompt clarification is needed.

Medicines Management.q: Bryony, 39, is nil by mouth after surgery. Her observations are stable and her prescription is for 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. The nurse is setting up the infusion and will ask a colleague to check it. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 166 mL/h on the volumetric pump
125 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.5 mL/h on the volumetric pump
80 mL/h on the volumetric pump
Medicines Management.w: Rate (mL/h) = volume / time = 1,000 mL / 8 h = 125 mL/h. Accurate dosage calculation is a patient safety proficiency (P4.14) and the setting should be checked against the prescription.

n.0: 166 mL/h corresponds to 6 hours, not 8.
n.2: 12.5 mL/h is a decimal place error, a tenfold underinfusion.
n.3: 80 mL/h would deliver 1,000 mL over 12.5 hours.

Medicines Management.q: During the breakfast round, Norma, 85, says she would like to take her tablets after she has eaten and asks the nurse to leave them on her table. Norma has capacity but no self-administration assessment has been done. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the tablets as refused and offer them at lunchtime
Return after breakfast to give them and record once taken
Leave the tablets and sign the chart as given
Leave the tablets and ask a support worker to check later
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) paras 3-4 and 15-17: unless a self-administration risk assessment allows it, the nurse administering remains accountable and must see the dose taken; the record is completed at the time of administration (NICE SC1: record only after the dose is taken).

n.0: Norma has not refused; she asked to take them later, which can be accommodated.
n.2: Signing before the dose is taken creates an inaccurate record and the tablets may be lost or taken by others.
n.3: Delegating a check does not confirm administration and leaves medicines unattended.

Medicines Management.q: Frank, 63, is prescribed oral morphine solution 2.5-5 mg as required every 2 hours for pain. He had 2.5 mg 4 hours ago with little effect and now rates his pain 8/10. He is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 2.5 mg now and repeat it in 30 minutes if needed
Give 7.5 mg, as the previous 2.5 mg dose was ineffective
Withhold the dose until the doctor increases the prescription
Give 5 mg, the top of the prescribed range, and reassess
Medicines Management.w: Titration within a prescribed range is a nurse's decision based on assessment (AnnexB.11.5). The previous dose was ineffective, he is not sedated and 2 hours have passed, so the higher dose within the range is appropriate, with reassessment of pain, sedation and respiratory rate.

n.0: Repeating at 30 minutes breaches the 2-hourly minimum interval.
n.1: 7.5 mg exceeds the prescribed range, which the nurse cannot change.
n.2: A suitable dose is available within the range; withholding leaves him in pain.

Medicines Management.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, which of these medicines is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
o: Diazepam 5 mg tablets
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Midazolam injection 10 mg in 2 mL
Medicines Management.w: Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 (Home Office controlled drugs list), oxycodone is in Schedule 2, alongside morphine, diamorphine and fentanyl, and needs a CD register entry (NICE NG46). Midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3; diazepam is Schedule 4 Part 1.

n.0: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 Part 1 benzodiazepine.
n.2: Tramadol is in Schedule 3.
n.3: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug, although many hospitals record it in the register by local policy.

Medicines Management.q: A ward's controlled drugs register has been completed and a new book started. The ward clerk asks how long the old register must be kept. Under NICE NG46, what is the minimum retention period?
o: 1 year from the date of the last entry
2 years from the date of the last entry
6 months from the date the book was closed
7 years from the date of the first entry
Medicines Management.w: NICE NG46: controlled drugs registers must be kept for 2 years from the date of the last entry, in line with the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. (Records of destruction of patients' own CDs are kept for a minimum of 7 years.)

n.0: 1 year is shorter than the legal minimum.
n.2: 6 months is well below the 2-year requirement.
n.3: 7 years applies to records of destruction of patients' own CDs, and the period runs from the last entry.

Medicines Management.q: Nurse Kemi is asked by a colleague to countersign the controlled drugs register for a dose of subcutaneous morphine that the colleague prepared and gave while Kemi was on her break. Trust policy requires a witness for CD administration. What should Kemi do?
o: Sign it and add a note that she did not see the dose given
Sign it, as she trusts her colleague's practice and experience
Sign the stock balance but leave the witness column blank for now
Decline, and offer to witness the next dose from preparation onwards
Medicines Management.w: NICE NG46 and RPS/RCN guidance: the CD administration record includes the person administering and any witness, and witnessing means observing the process. Signing for something not seen is a false record (NMC Code 10.3, records accurate). Kemi should decline and the colleague should report the gap per policy.

n.0: A witness signature with a disclaimer still misrepresents the record and breaches the witness policy.
n.1: Trust does not make a signature truthful; she did not witness the dose.
n.2: Countersigning the balance still implies checking a transaction she did not see.

Medicines Management.q: During a weekly stock check, two nurses find that the oxycodone 5 mg capsule count is one lower than the balance in the controlled drugs register. They have rechecked the cupboard and the most recent entries. What should they do next?
o: Report the discrepancy to the nurse in charge and pharmacy
Wait for the next weekly check to see if the count resolves
Borrow a capsule from another ward to restore the balance
Correct the register balance to match the stock and initial it
Medicines Management.w: NICE NG46: stock check SOPs include reporting and managing discrepancies between stock and records. Once rechecked, unresolved discrepancies are reported promptly to the person in charge and pharmacy (and the CD accountable officer as required) and an incident is recorded.

n.1: Delaying a week loses the trail needed to investigate a possible diversion or error.
n.2: Borrowing stock conceals the loss and creates a second unrecorded transfer.
n.3: Altering a balance to hide a discrepancy falsifies a legal record.

Medicines Management.q: At 07:30 the ward medicines refrigerator display reads 11°C and the overnight maximum recorded is 13°C. It contains insulin pens and influenza vaccines. Yesterday's readings were within range. What should the nurse do?
o: Quarantine the contents, report it, and seek pharmacy advice before use
Move the items to another fridge and use them as normal
Discard all the contents immediately into the pharmaceutical waste bin
Turn the thermostat down and recheck the temperature tomorrow
Medicines Management.w: Medicines such as insulin and vaccines are stored at 2-8°C (Green Book ch 3 cold chain). After a temperature excursion, the stock is quarantined in a working fridge and not used until pharmacy (or the vaccine manufacturer via pharmacy) advises; the excursion is reported and recorded (AnnexB.11.11).

n.1: Using stock after an excursion without advice risks giving ineffective vaccines or insulin.
n.2: Some stock may be usable after assessment; discarding everything without advice wastes medicines.
n.3: Adjusting the dial does not address whether the exposed stock is still safe.

Medicines Management.q: After Arthur, 89, dies at home, his son asks the district nurse what to do with Arthur's remaining tablets, including morphine sulfate modified-release tablets and blister packs from the pharmacy. What advice is most appropriate?
o: Put them in a sealed bag in the household waste collection
Return all the medicines to a community pharmacy for disposal
Hand them in at the GP surgery reception to be destroyed
Flush the tablets down the toilet so they cannot be misused
Medicines Management.w: Safe disposal of medicines (AnnexB.11.11; NICE NG46 on disposal of CDs that belonged to a person who has died): unwanted medicines, including controlled drugs, are returned to a community pharmacy, which disposes of them under the relevant regulations.

n.0: Household waste allows diversion and environmental contamination.
n.2: Surgery reception staff are not the route for patient-returned medicines; pharmacies accept them.
n.3: Flushing medicines contaminates water supplies and is not an approved disposal route.

Medicines Management.q: Eileen, 76, is prescribed morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously. The ward stocks morphine sulfate 10 mg in 1 mL ampoules. A second nurse witnesses throughout. Which controlled drugs register entry correctly records the dose and the remainder?
o: 2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.4 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.6 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) returned to the CD cupboard
2.5 mg (2.5 mL) given; ampoule recorded as used with no remainder
Medicines Management.w: Volume = 2.5 / 10 x 1 = 0.25 mL, leaving 7.5 mg (0.75 mL). NICE NG46: for CDs left over after administration, record the amount disposed of and the signatures of the person disposing and any witness. Opened ampoules are not returned to stock.

n.1: 0.4 mL contains 4 mg, so the volume is wrong for a 2.5 mg dose.
n.2: Opened ampoules cannot be returned to stock; the remainder is disposed of and recorded.
n.3: 2.5 mL exceeds the 1 mL ampoule and would be a tenfold miscalculation.

Medicines Management.q: Pharmacy has not yet collected four out-of-date diamorphine ampoules from a ward's CD cupboard. A nurse suggests destroying them in a denaturing kit with another registered nurse to tidy the cupboard before an audit. What is the correct action?
o: Destroy them in a denaturing kit with a second registered nurse
Keep them segregated and recorded until an authorised witness attends
Destroy them and record it once the ward manager has countersigned
Return them to pharmacy in the sealed internal post
Medicines Management.w: NICE NG46: stock Schedule 2 controlled drugs may only be destroyed in the presence of an authorised witness (for example someone appointed by the CD accountable officer). Until then they stay in the CD cupboard, clearly segregated and recorded.

n.0: A colleague who is not an authorised witness cannot witness destruction of stock Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: A ward manager is not an authorised witness by virtue of the role, and recording after the event does not fix this.
n.3: Internal post is not a secure, auditable transport route for Schedule 2 CDs.

Medicines Management.q: Oliver, 38, is prescribed an intramuscular injection into the ventrogluteal site. He has an average build. The nurse has located the site, cleaned it according to policy and stretched the skin. At what angle should the needle be inserted?
o: 30 degrees, angled towards the iliac crest
90 degrees to the skin, in a dart-like motion
10 to 15 degrees with the bevel facing up
45 degrees into a pinched fold of skin
Medicines Management.w: Intramuscular injections are given at 90 degrees to the skin so that the needle reaches muscle beneath the subcutaneous tissue (AnnexB.11.7). Lower angles deposit medicine in the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, changing absorption and causing tissue damage.

n.0: A shallow angle risks depositing the drug subcutaneously, not intramuscularly.
n.2: 10 to 15 degrees is the angle for an intradermal injection.
n.3: 45 degrees into a pinched fold is a subcutaneous technique.

Medicines Management.q: An occupational health nurse is giving an intradermal tuberculin skin test into the inner forearm of Leila, 24. Which finding confirms that the injection has been placed correctly?
o: The fluid flows freely and leaves no mark on the skin
Blood flashback is seen in the hub of the syringe
A small pale bleb forms raising the skin at the site
A bruise appears at the site within a few minutes
Medicines Management.w: Intradermal injections are given at a shallow angle of about 10-15 degrees with the bevel up, just under the epidermis; correct placement raises a small pale bleb (AnnexB.11.7). No bleb suggests a deeper, subcutaneous injection.

n.0: Free flow with no bleb suggests the fluid has gone into subcutaneous tissue.
n.1: Flashback indicates the needle is in a blood vessel, not the dermis.
n.3: Bruising suggests trauma to vessels, not correct dermal placement.

Medicines Management.q: Ronald, 80, is prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch, changed every 72 hours. The new patch is due today. His previous patch is on his upper left chest. What is the correct way to apply the new patch?
o: Apply the new patch to the same area once the old one has been removed
Remove the old patch and apply the new one to a different area of skin
Apply the new patch, then remove the old one at the next 72-hour change
Apply the new patch over the old one to maintain a steady dose
Medicines Management.w: For transdermal patches the old patch is removed before the new one is applied, sites are rotated to reduce skin irritation, and the patch goes on clean, dry, hairless skin (AnnexB.11.8). Leaving an old fentanyl patch in place causes opioid toxicity.

n.0: Reusing the same site raises the risk of skin irritation and altered absorption.
n.2: Leaving the old patch for another 72 hours doubles the dose for that period.
n.3: Two patches at once would double the fentanyl dose and risk respiratory depression.

Medicines Management.q: Ivan, 72, has COPD and is prescribed salbutamol 2 puffs via a pressurised metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. He tells the nurse he usually sprays both puffs into the spacer and then takes one big breath. What should the nurse advise?
o: Spray one puff and breathe it in, then repeat for the second
Spray both puffs together, then take several slow breaths
Spray one puff, wait a full minute, then breathe it in
Spray both puffs together, then take one breath and hold it
Medicines Management.w: With a spacer, one actuation is given at a time and inhaled straight away (by a slow deep breath or several tidal breaths), then the process is repeated for the next puff after shaking (AnnexB.11.8). Multiple actuations into the spacer reduce the dose delivered.

n.1: Firing two puffs together causes the drug to stick to the spacer walls, reducing the dose reaching the lungs.
n.2: Delaying inhalation lets the drug settle on the spacer walls.
n.3: This repeats his current error of firing both puffs into the spacer at once.

Medicines Management.q: Pauline, 67, has a fine-bore nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. Her morning medicines are due through the tube. The tube was placed and confirmed yesterday. What check should the nurse make before giving them?
o: Inject air and listen over the stomach for a 'whoosh'
Test an aspirate and confirm a pH of 5.5 or below
Check the tube is not coiled by looking in her mouth
Test an aspirate with blue litmus paper for a colour change
Medicines Management.w: NICE CG32 monitoring and NHS patient safety alerts on nasogastric tubes: confirm gastric placement before each use by testing an aspirate with CE-marked pH paper, accepting pH 5.5 or below; if no aspirate or pH above 5.5, do not use the tube and escalate (X-ray may be needed). A misplaced tube used for feeding is a Never Event.

n.0: The 'whoosh' test is unreliable and must not be used to confirm placement.
n.2: A mouth check may find coiling, but it does not confirm the tip is in the stomach.
n.3: Litmus paper is not sensitive enough to confirm gastric placement.

Medicines Management.q: Eric, 58, has a PEG tube. His paracetamol oral suspension, baclofen liquid and a dispersible aspirin tablet are due at 12:00. His feed is running. How should the nurse give these medicines?
o: Give all three, then flush once with water at the end
Give each separately, flushing with water before, between and after
Add the three medicines into the feed bag to run with the feed
Mix all three in one enteral syringe and give them together
Medicines Management.w: For enteral tubes, each medicine is given separately in a suitable liquid or dispersed form via an enteral syringe, with the tube flushed with water before, between and after each medicine to prevent interactions and blockage (AnnexB.11.9; RPS/RCN references the NEWT guidelines). The feed is paused while medicines are given.

n.0: Without flushing between medicines they may interact in the tube and block it.
n.2: Adding medicines to feed risks incompatibility and unpredictable dosing if the feed stops.
n.3: Mixing medicines can cause physical or chemical incompatibilities and tube blockage.

Medicines Management.q: Daniel, 41, is prescribed a 3 mL deep intramuscular injection. He is of average build and has no contraindications at any site. The nurse is choosing between the available sites. Which site is preferred for this volume?
o: The abdomen, at least 5 cm from the umbilicus
The ventrogluteal site over the gluteus medius
The dorsogluteal site in the upper outer buttock
The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
Medicines Management.w: The ventrogluteal site is the preferred IM site for larger volumes in adults: the muscle is thick, the subcutaneous layer is relatively thin and it is away from major nerves and vessels (AnnexB.11.7). The deltoid takes small volumes, and the dorsogluteal site risks sciatic nerve injury.

n.0: The abdomen is a subcutaneous site, not an intramuscular one.
n.2: The dorsogluteal site carries a risk of sciatic nerve and gluteal artery injury.
n.3: The deltoid is a small muscle used for small volumes such as vaccines, not 3 mL.

Medicines Management.q: Yusuf, 50, is prescribed co-amoxiclav 1.2 g by slow intravenous injection over 3 to 4 minutes via his peripheral cannula. The second check is complete. The ward is busy and his maintenance fluids are running. How should the nurse give the dose?
o: Add it to the maintenance fluid bag and let it run in with the fluids
Flush to confirm patency, give over 3 to 4 minutes, then flush again
Give it by rapid push over 30 seconds, then flush with saline
Give it without a flush, as the cannula was used this morning
Medicines Management.w: Safe IV administration via a vascular access device (AnnexB.11.9; NICE CG139 flushing with 0.9% sodium chloride): check patency and the site with a flush, give the drug at the prescribed rate, observe for reactions, then flush to clear the line.

n.0: Adding drugs to a bag changes the prescribed route and rate and risks incompatibility.
n.2: Giving faster than prescribed risks adverse reactions and does not follow the prescription.
n.3: Patency must be checked before each use; a morning flush does not confirm current patency.

Medicines Management.q: Shona, 44, started a new medicine marked with a black triangle (▼) two weeks ago. She now has a mild itchy rash on her arms and no other symptoms. The prescriber has reviewed her. Regarding the Yellow Card scheme, what is the most appropriate action for the nurse?
o: Report it if further tests prove the medicine caused the rash
Leave reporting to the prescriber, as nurses do not submit Yellow Cards
Report it on Yellow Card, as suspected reactions to ▼ medicines are reported
Record it in the notes and report it if the rash becomes severe
Medicines Management.w: The MHRA Yellow Card scheme accepts reports from anyone, including nurses and patients. Black triangle medicines are under additional monitoring, so all suspected adverse reactions to them should be reported, even mild ones; certainty of causation is not required.

n.0: A suspicion is enough to report; proof of causation is not required.
n.1: Anyone can report to the Yellow Card scheme, including nurses and patients.
n.3: For ▼ medicines, all suspected reactions are reported, not just serious ones.

Medicines Management.q: Five minutes into an intravenous antibiotic infusion, Graham, 60, develops a hoarse voice, wheeze, widespread urticaria and a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the infusion, call for help and give IM adrenaline 1 mg (1 mL)
Stop the infusion, call for help and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV chlorphenamine as first-line treatment, then call for help
Slow the infusion and give an oral non-sedating antihistamine
Medicines Management.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021): remove the trigger, call for help and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral thigh, 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) for adults, repeating after 5 minutes if no improvement. Antihistamines are third-line and not for airway, breathing or circulation problems.

n.0: 1 mg is double the adult IM dose in the RCUK algorithm.
n.2: Chlorphenamine is not first-line for anaphylaxis, and delaying help is unsafe.
n.3: Slowing the infusion continues exposure, and antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise.

Medicines Management.q: Bill, 71, takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation and has a stable INR. At a clinic appointment he tells the practice nurse he plans to buy ibuprofen from the supermarket for back pain. What advice is most appropriate?
o: Use ibuprofen at the lowest dose for no more than 3 days
Avoid ibuprofen, and discuss safer options such as paracetamol
Use topical ibuprofen gel, as it does not interact with warfarin
Take the ibuprofen with food to reduce the risk of side effects
Medicines Management.w: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase bleeding risk with warfarin, through antiplatelet effects, gastric irritation and possible INR change (P4.15, interactions and over-the-counter use). The person should avoid them and get advice on alternatives such as paracetamol from the pharmacist or prescriber.

n.0: Even short low-dose courses of NSAIDs raise bleeding risk with warfarin.
n.2: Topical NSAIDs are absorbed to some extent, and he should still seek advice before using them with warfarin.
n.3: Taking it with food does not prevent the interaction or bleeding risk.

Medicines Management.q: Maureen, 66, started ramipril for hypertension 6 weeks ago. She tells the community nurse she has had a persistent tickly dry cough since, with no fever or breathlessness. Her chest is clear. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain dry cough is a known ramipril effect and arrange a review
Advise buying a cough suppressant from the pharmacy and continue
Explain the cough is likely viral and should settle in 2 weeks
Advise her to stop the ramipril straight away and see her GP
Medicines Management.w: A persistent dry cough is a recognised adverse effect of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril (P4.5, supporting people with their medication). The prescriber should review, as an alternative such as an angiotensin II receptor blocker may be considered. Stopping without review leaves blood pressure untreated.

n.1: A cough suppressant masks a drug-induced cause without a medication review.
n.2: The timing and features point to an ACE inhibitor effect, not a viral illness.
n.3: Stopping an antihypertensive without review risks uncontrolled blood pressure.

Medicines Management.q: Cyril, 82, has heart failure and is on intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily. His morning bloods show potassium 3.1 mmol/L (previously 4.0). He feels weak. What best explains this result, and what should the nurse do?
o: IV furosemide dilutes the blood; increase his oral fluid intake
Loop diuretics cause potassium retention; repeat the bloods tomorrow
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; inform the prescriber now
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; give a banana with lunch
Medicines Management.w: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that increases urinary sodium and potassium excretion, so hypokalaemia is an expected effect (P4.17, applying pharmacology). A fall to 3.1 mmol/L with weakness needs prompt prescriber review for replacement and dose review; low potassium increases arrhythmia risk in heart failure.

n.0: Dilution is not the mechanism, and extra fluid may worsen heart failure.
n.1: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, not retention, and a day's delay is unsafe.
n.3: Dietary potassium will not correct this promptly and the prescriber still needs to know.

Medicines Management.q: Winifred, 86, lives alone and takes 12 regular medicines from three prescribers. She has fallen twice this month and her daughter reports increasing daytime drowsiness. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the community nurse's most appropriate action?
o: Request a structured medication review with her GP and pharmacist
Spread her doses across the day to reduce side effects
Advise her daughter to buy a pill organiser for the medicines
Stop the medicines most likely to cause drowsiness and falls
Medicines Management.w: Polypharmacy with falls and drowsiness is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5 medicines optimisation; P4.15). Prescribers and pharmacists can review the indication, risks and benefits of each medicine together with Winifred.

n.1: Retiming doses without review may cause errors and does not address inappropriate medicines.
n.2: A pill organiser may help adherence but does not address why she is falling.
n.3: Stopping medicines is a prescribing decision and abrupt withdrawal can cause harm.

Medicines Management.q: On admission, Gemma, 35, lists citalopram as her only regular medicine. When asked about other products, she says she has been taking St John's wort from a health food shop for low mood. What should the nurse do?
o: Record it as a herbal product that needs no further review or action
Remove it from her locker and dispose of it in the sharps bin
Record it and inform the prescriber, as it interacts with citalopram
Advise her to double her citalopram dose instead of using it
Medicines Management.w: Medicines reconciliation includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5; P4.15). St John's wort taken with an SSRI such as citalopram increases the risk of serotonin syndrome and interacts with many other drugs, so it is documented and the prescriber or pharmacist informed.

n.0: Herbal products can cause significant interactions and must be reviewed.
n.1: Patients' own products are not removed without consent, and sharps bins are not for medicines.
n.3: Changing a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision and could cause toxicity.

Medicines Management.q: On admission, Derek, 59, says he is 'allergic' to codeine. When asked, he explains that it made him nauseated and constipated, with no rash, swelling or breathing problems. How should the nurse record this?
o: Record a morphine allergy, as it is in the same group
Record a codeine allergy and apply a red allergy wristband
Record a codeine intolerance, noting nausea and constipation
Record no reaction, as nausea is not clinically relevant
Medicines Management.w: Responding to adverse reactions (AnnexB.11.10) includes accurate documentation: the drug, the reaction and its nature. Nausea and constipation are predictable side effects (intolerance), not an immune allergy; labelling them as allergy can deny appropriate analgesia later.

n.0: Extending an inaccurate label to morphine compounds the error.
n.1: An allergy label for a side effect is inaccurate and may restrict future treatment.
n.3: The reaction still matters to future prescribing and should be documented.

Medicines Management.q: Agnieszka, 52, uses an insulin pen at home and has brought it into hospital. Her lunchtime dose is due, but the ward has run out of pen needles. A colleague suggests drawing the dose out of the pen cartridge with an insulin syringe. What should the nurse do?
o: Obtain pen needles from pharmacy or another ward and give it
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using an insulin syringe
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using a 1 mL syringe
Omit the dose until pen needles are delivered tomorrow
Medicines Management.w: An NHS England patient safety alert (2016) warned of severe harm and death from withdrawing insulin from pen devices, as cartridges are not designed for this and dosing errors result. Insulin is a high-risk medicine (P4.14); the correct device should be obtained promptly so the dose is not omitted.

n.1: Withdrawing insulin from a pen cartridge is unsafe whichever syringe is used.
n.2: A standard 1 mL syringe adds a further risk of unit-to-mL confusion and overdose.
n.3: Omitting insulin for a day risks hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis when needles can be sourced.

Medicines Management.q: Before lunch, Rhys, 68, who takes gliclazide and insulin, feels shaky and sweaty. His capillary blood glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. He is alert, orientated and able to swallow safely. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Give IM glucagon 1 mg and recheck in 10 minutes
Give a starchy snack and recheck his glucose in 1 hour
Give him his lunch now and recheck his glucose before the evening meal
Give 15-20 g of quick-acting carbohydrate, then recheck in 10-15 minutes
Medicines Management.w: Hypoglycaemia (glucose below 4 mmol/L) in a conscious adult who can swallow is treated with 15-20 g of quick-acting carbohydrate, with glucose rechecked after 10-15 minutes and treatment repeated if still low, then a longer-acting carbohydrate (JBDS hospital hypoglycaemia guidance). Insulin and sulfonylureas are high-risk medicines (P4.15).

n.0: Glucagon is for people who cannot take oral treatment safely; Rhys can swallow.
n.1: Starchy snacks act too slowly as first-line treatment, and an hour is too long to recheck.
n.2: A meal is too slow and leaving the recheck until evening misses ongoing hypoglycaemia.

Medicines Management.q: Two hours after IV morphine, Brian, 79, is difficult to rouse, has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 7 breaths per minute. His SpO2 is 89% on air. Naloxone is prescribed as required. What is the priority?
o: Call for help, support his breathing and give the prescribed naloxone
Recheck his observations in 15 minutes and document the findings
Sit him upright and encourage him to take deep breaths until he wakes
Withhold the next morphine dose and inform the doctor on the ward round
Medicines Management.w: Opioid toxicity with respiratory depression is an emergency (P4.15): call for help, support airway and breathing with oxygen, and give naloxone, the opioid antagonist, titrating to restore adequate breathing while monitoring for recurrence. Opioids are high-risk medicines.

n.1: Delaying treatment of a respiratory rate of 7 risks respiratory arrest.
n.2: Repositioning does not reverse opioid respiratory depression in a barely rousable patient.
n.3: Withholding the next dose is needed but does not reverse the current toxicity.

Medicines Management.q: Irene, 72, is admitted with rheumatoid arthritis. Her new inpatient chart has methotrexate 10 mg once daily written in the regular section. Her repeat prescription list from home shows methotrexate 10 mg once weekly on Mondays. What should the nurse do?
o: Withhold it and contact the prescriber urgently to clarify
Give 10 mg on Monday, and correct the chart frequency herself
Give 10 mg daily until the pharmacist reviews the chart next week
Give 10 mg today, as it is written on the current drug chart
Medicines Management.w: Methotrexate for non-cancer conditions is usually taken once weekly; daily dosing causes serious toxicity, and overdose of methotrexate for non-cancer treatment is on the NHS Never Events list (2018, updated 2021). The discrepancy must be clarified with the prescriber before any dose (P4.14).

n.1: Changing a prescription is not within the nurse's role; the prescriber must amend it.
n.2: Daily dosing for a week would cause the very overdose the Never Events list targets.
n.3: Giving a daily dose that conflicts with her weekly regimen risks a fatal overdose.

Medicines Management.q: Jorge, 61, is prescribed potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours. The ward has no ready-mixed bags. A colleague suggests adding concentrated potassium chloride from an ampoule to a bag of saline. What should the nurse do?
o: Run plain saline now and add the potassium when the bag is changed
Obtain a ready-mixed bag from pharmacy or another area per policy
Give the concentrated potassium chloride as a slow IV bolus instead
Add the ampoule to the bag and invert it several times to mix
Medicines Management.w: Mis-selection of a strong potassium solution is a Never Event (2018 list, updated 2021); national guidance requires ready-diluted potassium infusions wherever possible, with concentrated ampoules restricted. Potassium is a high-risk medicine (P4.15).

n.0: Delaying and then adding concentrate later carries the same mis-selection risk.
n.2: Concentrated potassium must not be given as a bolus; it can cause cardiac arrest.
n.3: Ward addition of concentrated potassium risks mis-selection and poor mixing, causing fatal hyperkalaemia.

Medicines Management.q: Hamid, 74, takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. His INR today is 8.5 (target 2.5 to 3.5). He has no bleeding, bruising or other symptoms, and his 18:00 dose is due. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the usual dose, as he has no signs of bleeding
Give oral vitamin K from ward stock to lower the INR
Withhold the warfarin and inform the prescriber urgently
Give half the usual dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
Medicines Management.w: An INR well above target raises the risk of serious bleeding. Anticoagulants are high-risk medicines (P4.15): the dose is withheld and the prescriber informed promptly, who decides on dose changes or reversal such as vitamin K.

n.0: No bleeding now does not remove the high bleeding risk at INR 8.5.
n.1: Vitamin K must be prescribed; giving it from stock without a prescription is unlawful.
n.3: Altering the warfarin dose is a prescriber decision.

Medicines Management.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine solution instead of the prescribed 5 mg, 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16 and no sedation. What should Ola do?
o: Rewrite the chart entry to 5 mg to avoid confusing the next nurse
Monitor Leon, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report the incident
Observe Leon and report the error if he shows any signs of harm
Inform the ward manager and leave her to decide whether to tell Leon
Medicines Management.w: Medication incidents are reported and reflected on (P6.8; NMC Code 19): the priority is the person's safety (monitoring sedation and respiratory rate), then informing the prescriber, being open with Leon (professional duty of candour), and reporting through the local system feeding LFPSE.

n.0: Altering the record to hide an error is dishonest and breaches the Code.
n.2: Incidents, including those without harm, are reported so that learning can occur.
n.3: The professional duty of candour is personal; Ola should be open with Leon herself.

Medicines Management.q: Preparing the 14:00 dose, nurse Tamsin sees that Edna, 88, has been prescribed oral morphine solution 50 mg four-hourly. Edna is opioid-naive and her previous doses were 5 mg. Tamsin suspects a tenfold prescribing error. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold it, have the prescription corrected and report a near miss
Withhold it and ask for an amendment; reporting is not needed as no harm
Amend the chart to 5 mg, initial the change and give the dose
Give 5 mg, as this was clearly intended, then tell the prescriber
Medicines Management.w: A prescribing error intercepted before reaching the patient is a near miss and should be reported so learning can be shared (P6.8). The nurse checks that the prescription is unambiguous and appropriate before administration (RPS/RCN 2019 para 15) and raises concerns with the prescriber without delay.

n.1: Near misses are reported; no-harm events still reveal system weaknesses.
n.2: Nurses cannot amend a prescription; that is a prescribing act.
n.3: Giving a dose different from the written prescription is administering without a valid prescription.

Medicines Management.q: George, 80, lives in a care home and has been assessed as having capacity to make decisions about his medicines. He refuses his atorvastatin, saying he does not want it at his age. His daughter asks the nurse to crush it into his yoghurt without telling him. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a best interests meeting about covert administration
Agree after the GP signs a covert administration form
Respect his refusal, record it and inform the prescriber
Agree, as the statin is in his long-term interests
Medicines Management.w: Covert administration is used only for people who actively refuse medication and lack capacity, under an agreed plan (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21; NICE SC1). George has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (MCA 2005 s1(4): an unwise decision does not mean lack of capacity), documented and shared with the prescriber.

n.0: A best interests process applies to people who lack capacity; George has capacity.
n.1: A GP's signature cannot authorise covert administration to a person who has capacity.
n.3: Giving medicine covertly to a person with capacity is unlawful, whatever the benefit.

Medicines Management.q: After a stroke, Hilary, 77, can manage only pureed food and thickened fluids and cannot swallow tablets. Her prescription includes a modified-release tablet. A healthcare support worker suggests crushing it into her pudding. What should the nurse do first?
o: Crush it finely and mix it with a spoonful of pudding
Ask the pharmacist about a suitable alternative formulation
Omit the tablet and record that she is unable to swallow
Break the tablet in half so that it is easier to swallow
Medicines Management.w: Altering a medicine's form, such as crushing, can change how it works and makes its use unlicensed; modified-release tablets in particular must not be crushed because the whole dose may be released at once. Pharmacist advice is sought before crushing or opening (RPS guidance on crushing cited in RPS/RCN 2019; AnnexB.11.6).

n.0: Crushing a modified-release tablet can cause dose dumping and toxicity.
n.2: Omitting the dose without seeking an alternative leaves her untreated.
n.3: Splitting a modified-release tablet can also disrupt its release mechanism, and swallowing is unsafe.

Medicines Management.q: Dorothy, 86, has advanced dementia. For three days she has spat out her anticonvulsant and pushed staff away at medicine rounds. Her son suggests hiding it in her tea. What is the nurse's most appropriate first step?
o: Assess her capacity to make this specific decision about the medicine
Arrange for the medicine to be given by injection instead
Hide the medicine in her tea, as she has a diagnosis of dementia
Stop the anticonvulsant, as she is repeatedly refusing it
Medicines Management.w: The MCA 2005 (ss1-3) requires a capacity assessment that is decision-specific and time-specific; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. Only if she lacks capacity can a best interests decision about covert administration follow (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21).

n.1: Changing the route needs a prescriber and does not address capacity or consent.
n.2: A diagnosis does not prove lack of capacity (MCA s2(3)); covert use also needs a best interests process.
n.3: Stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures; the refusal needs assessment, not unilateral cessation.

Medicines Management.q: Ernest, 84, lacks capacity to decide about his medicines and actively refuses his antiepileptic. The care home manager arranges a best interests meeting about covert administration. According to NICE SC1, who should be involved?
o: The prescriber, the care home manager and the senior carer
Care staff, prescriber, pharmacist and a family member or advocate
The care home manager and the registered nurse on duty that day
The family, who make the final decision as his next of kin
Medicines Management.w: NICE SC1 (1.15) and RPS/RCN 2019: covert administration follows a best interests meeting involving care home staff, the health professional prescribing, a pharmacist and a family member or advocate, with a documented management plan.

n.0: Without a pharmacist and a family member or advocate the decision lacks key input.
n.2: The prescriber and pharmacist must also be involved, as must family or an advocate.
n.3: Next of kin have no legal power to decide unless they hold a relevant LPA or are deputies; the decision is made by the team in his best interests.

Medicines Management.q: A nurse joining a care home finds that Ada, 90, has been given her medicines covertly for 10 months. The best interests decision and management plan are filed, but there is no record of any review since. What should the nurse do?
o: Continue, as a plan is in place and signed
Ask Ada's daughter to confirm she still agrees with the plan
Stop all covert medicines until the GP's next visit
Arrange a review of the plan with the multidisciplinary team
Medicines Management.w: Covert administration requires a documented management plan that is reviewed regularly (NICE SC1 1.15; RPS/RCN 2019 paras 21-23). Ada's capacity, the need for each medicine and the method should be reconsidered by the team, including the prescriber and pharmacist.

n.0: A plan without review may be out of date; review is a required safeguard.
n.1: Family views are part of the review, but the daughter cannot authorise continuation alone.
n.2: Abruptly stopping all medicines could cause harm; a prompt review is needed instead.

Medicines Management.q: Maeve, 79, has dementia and lacks capacity. When she had capacity she made a written, signed and witnessed advance decision refusing antipsychotic medication. The team confirms it is valid and applicable. She is now refusing a newly prescribed antipsychotic. Her family ask for it to be given covertly. What applies?
o: Respect the advance decision and do not give the antipsychotic
Give it covertly, as a best interests meeting overrides the advance decision
Give it covertly until a court decides on the advance decision
Give it covertly if her family and the GP both agree
Medicines Management.w: Under the MCA 2005 ss24-26, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same effect as a capacitous refusal and binds professionals. Best interests decisions cannot override it, so the antipsychotic cannot be given, covertly or otherwise.

n.1: A best interests decision cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision.
n.2: Treatment may be given to prevent serious deterioration while a court decides on validity, but here validity is confirmed.
n.3: Family and GP agreement does not override a binding advance refusal.

Medicines Management.q: A covert administration plan for Sidney, 88, states that his dispersible aspirin and liquid antibiotic may be mixed with food on pharmacist advice. The nurse plans to stir them into his full bowl of porridge, which he often leaves half-eaten. What is the best approach?
o: Mix them into the whole bowl so they are well disguised
Mix them into the porridge and give the rest with lunch
Mix them into a small amount of the advised food first
Mix them into his tea, which he usually finishes
Medicines Management.w: The covert plan details how each medicine is given, with pharmacist advice (RPS/RCN 2019; NICE SC1). Using a small amount of the advised food, offered first, makes it more likely that the full dose is taken; mixing into a large portion risks a partial dose.

n.0: If he leaves half the bowl he receives only part of the dose.
n.1: Splitting a dose across meals is not in the plan and makes the dose taken uncertain.
n.3: Changing the vehicle to tea departs from the agreed plan and pharmacist advice on compatibility.

Medicines Management.q: Ken, 72, had severe delirium with sepsis and lacked capacity, so a covert plan was agreed for his antibiotics. Five days later his delirium has resolved, and an assessment shows he now has capacity to decide about his medicines. What should happen next?
o: Stop all his antibiotics, as the covert plan no longer applies
Stop covert administration and discuss his medicines with him
Continue covertly until the antibiotic course is complete
