n.0: Temporary registration is for people staying in an area for a short time; having no fixed address does not restrict her to it, and she is entitled to full registration.
n.2: Directing routine care to the emergency department is inappropriate and deepens inequality of access.
n.3: Lack of proof of address is not a reason to refuse registration.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. He brings a hospital passport describing how he communicates. On the ward round, staff talk to his mother and ignore Jamie. What should his nurse do?
o: Ask his mother to explain the ward round decisions to Jamie later
Allow the conversation to continue, as his mother knows him best
Share the passport details and invite staff to speak directly to Jamie
Ask the learning disability liaison nurse to attend the next ward round
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses advocate for people who are vulnerable or disabled and make reasonable adjustments (P7.9; Code 3.4; Equality Act 2010 s20). Using the hospital passport and speaking directly to Jamie in his preferred way respects his rights, involves him in decisions and supports any capacity assessment (MCA 2005 s1(3)).

n.0: Passing information on later excludes Jamie from the conversation about his own care.
n.1: His mother's knowledge is valuable, but Jamie must be involved directly in decisions about his care.
n.3: Liaison nurses offer valuable support, but the nurse should advocate for Jamie now rather than wait.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Leo, 19, is autistic and attends a busy emergency department with a wrist injury. He is covering his ears, rocking and becoming more distressed in the noisy waiting room. His triage category means he may wait two hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Suggest he returns tomorrow when the department is likely to be quieter
Move him up the triage queue ahead of patients with more urgent needs
Ask him to wait outside the department until a cubicle becomes free
Offer a quieter space to wait and explain clearly what will happen next
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Reasonable adjustments remove disadvantage arising from disability without compromising others' safety: a quieter waiting space and clear, predictable information reduce sensory overload while clinical priority is maintained (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7; P7.9). Two steps: recognise sensory distress, then select a proportionate adjustment.

n.0: Delaying treatment of an injury is not a reasonable adjustment and may worsen the outcome.
n.1: Triage order is based on clinical urgency; changing it could harm patients with more urgent needs.
n.2: Sending him outside removes him from observation and is not an adjustment that maintains his care.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Edna Fox, 83, is medically fit for discharge after a urinary tract infection. Before admission she managed alone at home. She will now go home with a new package of carers visiting twice a day for personal care. Which discharge pathway applies?
o: Pathway 1
Pathway 2
Pathway 3
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Hospital discharge and community support guidance (DHSC/NHS England, updated January 2024): pathway 1 is discharge home or to the usual place of residence with new or additional health and/or social care needs (P4.18; P7.10).

n.1: Pathway 2 is a community bed-based setting with recovery support, not home.
n.2: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new or additional care needs; Mrs Fox needs a new care package.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Gordon Bailey, 79, is recovering from a hip fracture repair. He is not yet safe at home but the team expects he will be able to return home after a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed. Which discharge pathway is this?
o: Pathway 3
Pathway 2
Pathway 1
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, where short-term care helps the person recover before living independently or receiving longer-term care (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.2: Pathway 1 is discharge home with new support; Mr Bailey is not yet ready to go home.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Claire Bennett, 42, who has multiple sclerosis, is due for discharge after a relapse. During discharge planning, Sunil, her nurse, learns that her 14-year-old son provides much of her care at home. What should Sunil do?
o: Ask Claire to arrange more help from other family members before discharge
Plan the discharge around the son's school hours, as he already provides her care
Leave the son out of discussions, as he is under 18 and cannot be a carer
Involve the son appropriately and notify the local authority so it can assess him
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NHS trusts must involve unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning as soon as feasible (Care Act 2014 s74 as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022). Where a young carer is identified, the local authority should be notified so it can carry out a young carer's needs assessment, including whether caring is appropriate or excessive (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Other support may help, but the young carer still needs to be identified and referred for assessment.
n.1: Relying on a child's care without assessment may place excessive responsibility on him and ignores safeguarding considerations.
n.2: Young carers are recognised in law and must be identified and involved appropriately, not excluded.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Joan Pike, 90, has social care needs and has been in hospital for a week with heart failure. Several professionals are involved and her daughter is confused about who to contact about discharge plans. According to NICE NG27, what should be in place?
o: A weekly letter to the daughter from the consultant in charge
A named discharge coordinator as the central point of contact
A rule that her daughter contacts the ward sister each morning
A referral to the hospital complaints team to manage contact
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NICE NG27 (2015) recommends a hospital-based multidisciplinary team and a named discharge coordinator who is the central point of contact for the person and their family during discharge planning (P7.10; P4.18).

n.0: A weekly letter is too infrequent and does not provide a single coordinating contact.
n.2: This places responsibility on the family rather than giving them a coordinator.
n.3: Her daughter's confusion is a coordination problem, not a complaint to be managed.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward wants to evaluate how well it plans discharges for people with complex care needs who go home with new support. Which approach would best capture the quality of their experience?
o: Count the number of discharges completed before midday each week
Review the ward's length-of-stay figures against other medical wards
Phone people and carers after discharge to ask about their experience
Audit how many discharge letters reached GPs within 24 hours
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The quality of people's experience of complex care is best evaluated by asking them and their carers directly about the discharge and transition, including whether support started as planned (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Discharge timing is a process measure that says little about the person's experience.
n.1: Length of stay measures efficiency, not experience.
n.3: Letter timeliness is an important process measure but does not capture the experience of people and carers.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: During a team meeting, Ellie, a nurse three months after registration, says that leadership is something for ward managers and that her job is to look after her own patients. How does the NMC Code describe leadership for registrants?
o: All registrants have opportunities to show leadership whatever their role
Leadership is required where a nurse is formally in charge of a shift
Leadership is expected once a nurse is appointed to a band 6 role or above
Leadership is expected after completing a recognised leadership course
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code standard 25 (provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences) applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position (P5.6 exhibit leadership potential).

n.1: Being in charge adds responsibilities (Code 25.1), but leadership is expected of all registrants at all times.
n.2: The Code links leadership to professional practice, not to pay band or grade.
n.3: Courses can develop leadership skills, but the Code's expectation does not depend on them.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward is moving from paper charts to electronic observations next month. Several experienced nurses tell Raj, the ward manager, that the system will slow them down and they do not want it. Which approach is most likely to support the change?
o: Ask the nurses who object to work on other wards during the changeover
Involve staff early, explain the reasons, act on concerns and pilot it
Delay the change until every member of the team agrees to it
Set a firm start date and tell staff the system is mandatory from that day
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Effective change management involves the people affected: explaining why the change is needed, listening to and addressing concerns, and testing the change on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1 principles of leadership and organisational culture; AnnexA.4.2.1 strengths-based approaches to managing change).

n.0: Removing staff who raise concerns loses their expertise and damages trust in the team.
n.2: Waiting for unanimous agreement can block necessary safety improvements indefinitely.
n.3: Imposing change without engagement tends to increase resistance and workarounds.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At her appraisal, Joy, a healthcare assistant, is praised by families for her skill in calming people living with dementia who are distressed. Her line manager, Paul, wants to use a strengths-based approach to developing the team. What should Paul do?
o: Concentrate the appraisal on the areas where Joy needs to improve
Move Joy to the dementia unit so that her skills are used there
Ask Joy to spend less time with families so she can do other tasks
Agree a plan for Joy to share her approach and support colleagues
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example by enabling a team member to share skills and act as a resource, which improves care and motivation (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2 strength-based approaches in teams).

n.0: Development needs matter, but a strengths-based approach starts from what the person does well.
n.1: Moving her removes the skill from the team rather than building on it within the team.
n.2: Reducing the activity she excels at undermines a strength that benefits patients and families.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a leadership study day, students are asked to distinguish leadership from management. Which activity is best described as leadership rather than management?
o: Preparing the ward's off-duty rota for the next four weeks
Setting a shared vision for care and motivating the team
Recording and reviewing staff sickness absence each month
Monitoring the ward's monthly spending against its budget
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Management is concerned with planning, organising and controlling resources (rotas, budgets, absence); leadership is concerned with direction, vision and influencing and motivating people. Nurses need both (P5.1 principles of effective leadership and management).

n.0: Rota planning organises resources, a management task.
n.2: Absence monitoring is a management process.
n.3: Budget monitoring is a management control activity.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Graham, 61, has central chest pain and a suspected acute coronary syndrome. He has no lung disease. A healthcare assistant has started oxygen at 15 L/min via a reservoir mask. His SpO2 on air before this was 97%. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue high-flow oxygen to limit the size of any infarct
Remove the oxygen and continue to monitor his saturation
Switch to a 28% Venturi mask aiming for 88-92%
Change to nasal cannulae at 2 L/min as a precaution
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE CG95 1.2.3.3: do not routinely give oxygen in suspected ACS; monitor SpO2 and give oxygen only if it falls below 94% (target 94-98%). BTS 2017 notes unnecessary high-concentration oxygen may increase infarct size.

n.0: Unnecessary high-concentration oxygen may increase infarct size; it is not a protective treatment.
n.2: The 88-92% range is for people at risk of hypercapnia; he is not, and he is not hypoxaemic.
n.3: Low-flow oxygen is still not indicated when SpO2 is 94% or above in suspected ACS.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Chloe, 24, attends the emergency department feeling panicky. Her respiratory rate is 32/min, SpO2 99% on air and she has tingling fingers. A colleague offers her a paper bag to breathe into. Organic causes are still being excluded. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Support her to rebreathe from the paper bag for several minutes
Apply a reservoir mask at 15 L/min to settle her breathing
Apply a 24% Venturi mask aiming for a saturation of 88-92%
Coach slow breathing and advise against paper-bag rebreathing
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017: oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness. Pure hyperventilation from anxiety is unlikely to need oxygen, and paper-bag rebreathing may cause hypoxaemia. Other causes (for example PE or DKA) must still be excluded.

n.0: BTS warns that paper-bag rebreathing may cause hypoxaemia, so it is not advised.
n.1: Her saturation is normal; oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not anxiety-related breathlessness.
n.2: She is not hypoxaemic and has no hypercapnia risk factor, so controlled oxygen is not indicated.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Ivan, 69, has COPD and was started on oxygen via a 28% Venturi mask with a target of 88-92%. His SpO2 is now 89%. Blood gases show pH 7.40 and PaCO2 5.1 kPa. He has never needed NIV or intubation. What should the nurse ask the doctor to do?
o: Keep the 88-92% target because of his COPD diagnosis
Increase to a 60% Venturi mask to reach 99-100%
Revise his prescribed target range to 94-98%
Stop oxygen because his carbon dioxide level is normal
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Two steps: interpret the gas (normal pH and PaCO2, so no hypercapnia), then apply BTS 2017 Table 4: if PaCO2 is normal, adjust the target to 94-98% unless the person has previously needed NIV or invasive ventilation, and recheck gases after 30-60 minutes.

n.0: BTS advises moving to 94-98% when PaCO2 is normal and there is no history of NIV or invasive ventilation.
n.1: BTS does not aim for 100%; the upper limit of the target is 98%.
n.3: His SpO2 is 89%, which is below the revised range, so he still needs oxygen.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Bernard, 77, has COPD with a prescribed target of 88-92%. He is receiving oxygen at 4 L/min via nasal cannulae. On your round he is drowsy and difficult to rouse, and his SpO2 is 99%. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Sit him upright and repeat the observations in 4 hours
Reduce the oxygen to reach 88-92% and request urgent blood gases
Continue the current flow because his saturation is satisfactory
Stop the oxygen straight away and recheck his saturation
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Assess then act: drowsiness with SpO2 above target in an at-risk patient suggests hypercapnic respiratory failure. BTS 2017 advises stepping oxygen down to the target range (not stopping it suddenly) and urgent blood gases with medical review.

n.0: New drowsiness with high saturation needs urgent action and blood gases, not routine monitoring.
n.2: 99% is above his target; with new drowsiness this suggests hypercapnia from excess oxygen.
n.3: Sudden withdrawal can cause rebound hypoxaemia; oxygen should be stepped down to the target, not stopped abruptly.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Sandra, 58, is admitted with sepsis. She is pale and clammy, her SpO2 is 82% on air and her blood pressure is 84/50 mmHg. She has no chronic lung disease. Which oxygen delivery is most appropriate initially?
o: Nasal cannulae at 4 L/min
Reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Simple face mask at 5 L/min
28% Venturi mask at 4 L/min
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017: in critical illness (shock, sepsis, major trauma) or SpO2 below 85%, start a reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then titrate down to 94-98% once stable.

n.0: Nasal cannulae suit mild hypoxaemia; critical illness with SpO2 below 85% needs a reservoir mask.
n.2: A simple mask delivers a lower and variable concentration than she needs in critical illness.
n.3: Controlled low-concentration oxygen is for people at risk of hypercapnia, not critical illness.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Peter, 70, has COPD and is breathless. The doctor prescribes oxygen via a 28% Venturi mask with a target of 88-92%. At what flow rate should the oxygen be set?
o: 15 L/min
2 L/min
4 L/min
10 L/min
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 Table 4: for at-risk patients use a 24% Venturi at 2-3 L/min or a 28% Venturi at 4 L/min (or nasal cannulae 1-2 L/min), aiming for 88-92%.

n.0: 15 L/min is the reservoir mask flow for critical illness.
n.1: 2-3 L/min is the flow for a 24% Venturi valve, not 28%.
n.3: 10 L/min is used with higher-concentration Venturi valves or simple masks, not the 28% valve.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Joan, 63, has a chest infection and no risk factors for hypercapnia. Her SpO2 is 91% on air and she is talking comfortably. The prescribed target is 94-98%. Which delivery device is preferred to start with?
o: Reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Simple face mask at 2 L/min
Nasal cannulae at 2-6 L/min
24% Venturi mask at 2 L/min
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 Figure 1: for other hypoxaemic patients use nasal cannulae at 2-6 L/min (preferred) or a simple face mask at 5-10 L/min, titrated to 94-98%.

n.0: A reservoir mask is for critical illness or SpO2 below 85%; Joan is mildly hypoxaemic.
n.1: Simple masks need 5-10 L/min; lower flows risk rebreathing carbon dioxide.
n.3: Low-concentration Venturi oxygen is aimed at people at risk of hypercapnia.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Rosa, 66, has been on oxygen 1 L/min via nasal cannulae with a target of 94-98%. For the last 12 hours she has kept her SpO2 at 95-96% on air during trial breaks and is clinically stable. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop the oxygen and cross off the oxygen prescription
Continue 1 L/min overnight in case she desaturates
Stop the oxygen and keep the target range on her drug chart
Stop the oxygen and discontinue her saturation monitoring
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 weaning: discontinue oxygen once the patient is stable and maintaining the target saturation on air, but leave the target range prescription in place to guide future care and NEWS2 scoring.

n.0: BTS advises keeping the target range in place so that any later fall in saturation is recognised and acted on.
n.1: She meets the criteria to discontinue; continuing oxygen she does not need is not recommended.
n.3: Monitoring continues after weaning; the target range guides scoring and escalation.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: A student nurse sets up a simple face mask at 3 L/min for Faisal, 55, whose prescribed target is 94-98%. Which explanation should you give the student before adjusting the flow?
o: Below 5 L/min a simple mask can cause carbon dioxide rebreathing
Simple masks deliver 100% oxygen at any flow rate
Simple masks are designed to run between 1 and 2 L/min
A simple mask needs 15 L/min to keep its reservoir bag inflated
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017: simple face masks are used at 5-10 L/min. At lower flows exhaled carbon dioxide may be rebreathed from the mask, so a nasal cannula is preferable if low flow is needed.

n.1: Simple masks give a variable, lower concentration; they do not deliver 100% oxygen.
n.2: 1-2 L/min is a nasal cannula range for at-risk patients, not a simple mask setting.
n.3: A simple mask has no reservoir bag; 15 L/min applies to the reservoir mask.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Olu, 49, has pneumonia and is on nasal cannulae at 4 L/min with a target of 94-98%. Over two hours his SpO2 falls from 95% to 89% and his respiratory rate rises from 20 to 27/min. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase the oxygen and recheck at the next routine observations
Increase the oxygen to regain 94-98% and inform the medical team
Switch to a 28% Venturi mask and aim for 88-92%
Document the change and recheck his saturation in 1 hour
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Assess then act: SpO2 below target with a rising respiratory rate shows deterioration. BTS 2017 advises titrating oxygen to the target and treating any increase in oxygen requirement as a trigger for clinical review (NEWS2 escalation).

n.0: A rising oxygen requirement is a sign of deterioration that needs prompt clinical review, not routine checks.
n.2: He has no hypercapnia risk factor, so his target remains 94-98%.
n.3: His falling saturation needs treatment now; delaying leaves him hypoxaemic.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Edith, 72, has COPD. Her oxygen was changed from a 24% to a 28% Venturi mask because her SpO2 was 85%. Her target is 88-92%. When should her blood gases be rechecked?
o: After 30-60 minutes on the new setting
At the next consultant-led ward round
When her saturation reaches 98%
After 4 hours on the new setting
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 Table 4: in people at risk of hypercapnia, recheck blood gases 30-60 minutes after starting or increasing oxygen to detect rising PaCO2 or falling pH.

n.1: Repeat gases are timed from the oxygen change, not from the ward round.
n.2: 98% is above her target; gases are rechecked at a set interval after any change.
n.3: Waiting 4 hours could miss rising carbon dioxide; BTS advises 30-60 minutes.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Thomas, 68, is receiving oxygen 2 L/min via nasal cannulae with a prescribed target of 94-98%. You are on the morning medicines round. How should the oxygen be recorded?
o: Sign the prescription chart once, when oxygen was first started
Record the device in the nursing notes at handover
Sign the prescription chart at each round to confirm oxygen is in use
Ask the doctor to sign the oxygen chart each day
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017: oxygen is a drug. Sign the drug chart on each drug round to confirm it is being given, and record the device, flow and SpO2 on the observation chart.

n.0: BTS expects the oxygen prescription to be signed on each drug round, like other medicines.
n.1: The nursing notes are not the place to confirm administration of a prescribed drug.
n.3: Administration is signed by the nurse giving it; the doctor prescribes the target range.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Martin, 58, attends a respiratory clinic. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years. The nurse calculates his pack-year history for the referral letter. What is his pack-year history?
o: 1,200 pack-years
60 pack-years
40 pack-years
30 pack-years
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115 1.2.1: pack-years = (cigarettes per day / 20) x years smoked = (30 / 20) x 40 = 1.5 x 40 = 60 pack-years.

n.0: 1,200 is cigarettes a day multiplied by years without dividing by 20.
n.2: 40 is the number of years smoked; it ignores that he smokes 1.5 packs a day.
n.3: 30 is the number of cigarettes a day, not the pack-year total.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Lorraine, 61, has a chronic productive cough and exertional breathlessness. Post-bronchodilator spirometry is performed. Which result confirms airflow obstruction consistent with COPD?
o: FEV1/FVC ratio above 0.8
FeNO level of 50 ppb or more
FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7
FEV1 increase of 12% after bronchodilator
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: airflow obstruction is defined as a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7, interpreted with the clinical picture.

n.0: A ratio above 0.8 is within the normal range and does not show obstruction.
n.1: A raised FeNO supports a diagnosis of asthma, not COPD.
n.3: Significant reversibility suggests asthma rather than confirming COPD.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Victor, 66, has COPD. He tells you he has to stop for breath after walking about 100 metres on level ground but can still dress himself and leave the house. What is his MRC dyspnoea grade?
o: Grade 5
Grade 2
Grade 3
Grade 4
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115 Table 1 (MRC dyspnoea scale): grade 4 = stops for breath after walking about 100 metres or after a few minutes on level ground.

n.0: Grade 5 is too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing.
n.1: Grade 2 is breathlessness when hurrying or walking up a slight hill.
n.2: Grade 3 is walking slower than contemporaries or stopping at own pace on the level.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Annette, 64, has COPD with MRC grade 3 breathlessness. She has stopped going to the shops because she feels too breathless and sees herself as limited. She is on LAMA+LABA with good technique. Which referral is most appropriate?
o: Home non-invasive ventilation assessment
Respiratory physiotherapy for airway clearance
Long-term oxygen therapy assessment
Pulmonary rehabilitation
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: offer pulmonary rehabilitation to people with COPD who view themselves as functionally disabled, usually MRC grade 3 and above.

n.0: Home NIV is for chronic hypercapnic failure, which is not described here.
n.1: Airway clearance helps sputum problems; it is not the structured programme she needs.
n.2: LTOT is assessed on blood gas criteria, not on functional disability alone.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Ronald, 71, has COPD and still smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Two arterial blood gases taken 3 weeks apart while stable show PaO2 of 7.1 kPa and 7.0 kPa. He asks about home oxygen. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain LTOT is not offered while he smokes and offer cessation support
Repeat the arterial blood gases in another 3 weeks before deciding
Arrange LTOT for 15 hours a day with fire safety advice
Arrange ambulatory oxygen for use when walking outdoors
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Two steps: his PaO2 is below 7.3 kPa on two stable readings 3 weeks apart, so he meets the LTOT threshold, but NICE NG115 says do not offer LTOT to people who continue to smoke (fire and burns risk). Smoking cessation is offered at every opportunity.

n.1: Two qualifying gases 3 weeks apart are already available; smoking is the barrier.
n.2: His gases meet the threshold, but NICE advises not to offer LTOT to people who continue to smoke.
n.3: Ambulatory oxygen is not a substitute when smoking rules out home oxygen; the fire risk is the same.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Doreen, 75, has started long-term oxygen therapy. She tells you she uses it for about 8 hours overnight because the tubing gets in the way during the day. What is the best advice?
o: Use it for 12 hours a day split across day and night
Benefit needs use for at least 15 hours a day
Overnight use for 8 hours gives the full benefit
Use it during the day when she feels breathless
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: people prescribed LTOT should breathe supplemental oxygen for at least 15 hours a day.

n.0: 12 hours is below the 15-hour minimum.
n.2: NICE sets a minimum of 15 hours a day; 8 hours falls short of this.
n.3: LTOT is a planned daily treatment, not a symptom-driven reliever.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Kevin, 63, has COPD with no asthmatic features and no evidence of steroid responsiveness. He remains breathless despite using his as-needed salbutamol and has had smoking cessation support and vaccinations. Which inhaled treatment is recommended next?
o: A long-acting antimuscarinic plus a long-acting beta2 agonist
Regular nebulised short-acting bronchodilator four times a day
A long-acting beta2 agonist plus an inhaled corticosteroid
An inhaled corticosteroid as a single regular inhaler
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: if no asthmatic features or features suggesting steroid responsiveness, offer LAMA+LABA when breathlessness limits daily activities despite short-acting bronchodilators and non-pharmacological measures.

n.1: Nebulisers are for people still distressed despite maximal inhaled therapy.
n.2: LABA+ICS is considered when there are asthmatic features or steroid responsiveness, which he does not have.
n.3: ICS monotherapy is not recommended in COPD.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Iris, 68, has COPD and had two exacerbations last year. She has a personalised action plan and a rescue pack of prednisolone and an antibiotic at home. She asks how to use it. What is the best advice?
o: Take the antibiotic first and keep the steroid for a second flare
Start it at the first sign of a cold and continue for 14 days
Start it as your plan says and tell your practice you have used it
Keep it for when you are admitted so the hospital can use it
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: offer rescue packs as part of an individualised exacerbation action plan, ask people to tell their healthcare professional when they use it, and review use at every appointment (investigate if 3 or more courses a year).

n.0: The plan sets out how both are used; holding back the steroid delays treatment.
n.1: Rescue courses are short courses guided by the plan, not 14-day courses for any cold.
n.3: A rescue pack is for early self-treatment at home, not for hospital use.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Gerald, 70, is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. He can swallow tablets and has no contraindication to corticosteroids. Which oral corticosteroid regimen is recommended?
o: Prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for 5 days
Prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days
Prednisolone 60 mg daily for 7 days
Prednisolone 30 mg daily for 14 days
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115 (2019): for COPD exacerbations offer oral prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days.

n.0: 40-50 mg is the regimen for acute asthma attacks, not COPD exacerbations.
n.2: This dose and duration do not match NICE NG115.
n.3: NICE recommends 5 days; longer courses add side effects without extra benefit.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Brenda, 73, has an exacerbation of COPD. Her blood gases show pH 7.32 and PaCO2 7.6 kPa. A salbutamol nebuliser is prescribed. How should the nebuliser be given?
o: Driven by compressed air, with oxygen by nasal cannulae alongside
Through a spacer instead, because nebulisers are unsafe here
Driven by compressed air, with oxygen stopped during the dose
Driven by oxygen at 8 L/min through the nebuliser mask
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: if a person is hypercapnic or acidotic, nebulisers should be driven by compressed air; if oxygen is needed it is given simultaneously by nasal cannulae (BTS 2017 agrees).

n.1: Nebulisers can be used; the issue is the driving gas, not the device.
n.2: Stopping oxygen during the nebuliser risks hypoxaemia; oxygen continues by cannulae.
n.3: Oxygen-driven nebulisers can worsen hypercapnia when PaCO2 is raised and pH is low.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Stanley, 67, arrives in the emergency department with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 90% on a 28% Venturi mask. A colleague says blood gases are unnecessary because his saturation is within the target. Which reply is best?
o: Blood gases are needed because his saturation is above target
Blood gases are needed to measure his haemoglobin level
Oximetry tells us nothing about his carbon dioxide or pH
Blood gases are needed before any nebuliser can be given
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: pulse oximetry gives no information about PaCO2 or pH, so measure arterial blood gases (noting the inspired oxygen) in everyone arriving at hospital with an exacerbation.

n.0: His saturation of 90% is within the 88-92% target; the reason for gases is the missing CO2 and pH data.
n.1: Haemoglobin is not the reason NICE gives for measuring gases in exacerbations.
n.3: Bronchodilators are not delayed for gas results; the gas guides oxygen and ventilation.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Wilfred, 76, has an exacerbation of COPD. On 28% oxygen his blood gases are: pH 7.31, PaCO2 7.8 kPa, PaO2 8.2 kPa, bicarbonate 27 mmol/L. How should these results be interpreted?
o: Compensated respiratory alkalosis
Type 2 respiratory failure with acute respiratory acidosis
Type 1 respiratory failure with normal carbon dioxide
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Two steps: pH below 7.35 is acidaemia, and a raised PaCO2 (above about 6 kPa) explains it, so this is a respiratory acidosis. Hypercapnia (raised PaCO2) defines type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure; his PaO2 of 8.2 kPa is only being reached on 28% oxygen.

n.0: A pH of 7.31 is acidaemic, not alkalotic.
n.2: Type 1 failure has a normal or low PaCO2; his is raised at 7.8 kPa.
n.3: In metabolic acidosis bicarbonate falls; his is normal to high and PaCO2 is raised.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Alfred, 72, has COPD. After an hour of optimal treatment (controlled oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators, prednisolone and antibiotics) his repeat blood gas shows pH 7.28 and PaCO2 8.9 kPa. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Prepare for NIV in a dedicated setting with an agreed treatment ceiling
Increase oxygen to a 60% Venturi mask to raise his PaO2
Continue the current treatment and repeat the blood gases in 4 hours
Give a second dose of prednisolone and recheck gases tomorrow
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: NIV is the treatment of choice for persistent hypercapnic ventilatory failure during exacerbations despite optimal medical therapy, delivered by trained staff in a dedicated setting with a documented plan and ceiling of treatment.

n.1: More oxygen would worsen hypercapnia; ventilatory support is needed.
n.2: Delay risks further acidosis; NICE recommends NIV for persistent hypercapnic failure.
n.3: Steroids act slowly; persistent acidosis needs ventilatory support now.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Norman, 79, has severe COPD and is about to start NIV for hypercapnic respiratory failure. His notes contain no plan about what will happen if NIV does not work. He has capacity. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the medical team to agree and record a ceiling of care with him
Ask his daughter to decide what should happen if NIV fails
Record him as not for resuscitation because he has severe COPD
Start NIV and leave escalation planning until it has had time to work
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: before starting NIV there should be a clear plan covering what to do if it fails, with the ceiling of treatment agreed and documented, involving the person (MCA: a person with capacity makes their own decisions).

n.1: He has capacity, so the discussion is with him; family do not decide for him.
n.2: Severity alone does not set a ceiling; decisions are made with him and the senior team.
n.3: NICE expects the plan, including what happens if NIV fails, to be agreed at the start.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Agnes, 69, is going home after a COPD exacerbation with a prescription for prednisolone 30 mg daily. She asks how to take it. Which advice is correct?
o: Reduce the dose gradually over 2 weeks before stopping
Continue until your breathing is back to normal
Take 30 mg each morning for 5 days, then stop
Take 15 mg twice daily for 5 days with food
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: prednisolone 30 mg orally once daily for 5 days, with clear instructions about when to stop. Morning dosing matches the natural cortisol rhythm.

n.0: A 5-day course does not usually need tapering; NICE advises clear instructions to stop.
n.1: The course has a set length; open-ended use adds steroid harms.
n.3: Prednisolone is given once daily in the morning; splitting the dose is not the regimen.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Clifford, 66, is recovering from his second hospital admission this year with a COPD exacerbation. He is now stable and ready for discharge. He has MRC grade 3 breathlessness. Which referral is most appropriate to arrange?
o: Pulmonary rehabilitation after this admission
Home nebuliser for regular four-times-daily use
Home NIV assessment because he has had two admissions
Long-term oxygen assessment using today's blood gases
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NICE NG115: offer pulmonary rehabilitation to people who have had a recent hospitalisation for an acute exacerbation. LTOT assessment needs two stable ABGs at least 3 weeks apart.

n.1: Nebulisers are for distress despite maximal inhaled therapy, not a routine discharge step.
n.2: Two admissions alone do not establish chronic hypercapnic failure needing home NIV.
n.3: LTOT is assessed on two stable gases at least 3 weeks apart, not during recovery from an exacerbation.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Sophie, 29, has newly diagnosed asthma confirmed by a raised FeNO. She has symptoms twice a week and has never had an attack. Which treatment is recommended to start?
o: Regular low-dose ICS plus as-needed salbutamol
As-needed salbutamol with no regular inhaler
A leukotriene receptor antagonist taken daily
As-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN NG245 (2024): for people aged 12 and over with newly diagnosed asthma, offer as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (anti-inflammatory reliever, AIR therapy).

n.0: This was the older NICE pathway; NG245 starts with as-needed ICS/formoterol.
n.1: NG245 moves away from SABA-only treatment because it does not treat airway inflammation.
n.2: LTRAs are add-on options, not first-line in NG245.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Hamid, 34, has a history suggestive of asthma. His blood eosinophil count is normal and his FeNO is 56 ppb. How does this result guide diagnosis under NG245?
o: It needs a bronchial challenge test to confirm
It confirms asthma without further testing
It is a normal result, so asthma is unlikely
It needs bronchodilator reversibility testing to confirm
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NG245 (2024): in adults, diagnose asthma if the blood eosinophil count is above the reference range or FeNO is 50 ppb or more. If neither confirms it, measure bronchodilator reversibility, then PEF variability, then bronchial challenge.

n.0: Challenge testing comes later in the sequence, after reversibility and peak flow variability.
n.2: In adults, 50 ppb or more is raised and supports asthma.
n.3: Reversibility testing is the next step when eosinophils and FeNO do not confirm asthma.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Grace, 42, uses as-needed ICS/formoterol. She says she is still using it most days and wakes with cough twice a week. Before her treatment is stepped up, what should the nurse check first?
o: Her suitability for a leukotriene receptor antagonist
Her eligibility for a course of oral prednisolone
Her adherence, inhaler technique and exposure to triggers
Her suitability for moderate-dose MART
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NG245: for uncontrolled asthma, check adherence, inhaler technique and triggers (including smoking and occupational exposure) before increasing treatment.

n.0: Add-on treatment is considered after checking adherence, technique and triggers.
n.1: Oral steroids treat attacks; uncontrolled day-to-day asthma is reviewed for causes first.
n.3: Low-dose MART is the next step after AIR, and only after checking adherence and technique.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Paula, 38, has a reversibility test. Her FEV1 is 2.0 L before and 2.3 L after a bronchodilator. How should this result be interpreted?
o: Negative, as FEV1 needs to rise by 20%
Positive, as FEV1 rose by 15% and 300 mL
Positive, as FEV1 rose by 10% and 200 mL
Negative, as FEV1 needs to rise by 400 mL
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Two steps: change = 2.3 - 2.0 = 0.3 L (300 mL); 0.3 / 2.0 x 100 = 15%. NG245 counts an FEV1 increase of 12% or more AND 200 mL or more as a positive bronchodilator reversibility test.

n.0: The NG245 threshold is 12%, not 20%.
n.2: The rise is 300 mL (15%), not 200 mL (10%); the working is wrong.
n.3: 400 mL is not the NG245 threshold; the test needs 12% and 200 mL or more.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Tariq, 50, has used as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol for 3 months with good technique and adherence. His asthma remains uncontrolled. What is the recommended next step?
o: Add a separate salbutamol inhaler for relief
Regular high-dose inhaled corticosteroid with salbutamol
Low-dose maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
Moderate-dose maintenance and reliever therapy
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NG245: if asthma is uncontrolled on as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (after checking adherence, technique and triggers), offer low-dose MART, then moderate-dose MART.

n.0: Adding SABA does not treat inflammation and goes against the AIR/MART model.
n.1: Regular high-dose ICS with a SABA reliever is not the next step after AIR in NG245.
n.3: Moderate-dose MART follows low-dose MART, not AIR.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Bethany, 33, has had asthma for years. She uses a salbutamol inhaler about three times a week and takes no other asthma medicine. At her annual review, what is the recommended change?
o: Continue salbutamol as her asthma sounds well controlled
Add a regular long-acting beta2 agonist on its own
Add a daily leukotriene receptor antagonist to salbutamol
Switch her to as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NG245 (2024): people with asthma treated with a SABA alone should be moved to as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol.

n.0: SABA-only treatment leaves inflammation untreated; NG245 recommends moving these people on.
n.1: A LABA without an inhaled corticosteroid is unsafe in asthma.
n.2: This is not the NG245 recommendation for SABA-only users.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Four adults attend asthma review. Each has an FEV1 above 80% of predicted. Which person's asthma is NOT completely controlled?
o: Priya, who has not needed her reliever for a month
Owen, who has had no attacks in the last year
Lena, who wakes with cough about once a week
Sam, who plays football with no limitation
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NG245 defines complete control as no daytime symptoms, no night-time waking due to asthma, no attacks, no need for rescue medication, no limitation on activity and normal lung function (FEV1 or PEF above 80%). Night waking means control is not complete.

n.0: No rescue medication is one of the features of complete control.
n.1: No attacks is one of the features of complete control.
n.3: No limitation of activity is one of the features of complete control.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Nadia, 47, has just started low-dose MART with a budesonide/formoterol inhaler. You check her understanding. Which statement shows she has understood?
o: I can stop the daily doses once I feel well for a week
I take my daily doses and use the same inhaler for symptoms
I use it for symptoms and skip the daily doses
I take my daily doses and use salbutamol for symptoms
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: NG245: MART uses one ICS/formoterol inhaler both as regular maintenance and as the reliever for symptoms, with a personalised action plan.

n.0: Maintenance doses continue; stopping when well risks loss of control.
n.2: That describes AIR therapy, not MART, which includes regular maintenance doses.
n.3: With MART the same ICS/formoterol inhaler is the reliever; a separate SABA is not used.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Jade, 27, has an asthma attack. Her PEF is 45% of her best, respiratory rate 26/min, heart rate 105/min and SpO2 95%. She can complete sentences. How should the severity of this attack be classified?
o: Acute severe asthma
Moderate asthma attack
Life-threatening asthma
Near-fatal asthma
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: SIGN 158 (retained via NG244): acute severe asthma is any one of PEF 33-50% best or predicted, respiratory rate 25/min or more, heart rate 110/min or more, or inability to complete sentences in one breath.

n.1: Moderate attacks have PEF above 50% and no severe features; her PEF and respiratory rate are severe features.
n.2: There are no life-threatening features: PEF is above 33% and SpO2 is above 92%.
n.3: Near-fatal asthma means raised PaCO2 or needing mechanical ventilation.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Martin, 35, has an acute asthma attack. His PEF is 40% of predicted and his SpO2 is 90% on air. He is talking in short phrases. Which classification applies?
o: Life-threatening asthma
Near-fatal asthma
Moderate asthma attack
Acute severe asthma
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: SIGN 158: any one life-threatening feature in a person with severe asthma, including SpO2 below 92%, PEF below 33%, silent chest, cyanosis or exhaustion, makes the attack life-threatening.

n.1: Near-fatal asthma needs a raised PaCO2 or mechanical ventilation.
n.2: Moderate attacks have PEF above 50% and no severe or life-threatening features.
n.3: His PEF fits acute severe, but SpO2 below 92% is a life-threatening feature.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Lucy, 31, is having an acute severe asthma attack with SpO2 91% on air. She has no other lung disease. What saturation target should guide her oxygen therapy?
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: SIGN 158 and BTS 2017: in acute asthma give controlled oxygen to maintain SpO2 94-98%.

n.1: BTS does not aim for 100%; the upper limit is 98%.
n.2: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as COPD.
n.3: This is not the SIGN 158 or BTS target range.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Kieran, 40, is treated for an acute severe asthma attack and is able to swallow. Which corticosteroid regimen is recommended?
o: Prednisolone 10 mg daily for 14 days
Prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days
Prednisolone 40-50 mg given as a single one-off dose
Prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for at least 5 days
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: SIGN 158: give prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for at least 5 days (or IV hydrocortisone if unable to take oral) in acute asthma.

n.0: This dose is too low for an acute attack.
n.1: 30 mg for 5 days is the COPD exacerbation regimen.
n.2: SIGN 158 recommends continuing for at least 5 days, not one dose.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Abigail, 22, has been wheezy for hours. She is now drowsy, her chest is quiet with almost no wheeze, and her SpO2 is 89% on oxygen. Her friend says she must be getting better. What is the priority?
o: Reassure her friend that the reduced wheeze is improvement
Measure her peak flow first to confirm how severe the attack is
Give salbutamol by spacer and reassess her breathing in 1 hour
Call for immediate senior and critical care help while giving oxygen
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: SIGN 158: silent chest, altered conscious level and SpO2 below 92% are life-threatening features. They need immediate senior and critical care involvement alongside oxygen and bronchodilators.

n.0: A silent chest means very little air movement and is a life-threatening sign.
n.1: PEF measurement must not delay emergency help; her features are already life-threatening.
n.2: A silent chest with drowsiness needs immediate escalation, not hourly review.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Robert, 45, has had acute severe asthma for 6 hours and looks exhausted. His blood gas shows PaO2 7.6 kPa and PaCO2 5.4 kPa. A colleague says the carbon dioxide is normal so he is coping. What is the best interpretation?
o: This is near-fatal asthma because PaCO2 is raised
A normal PaCO2 shows he is ventilating adequately
A 'normal' PaCO2 here is a life-threatening sign
His PaO2 of 7.6 kPa fits a moderate attack
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Two steps: identify each finding against SIGN 158. PaO2 below 8 kPa and a 'normal' PaCO2 (4.6-6.0 kPa) are both life-threatening features because a normal PaCO2 in a severe attack shows exhaustion.

n.0: Near-fatal asthma needs a raised PaCO2; 5.4 kPa is in the normal range.
n.1: In a severe attack PaCO2 should be low from fast breathing; a normal value signals tiring.
n.3: PaO2 below 8 kPa is a life-threatening feature, not a moderate one.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Fiona, 26, knows her best peak flow is 500 L/min. During an attack her PEF is 150 L/min. She can speak in full sentences and her SpO2 is 95%. What is her PEF as a percentage of best, and how is this classified?
o: 30%, which is life-threatening
30%, which is classed as acute severe
33%, which is classed as acute severe
40%, which is classed as acute severe
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: Two steps: 150 / 500 x 100 = 30%. SIGN 158: PEF below 33% best or predicted is a life-threatening feature.

n.1: Acute severe is PEF 33-50%; 30% is below 33% and so is life-threatening.
n.3: The calculation is wrong: 150/500 x 100 = 30%.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Callum, 39, has an asthma attack. His PEF is 55% of best, respiratory rate 22/min, heart rate 114/min and he completes sentences. SpO2 is 96%. How should this attack be classified?
o: Acute severe asthma
Mild asthma with no severe features
Moderate asthma attack
Life-threatening asthma
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: SIGN 158: any one feature (PEF 33-50%, RR 25/min or more, HR 110/min or more, unable to complete sentences) classifies an attack as acute severe.

n.1: His heart rate of 114/min is a severe feature.
n.2: His PEF fits moderate, but a heart rate of 110/min or more is an acute severe feature.
n.3: There are no life-threatening features such as SpO2 below 92% or PEF below 33%.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Margaret, 74, has known COPD and is admitted to the medical assessment unit with pneumonia. Her SpO2 is 85% on air and her respiratory rate is 26/min. Blood gases have not yet been taken. Which target saturation range should be prescribed for her oxygen?
o: 85-88% to match her usual resting saturation
94-98% as for most acutely ill adults
92-96% as a compromise for chronic lung disease
88-92% until blood gas results are available
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 emergency oxygen guideline: prescribe oxygen to a target range. People at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, including COPD, have a target of 88-92% pending blood gas results; most other acutely ill adults have 94-98%.

n.0: BTS does not set a target below 88% for acute oxygen therapy; 85% is the hypoxaemia being treated.
n.1: 94-98% is the standard target, but COPD puts her at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, so BTS sets 88-92% pending gases.
n.2: 92-96% is not a BTS target range; the two recognised ranges are 94-98% and 88-92%.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Daniel, 45, has no history of lung disease. He is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. His SpO2 is 91% on air, respiratory rate 22/min and he is alert. Which target saturation range is appropriate for his prescribed oxygen?
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017: most acutely ill adults without risk factors for hypercapnia should be given oxygen to achieve a target SpO2 of 94-98%.

n.0: 90-94% is not a BTS target range and would leave him below the standard lower limit of 94%.
n.1: 88-92% is reserved for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as COPD; Daniel has no such risk factor.
n.2: BTS advises against aiming for 100%; hyperoxaemia gives no benefit and may cause harm, so the upper limit is 98%.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: You are reviewing four newly admitted adults with low oxygen saturation. None has had blood gases taken yet. Which person should have an initial oxygen target of 88-92%?
o: Raj, 66, with lobar pneumonia and no chronic lung disease
Ahmed, 52, with motor neurone disease and respiratory weakness
Helen, 71, admitted with acute left ventricular failure and oedema
Lucy, 30, with an acute asthma attack and no other illness
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 lists COPD and other fixed airflow obstruction, cystic fibrosis, neuromuscular disease, chest wall deformity and morbid obesity as risks for hypercapnic respiratory failure. Neuromuscular weakness from motor neurone disease means an 88-92% target pending gases.

n.0: Pneumonia without a chronic hypercapnia risk factor uses the standard 94-98% range.
n.2: Heart failure is not listed among the BTS risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure; her target is 94-98%.
n.3: Acute asthma is not a BTS hypercapnia risk factor for target-setting; SIGN 158 sets a target of 94-98% in an asthma attack.

Respiratory Care & Oxygen.q: Kwame, 38, is brought to the emergency department after a house fire. He has a headache and nausea. The pulse oximeter reads 99% on air. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?
o: Oxygen should be titrated to keep his reading between 94% and 98%
A 24% Venturi mask is enough because his airway is clear
The oximeter cannot detect carbon monoxide, so give high-flow oxygen
His saturation of 99% shows he does not need supplemental oxygen
Respiratory Care & Oxygen.w: BTS 2017 Table 1: in carbon monoxide poisoning give as much oxygen as possible (reservoir mask 15 L/min). Pulse oximetry is unreliable because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading does not exclude poisoning.

n.0: Titrating to the oximeter is unsafe here because the reading is unreliable in carbon monoxide poisoning.
n.1: Low-concentration oxygen is for people at risk of hypercapnia; carbon monoxide poisoning needs as much oxygen as possible.
n.3: Oximeters cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so 99% may be falsely reassuring after smoke exposure.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Florence, 84, has treated hypertension and no other major conditions. She asks what clinic blood pressure she should aim for. What is the NICE target?
o: Below 150/90 mmHg
Below 130/80 mmHg
Below 135/85 mmHg
Below 140/90 mmHg
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG136 1.4.20: for people aged 80 and over, the clinic target is below 150/90 mmHg (145/85 with ABPM/HBPM), using clinical judgement for frailty.

n.1: 130/80 is not the NICE NG136 clinic target for someone aged 80 or over.
n.2: 135/85 is the ABPM/HBPM target for people aged under 80.
n.3: Below 140/90 is the clinic target for people aged under 80.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Gordon, 62, monitors his blood pressure at home. He is treated for hypertension and has no other conditions. What home (HBPM) average should he aim for?
o: Below 145/85 mmHg
Below 150/90 mmHg
Below 140/90 mmHg
Below 135/85 mmHg
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG136 1.4.20: under 80, clinic target below 140/90 and ABPM/HBPM average below 135/85 mmHg.

n.0: 145/85 is the ABPM/HBPM target for people aged 80 or over.
n.1: 150/90 is the clinic target for people aged 80 or over.
n.2: 140/90 is the clinic target; home readings run about 5 mmHg lower.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Abena, 48, of Black African family origin, has confirmed stage 1 hypertension. She does not have diabetes. Lifestyle advice has been given and treatment is agreed. Which step 1 drug class is recommended?
o: A thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide
An ACE inhibitor such as ramipril
A beta-blocker such as bisoprolol
A calcium-channel blocker such as amlodipine
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG136: offer a CCB as step 1 to people aged 55 and over, and to people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin of any age, who do not have type 2 diabetes.

n.0: A thiazide-like diuretic is offered if a CCB is unsuitable, not first choice here.
n.1: ACE inhibitors are step 1 for under-55s who are not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, or with type 2 diabetes.
n.2: Beta-blockers are not a NICE step 1 treatment for hypertension.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Reginald, 66, attends the practice with a headache. His clinic blood pressure is 188/124 mmHg on repeat. His wife says he has been confused since this morning. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange same-day specialist assessment
Offer ABPM to confirm the diagnosis
Start amlodipine and recheck in 1 week
Recheck his blood pressure after 1 hour of rest
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: 188/124 is severe hypertension (180/120 or higher); new confusion is a life-threatening symptom. NICE NG136 1.5.1: refer for same-day specialist assessment.

n.1: ABPM delays care; severe hypertension with red flags is managed urgently.
n.2: New confusion with severe hypertension is a life-threatening symptom needing same-day assessment.
n.3: Resting and rechecking delays urgent review of a possible hypertensive emergency.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Lionel, 72, has ankle swelling and breathlessness on exertion. His GP finds an NT-proBNP of 2,600 ng/L. Within what time should he have specialist assessment and echocardiography?
o: Within 2 weeks
Within 12 weeks
Within 6 weeks
Within 48 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106: NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L, refer urgently for specialist assessment and transthoracic echocardiography within 2 weeks.

n.1: 12 weeks is too long for an NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L.
n.2: 6 weeks applies to NT-proBNP between 400 and 2,000 ng/L.
n.3: 48 hours is not the NG106 timeframe for this level.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Edna, 68, has fatigue and mild breathlessness. Her NT-proBNP is 850 ng/L. What is the appropriate referral timeframe for specialist assessment and echocardiography?
o: Within 2 weeks
Within 6 weeks
No referral, as heart failure is excluded
Within 24 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106: NT-proBNP between 400 and 2,000 ng/L, refer for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 6 weeks.

n.0: 2 weeks is for NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L.
n.2: Heart failure is unlikely below 400 ng/L; 850 ng/L needs referral.
n.3: This is not an NG106 timeframe for suspected chronic heart failure.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Morris, 64, has newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. He has no contraindications. Which combination does NICE NG106 (2025) recommend as first-line treatment?
o: ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor together
ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, loop diuretic and digoxin
Beta-blocker and SGLT2 inhibitor, adding an ACE inhibitor if needed
ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker, adding an MRA months later
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106 (updated Sep 2025): for HFrEF offer an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor; it is not necessary to optimise one before starting the next.

n.1: Diuretics relieve congestion and digoxin is not a first-line pillar.
n.2: The ACE inhibitor (or ARNI) is one of the four first-line drugs.
n.3: The 2025 update offers all four together rather than one after another.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Patrick, 70, has stable heart failure and normal sodium. He asks whether he should limit his fluids to a litre a day and use a low-sodium salt substitute. What is the best advice?
o: Limit fluids to 1.5 litres a day and use a salt substitute
Keep fluids under a litre a day and use the substitute sparingly
No routine fluid limit, and avoid potassium-based salt substitutes
Use the salt substitute freely as it contains no sodium
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106 1.9.10-1.9.11: do not routinely advise restricting sodium or fluid; ask about intake and advise if needed (for example fluid restriction in dilutional hyponatraemia). Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium.

n.0: NICE does not routinely advise fluid restriction, and potassium salt substitutes risk hyperkalaemia.
n.1: Routine strict fluid restriction is not recommended in NG106, and potassium-based substitutes are unsafe with his medicines.
n.3: Many substitutes contain potassium, which is dangerous with ACE inhibitors and MRAs.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Ivy, 75, has heart failure and takes ramipril and spironolactone. Today's blood results show potassium 5.8 mmol/L; it was 4.9 a month ago. Her spironolactone is due. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose and advise foods rich in potassium
Inform the prescriber before giving the next spironolactone dose
Give the dose and recheck her electrolytes in 3 months
Give the dose, as 5.8 mmol/L is expected with these two drugs
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Assess then act: potassium has risen above 5.5 mmol/L on an ACE inhibitor and an MRA, both of which raise potassium. NICE NG106 (2025) says follow local guidance if potassium exceeds 5.5 mmol/L, so the prescriber must review before more spironolactone is given.

n.0: Increasing potassium intake would make hyperkalaemia worse.
n.2: A potassium above 5.5 needs action now under NG106 monitoring advice.
n.3: NICE sets 5.5 mmol/L as the level that triggers action.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Bill, 69, has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and is due to start bisoprolol today. Before the first dose his pulse is 46/min and regular. His ECG is awaited. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the dose and record a lying and standing BP
Give the dose because beta-blockers improve survival
Withhold the first dose and discuss with the prescriber
Give half the dose and recheck the pulse in an hour
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106 (2025): perform a 12-lead ECG before starting a beta-blocker and do not offer one to people with second or third degree heart block (without a pacemaker) or a heart rate below 50/min.

n.0: Postural BP does not address a heart rate below 50/min.
n.1: NICE advises not to start a beta-blocker if heart rate is below 50/min.
n.3: Changing the dose is a prescribing decision and does not remove the contraindication.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Maud, 82, has COPD and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. She is prescribed bisoprolol. Her pulse is 74/min, BP 128/76 mmHg and her ECG shows sinus rhythm. Her daughter asks if it is safe given her age and lungs. What is the best response?
o: Give it as prescribed; age and COPD are not reasons to withhold
Withhold it until a respiratory specialist has reviewed her
Swap it for a calcium-channel blocker to protect her lungs
Withhold it because beta-blockers are unsuitable after 80
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106: do not withhold treatment with a beta-blocker solely because of age, peripheral vascular disease, erectile dysfunction, diabetes, interstitial pulmonary disease or COPD without reversibility.

n.1: NICE says beta-blockers should not be withheld because of COPD.
n.2: Rate-limiting CCBs are not a substitute in HFrEF and the change is not indicated.
n.3: NICE says not to withhold beta-blockers because of age.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Harold, 67, has stable heart failure after a recent admission. He is keen to get fitter but worried exercise will strain his heart. What should the nurse discuss with him?
o: Avoiding exercise until his ejection fraction has improved
A personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme
Bed rest for 6 weeks to reduce cardiac workload
Unsupervised gym training at the highest intensity he can
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG106 1.11.1: offer people with heart failure a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme with psychological and educational components.

n.0: NICE recommends exercise-based rehabilitation rather than avoiding activity.
n.2: Prolonged rest leads to deconditioning and is not recommended.
n.3: Rehab is personalised and structured, not unsupervised maximal training.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: During routine observations, Cyril, 71, has an irregularly irregular radial pulse of 92/min. He has no chest pain and his blood pressure is stable. How should possible atrial fibrillation be confirmed?
o: Record a 12-lead ECG
Arrange an echocardiogram
Recount the pulse at the apex for 1 minute
Recheck the radial pulse in 4 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG196 1.1.1-1.1.2: manual pulse palpation to detect an irregular pulse in suspected AF, then a 12-lead ECG to confirm the diagnosis.

n.1: Echo assesses heart structure and function; it does not diagnose AF.
n.2: Apical counting confirms the rate but cannot diagnose the rhythm.
n.3: Rechecking delays diagnosis; NICE asks for an ECG.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Winifred, 76, has newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation and treated hypertension. She has no other conditions. What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score and the recommended action?
o: Score 4: offer a DOAC
Score 4: offer aspirin
Score 3: offer a DOAC
Score 2: consider a DOAC
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: age 75 or over = 2, female sex = 1, hypertension = 1, total 4. NICE NG196 1.6.3: offer anticoagulation with a DOAC if CHA2DS2-VASc is 2 or above, taking bleeding risk into account.

n.1: NICE says do not offer aspirin monotherapy for stroke prevention in AF.
n.2: Age 75 or over scores 2, not 1, so the total is 4.
n.3: Her total is 4, and at 2 or above a DOAC is offered, not considered.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Before starting apixaban for Leonard, 70, who has atrial fibrillation, the team assesses his bleeding risk. Which tool does NICE NG196 recommend for this?
o: HAS-BLED
ABCD2
CHA2DS2-VASc
ORBIT
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG196 1.3: use the ORBIT bleeding risk score to assess bleeding risk in people with AF, alongside CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk.

n.0: NG196 replaced HAS-BLED with ORBIT as the preferred bleeding risk tool.
n.1: ABCD2 was a TIA risk score and is not used for bleeding risk.
n.2: CHA2DS2-VASc assesses stroke risk, not bleeding risk.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Elsie, 84, has atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban. She fell at home last week without injury. Her son asks the nurse to stop the apixaban because he worries about bleeding if she falls again. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Halve the apixaban dose to reduce her bleeding risk
Withhold the apixaban until a falls assessment is complete
Suggest switching to aspirin as a safer option for falls
Explain falls are not a reason to stop it and ask for a review
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG196 1.6.8: do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of a person's age or their risk of falls. Explain this, address falls risk separately (NG249) and refer the concern for prescriber review.

n.0: Nurses do not change doses, and dose reduction follows set criteria, not falls.
n.1: NICE says do not withhold anticoagulation because of falls risk; withholding exposes her to stroke.
n.2: Aspirin is not recommended for AF stroke prevention and still carries bleeding risk.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Ernest, 73, has had atrial fibrillation for years. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3. He takes aspirin 75 mg daily, prescribed only for stroke prevention, and has no other indication for it. What should the nurse raise at his review?
o: Aspirin is adequate stroke protection at his level of risk
He should add clopidogrel to the aspirin for better protection
He should increase his aspirin dose to 300 mg daily
Aspirin is not recommended for AF stroke prevention; a DOAC is
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG196 1.6.14: do not offer aspirin monotherapy solely for stroke prevention in AF. With a score of 2 or above, offer a DOAC.

n.0: Aspirin monotherapy is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF.
n.1: Dual antiplatelet therapy is not the NG196 alternative to anticoagulation.
n.2: A higher aspirin dose does not make it an effective AF treatment.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Rita, 66, has permanent atrial fibrillation with a resting heart rate of 118/min. She has no heart failure and the team chooses rate control. Which drug is an appropriate first-line choice?
o: Amiodarone
Bisoprolol
Sotalol
Flecainide
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG196 1.7.2: offer a standard beta-blocker (that is, a beta-blocker other than sotalol) or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker as initial rate-control monotherapy.

n.0: Amiodarone is a rhythm-control drug, not first-line for rate control.
n.2: NICE specifies a standard beta-blocker other than sotalol for rate control.
n.3: Flecainide is a rhythm-control drug, not used for rate control.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Cecil, 68, develops new-onset atrial fibrillation with a rate of 170/min. His blood pressure is 76/40 mmHg, he is confused and clammy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Start apixaban now and plan electrical cardioversion after 3 weeks
Arrange an urgent echocardiogram before treatment
Emergency electrical cardioversion without waiting for anticoagulation
Give oral bisoprolol and reassess in one hour
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Assess then act: hypotension, confusion and clamminess show life-threatening haemodynamic instability. NICE NG196 1.8.1: perform emergency electrical cardioversion without delaying to achieve anticoagulation.

n.0: Elective delay is for stable patients; he is in life-threatening shock.
n.1: Investigations must not delay emergency cardioversion in shock.
n.3: Oral rate control is too slow for haemodynamic collapse.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Joanne, 52, has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. She has no hypertension, diabetes, heart failure or vascular disease and no history of stroke. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 1. What is the recommended approach?
o: Offer a DOAC because her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 1
Consider a DOAC, as for men with a score of 1
Do not offer anticoagulation for stroke prevention
Offer aspirin 75 mg as a lower-risk option
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG196 1.6.7: do not offer stroke prevention therapy to people aged under 65 with AF and no risk factors other than their sex (score 0 for men, 1 for women).

n.0: Her only point is female sex; NICE does not offer anticoagulation in this case.
n.1: Consideration at a score of 1 applies to men, whose point reflects a real risk factor.
n.3: Aspirin is not used for stroke prevention in AF.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Norma, 59, has central chest pain. It eases 3 minutes after sublingual GTN. The foundation doctor says this means the pain is cardiac and an ACS is confirmed. Which statement is correct?
o: Relief with GTN confirms that the pain is cardiac angina
Relief with GTN cannot be used to confirm or exclude ACS
Relief with GTN rules out a myocardial infarction
Relief with GTN means a troponin is not needed
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE CG95 1.2.1.4: do not use a person's response to GTN to make a diagnosis of ACS.

n.0: NICE says not to use the response to GTN to make a diagnosis.
n.2: Pain can ease with GTN during an MI; it does not exclude one.
n.3: Troponin and ECG are still needed; GTN response is not diagnostic.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Raymond, 62, has an ECG showing ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His pain started 4 hours ago. Primary PCI can be delivered within 90 minutes. What is the recommended reperfusion strategy?
o: Coronary angiography with follow-on primary PCI
Thrombolysis followed by elective angiography in 6 weeks
Fibrinolysis in the emergency department
Medical treatment and angiography within 72 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG185 1.1.6: coronary angiography with follow-on primary PCI if presentation is within 12 hours of onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given.

n.1: This does not reflect NG185 reperfusion timings for STEMI.
n.2: Fibrinolysis is used if primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes.
n.3: This approach applies to NSTEMI, not STEMI within 12 hours.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Stuart, 57, is recovering from a myocardial infarction. You are checking his discharge prescription against NICE secondary prevention advice. Which set of drugs should normally be included?
o: Beta-blocker, warfarin, aspirin and a statin
ACE inhibitor, dual antiplatelets, beta-blocker and a statin
ACE inhibitor, aspirin, calcium-channel blocker and a statin
Dual antiplatelets, a nitrate patch, statin and a diuretic
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG185 1.4.1: offer all people who have had an MI an ACE inhibitor, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a second antiplatelet), a beta-blocker and a statin.

n.0: Warfarin is not routine secondary prevention after MI.
n.2: A beta-blocker, not a CCB, and dual antiplatelets are recommended after MI.
n.3: Nitrates and diuretics are not among the four secondary prevention drugs.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Pauline, 61, had an MI 2 months ago. She takes aspirin and ticagrelor. She asks how long she must take both. What is the most accurate answer?
o: Both are taken for the rest of her life
Usually up to 12 months, with aspirin continuing after that
Usually 6 weeks, then both can stop
Usually 3 months, then she switches to warfarin long term
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG185 1.4.15: continue dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months after an ACS (unless contraindicated); aspirin is continued indefinitely as part of secondary prevention.

n.0: The second antiplatelet normally stops after up to 12 months.
n.2: Dual therapy normally continues for up to 12 months and aspirin continues long term.
n.3: Warfarin is not a routine follow-on after DAPT.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Arthur, 86, has had a myocardial infarction. A colleague suggests not referring him to cardiac rehabilitation because of his age. He lives independently. What should the nurse do?
o: Delay any referral for 6 months to let him recover first
Agree not to refer, as rehabilitation is aimed at working-age adults
Refer him for a home exercise leaflet in place of a programme
Offer him cardiac rehabilitation, as age is not a barrier
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG185 1.8.1: offer cardiac rehabilitation with an exercise component to all people after an MI, regardless of age, and encourage attendance.

n.0: Rehabilitation should start early after MI, not be deferred.
n.1: NICE says cardiac rehabilitation should be offered to all, regardless of age.
n.2: A leaflet is not a substitute for an offered rehabilitation programme.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Gwen, 64, has suspected ACS. She has no lung disease. Her SpO2 is 92% on air and her respiratory rate is 22/min. What is the most appropriate oxygen management?
o: Give 15 L/min via reservoir mask aiming for 100%
Give oxygen aiming for SpO2 88-92%
Withhold oxygen because routine oxygen harms ACS patients
Give oxygen aiming for SpO2 94-98%
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Assess then act: SpO2 92% is below 94%. NICE CG95 1.2.3.3: do not routinely give oxygen in ACS, but give it if SpO2 is below 94%, aiming for 94-98% (88-92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure).

n.0: The aim is 94-98%, not 100%; excess oxygen may increase infarct size.
n.1: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnia, which she is not.
n.2: Oxygen is withheld in ACS when SpO2 is 94% or more; she is hypoxaemic.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: A 12-lead ECG for Leslie, 55, with chest pain shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which area of the heart does this pattern suggest is affected?
o: Anterior
Inferior
Septal
Lateral
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Leads II, III and aVF view the inferior surface of the heart, usually supplied by the right coronary artery, so ST elevation there suggests an inferior STEMI. Report it immediately for reperfusion (NG185).

n.0: Anterior changes appear in leads V1-V4.
n.2: Septal changes appear in leads V1 and V2.
n.3: Lateral changes appear in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Dennis, 60, has an ECG showing STEMI. He has had two doses of sublingual GTN but still reports severe central chest pain. What pain relief is recommended next?
o: A third GTN dose with no further drug
An intravenous opioid such as morphine
Oral paracetamol and codeine
Intramuscular morphine into the deltoid
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE CG95 1.2.3.1: offer pain relief as soon as possible, with GTN (sublingual or buccal) and an intravenous opioid such as morphine, particularly if an acute MI is suspected.

n.0: Persisting pain after GTN in suspected MI calls for an IV opioid.
