n.2: Oral analgesia is too slow and weak for suspected MI pain.
n.3: IV is preferred; IM absorption is unpredictable and can interfere with later investigations.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Joyce, 74, is admitted with pneumonia. Her VTE risk outweighs her bleeding risk and enoxaparin is prescribed. Within what time of the decision to admit should the first dose be given?
o: Within 14 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 4 hours
Within 48 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG89: start pharmacological VTE prophylaxis as soon as possible and within 14 hours of admission (decision to admit) for people whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk.

n.1: 24 hours is later than the NICE timeframe for starting prophylaxis.
n.2: 4 hours is the DVT ultrasound timeframe, not the LMWH start time.
n.3: 48 hours is far later than NICE recommends.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Simon, 66, is an acutely ill medical inpatient on enoxaparin prophylaxis. On day 4 he is walking again and asks to stop the injections. He remains in hospital. What is the minimum NICE duration of pharmacological prophylaxis for him?
o: At least 7 days
At least 3 days
At least 28 days
Until he walks unaided
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG89 1.4.6: offer pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days to acutely ill medical patients whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk. The patient's concerns are explored and any decision is made with him.

n.1: NICE sets a minimum of 7 days in acutely ill medical patients.
n.2: 28 days is not the NG89 minimum for medical patients.
n.3: The NG89 minimum is a time period, not a mobility milestone.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Rupert, 58, was admitted mobile with cellulitis and assessed as low VTE risk. Three days later he falls, fractures his ankle and is now immobile in a cast. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassess his VTE and bleeding risk now
Reassess his risk when he is discharged home
Reassess his risk at the weekly multidisciplinary meeting
Keep his admission assessment, as it remains valid
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG89 1.1.8: reassess VTE and bleeding risk at the consultant review and whenever the clinical condition changes.

n.1: Waiting until discharge leaves him unprotected during a higher-risk period.
n.2: NICE asks for reassessment when the clinical condition changes, not at a fixed weekly point.
n.3: His risk has changed with immobility; the admission assessment is out of date.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Bridget, 77, is admitted with an acute ischaemic stroke and is immobile. The healthcare assistant asks whether to fit anti-embolism stockings. What is the most appropriate VTE prevention?
o: Thigh-length anti-embolism stockings on both legs
Intermittent pneumatic compression to both legs
Leg elevation and ankle exercises with no device
Knee-length anti-embolism stockings on the weak leg
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG89 1.4.2-1.4.3: do not offer anti-embolism stockings for VTE prophylaxis to people admitted for acute stroke; consider intermittent pneumatic compression for those who are immobile.

n.0: NICE advises not to offer anti-embolism stockings for VTE prevention after stroke.
n.2: IPC is recommended for immobile stroke patients; exercises alone are not enough.
n.3: Stockings of any length are not recommended for VTE prevention in acute stroke.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Maurice, 70, is immobile after an acute stroke and intermittent pneumatic compression was started on day 2. How long should IPC usually continue?
o: Until he can transfer from bed to chair
14 days, or until a swallow assessment is passed
30 days, or until mobile or discharged if sooner
7 days, then switch to anti-embolism stockings
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG89 1.4.3 and 1.4.5: if intermittent pneumatic compression is used for an immobile person with acute stroke, start it within 3 days of the stroke and continue for 30 days or until the person is mobile or discharged, whichever is sooner.

n.0: Mobility rather than transfer ability ends IPC, within the 30-day limit.
n.1: Swallowing is not the criterion for stopping IPC.
n.3: Stockings are not used after stroke, and IPC continues beyond 7 days.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Hazel, 55, has a painful swollen left calf. The doctor calculates a two-level DVT Wells score of 3. What is the recommended next investigation?
o: A D-dimer test first, then an ultrasound if it is positive
Proximal leg vein ultrasound, with results within 4 hours
Repeat the Wells score in 24 hours
CT pulmonary angiogram
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: a two-level DVT Wells score of 2 or more means DVT is likely. NICE NG158: offer a proximal leg vein ultrasound with results within 4 hours (or interim anticoagulation and a D-dimer if this is not possible).

n.0: D-dimer first is the pathway when DVT is 'unlikely' (score 1 or less).
n.2: A 'likely' score needs imaging now, not repeat scoring.
n.3: CTPA investigates PE, not DVT.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Kenneth, 63, has a confirmed proximal DVT with no cancer and normal kidney function. Which treatment does NICE NG158 recommend first-line?
o: Apixaban or rivaroxaban for 4 weeks
LMWH for 5 days then aspirin for 3 months
Apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least 3 months
Warfarin for at least 6 weeks
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG158 1.3.5 and 1.3.8: offer apixaban or rivaroxaban to people with confirmed proximal DVT or PE, and continue anticoagulation for at least 3 months.

n.0: The minimum treatment duration is 3 months, not 4 weeks.
n.1: Aspirin is not a treatment for confirmed DVT.
n.3: A VKA is not first-line, and NICE sets at least 3 months of treatment.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Glenys, 72, is admitted for a hip replacement. She has type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy and reduced sensation in both feet. She is due to be measured for anti-embolism stockings. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Check her ankle brachial pressure index, then fit if normal
Do not fit stockings and discuss other prophylaxis with the team
Fit knee-length stockings to reduce pressure on her feet
Fit thigh-length stockings and check her skin each day
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG89 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with peripheral neuropathy or other causes of sensory impairment (or peripheral arterial disease, severe oedema, local skin conditions). Discuss alternative mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis.

n.0: A normal ABPI excludes arterial disease but not her neuropathy.
n.2: Stockings of any length are contraindicated with sensory impairment.
n.3: Peripheral neuropathy is a contraindication; daily checks do not remove the risk.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Mabel, 74, arrives in the emergency department with sudden right arm weakness and slurred speech. The paramedics used FAST on scene. Which tool should the emergency department use to establish the diagnosis rapidly?
o: FAST again
NIHSS
ABCD2
ROSIER
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.1.1 and 1.1.3: use a validated tool such as FAST outside hospital; in the emergency department use ROSIER to establish the diagnosis rapidly.

n.0: FAST is for use outside hospital; NICE recommends ROSIER in the ED.
n.1: NIHSS grades stroke severity; it is not the NICE ED recognition tool.
n.2: ABCD2 was a TIA risk score and is no longer recommended.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Victor, 67, had 30 minutes of left arm weakness this morning that has fully resolved. He has no contraindication to aspirin and no bleeding disorder. Which actions are recommended?
o: Aspirin 75 mg now and a specialist clinic within 7 days
No aspirin until a CT scan has been done
Calculate an ABCD2 score to decide on referral timing
Aspirin 300 mg now and specialist assessment within 24 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.1.4-1.1.5: offer aspirin 300 mg immediately to people with suspected TIA (unless contraindicated) and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset.

n.0: NICE recommends 300 mg and assessment within 24 hours of onset.
n.1: For suspected TIA with resolved symptoms, NICE advises aspirin 300 mg straight away.
n.2: NICE no longer uses ABCD2; all suspected TIAs are seen within 24 hours.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Norman, 59, collapses at home. His wife notices his face has dropped on one side and he cannot lift his left arm. He is awake and breathing. What should she be advised to do?
o: Lie him down and call 999 if not better in 30 minutes
Book an urgent GP appointment for later today
Call 999 straight away
Give him aspirin 300 mg and call the GP
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time): any positive sign means Time to call 999. NICE NG128 1.1.1 recommends FAST outside hospital to identify stroke quickly for urgent transfer.

n.0: Waiting loses time for thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
n.1: A suspected stroke is an emergency needing ambulance transfer.
n.3: Aspirin before imaging could worsen a haemorrhagic stroke; he needs emergency transfer.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Amira, 63, has type 1 diabetes. Her carer finds her with sudden slurred speech and right-sided weakness. You are the first nurse to see her. Which assessment is a priority to exclude a stroke mimic?
o: Capillary blood glucose
Mini-mental state examination
Urinalysis for infection
Lying and standing blood pressure
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.1.2-1.1.3: exclude hypoglycaemia as the cause of sudden-onset neurological symptoms. A capillary glucose is quick and reversible causes are treated immediately.

n.1: Cognitive testing does not exclude the urgent reversible mimic.
n.2: Infection can cause confusion, but hypoglycaemia is the urgent mimic to exclude.
n.3: Postural BP is not a priority in suspected stroke and delays assessment.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Lilian, 78, has left-sided weakness that began 7 hours ago. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. She is not a candidate for thrombolysis. When should she have brain imaging?
o: Within 1 hour, if her GCS falls below 13
Within 24 hours, as she is outside the thrombolysis window
Immediately, because she is on an anticoagulant
At the next scheduled CT list tomorrow morning
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: identify the criterion (on anticoagulant treatment), then apply NICE NG128 1.3.2: perform non-enhanced CT immediately if the person is on anticoagulants, has a known bleeding tendency, GCS below 13, unexplained progressive or fluctuating symptoms, papilloedema, neck stiffness or fever, or severe headache at onset.

n.0: She already meets an immediate-imaging criterion through her anticoagulant.
n.1: Anticoagulant use is an indication for immediate imaging in its own right.
n.3: Waiting until tomorrow could miss a haemorrhage needing urgent reversal.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Bernard, 69, has a suspected stroke. He reports that his symptoms began with a sudden, very severe headache. His GCS is 15. When should brain imaging be done?
o: Within 24 hours
Within 4 hours
Immediately
Within 12 hours
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.3.2: severe headache at onset of stroke symptoms is an indication for immediate non-enhanced CT, as it suggests possible haemorrhage. NG128 defines 'immediately' as ideally the next slot and definitely within 1 hour, whichever is sooner.

n.0: 24 hours applies when no immediate criterion is present.
n.1: Severe headache at onset needs immediate CT, which NICE defines as the next slot and definitely within 1 hour; 4 hours is too long.
n.3: 12 hours is not an NG128 imaging timeframe.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Eileen, 72, had 20 minutes of slurred speech yesterday afternoon that fully resolved. She attends her GP today. She has not had aspirin. Which statement about her assessment timing is correct?
o: She needs specialist assessment within 7 days as symptoms resolved
She needs a carotid ultrasound before any referral is made
She needs specialist assessment within 24 hours of her symptom onset
She needs specialist assessment within 24 hours of today's visit
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.1.5: refer immediately people who have had a suspected TIA for specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset of symptoms (and give aspirin 300 mg unless contraindicated).

n.0: Resolution does not change the 24-hour standard for recent TIA.
n.1: Imaging is arranged by the specialist service and must not delay referral.
n.3: The 24-hour clock runs from symptom onset, not from presentation.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Ethel, 81, is brought to the emergency department with sudden weakness of her left leg and arm, which started 50 minutes ago and is still present. A student asks why aspirin has not been given. What is the best explanation?
o: Aspirin is given after 2 weeks of anticoagulation
Aspirin is held because her symptoms may resolve
Bleeding into the brain must be excluded by imaging first
Aspirin is not used in ischaemic stroke at any stage
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.4.9: offer aspirin 300 mg as soon as possible within 24 hours to people with acute ischaemic stroke once a diagnosis of primary intracerebral haemorrhage has been excluded by brain imaging. TIA with resolved symptoms is managed differently (aspirin immediately).

n.0: Aspirin is started early and continued for 2 weeks.
n.1: Treatment is not delayed to see if symptoms resolve.
n.3: Aspirin 300 mg is given within 24 hours once haemorrhage is excluded.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Harriet, 70, has an acute ischaemic stroke confirmed on CT, with haemorrhage excluded. Her symptoms started 3 hours ago. What is the time limit for giving thrombolysis?
o: 24 hours from onset
3 hours from onset
4.5 hours from onset
6 hours from onset
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.4 and TA990: thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of known onset once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded.

n.0: 24 hours is the extended thrombectomy window for selected people.
n.1: The licensed window was extended to 4.5 hours.
n.3: 6 hours is the standard thrombectomy window, not thrombolysis.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Clifford, 64, woke with a dense left hemiparesis. He was last known well 14 hours ago. Imaging shows a proximal anterior circulation occlusion with salvageable brain. Which treatment may still be offered?
o: Mechanical thrombectomy
IV heparin infusion
Thrombolysis with alteplase
Aspirin 300 mg and observation
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.4.6-1.4.7: thrombectomy can be offered up to 24 hours from last known well (including wake-up strokes) in selected people with potential to salvage brain tissue on imaging.

n.1: Anticoagulation is not an acute reperfusion treatment for stroke.
n.2: He is beyond the 4.5-hour thrombolysis window.
n.3: Aspirin is given, but thrombectomy can still be offered within 24 hours.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Thomas, 68, is being assessed for thrombolysis after an ischaemic stroke. His blood pressure is 196/112 mmHg. What blood pressure should be achieved before thrombolysis?
o: 140/90 mmHg or lower
220/120 mmHg or lower
160/100 mmHg or lower
185/110 mmHg or lower
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.5.10: consider blood pressure reduction to 185/110 mmHg or lower in people who are candidates for thrombolysis.

n.0: This is a long-term target, not the pre-thrombolysis threshold.
n.1: This is above the NG128 threshold for thrombolysis.
n.2: This is lower than NG128 requires before thrombolysis.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Edwin, 72, is on the stroke unit after an acute ischaemic stroke. He has type 2 diabetes. Within what range should his blood glucose be maintained?
o: 4 to 11 mmol/L
7 to 14 mmol/L
6 to 12 mmol/L
4 to 7 mmol/L
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.5.2: maintain blood glucose between 4 and 11 mmol/L in people with acute stroke.

n.1: Levels above 11 mmol/L are linked with worse stroke outcomes.
n.2: This is not the NG128 range for acute stroke.
n.3: This tighter range is not the NG128 target in acute stroke.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Margot, 75, is 6 hours into an acute ischaemic stroke. Her SpO2 is 93% on air and she has no lung disease. What is the most appropriate oxygen management?
o: Give supplemental oxygen as her SpO2 is below 95%
Withhold oxygen as routine oxygen is not used in stroke
Give 15 L/min via reservoir mask to protect the brain
Give oxygen aiming for 88-92% to limit oxygen toxicity
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.5.1: give supplemental oxygen only if oxygen saturation drops below 95%; routine use in people who are not hypoxic is not recommended. BTS target 94-98%.

n.1: Routine oxygen is not used, but she is below the 95% threshold.
n.2: High-concentration oxygen is not advised in non-critical stroke.
n.3: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnia, which she is not.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Henry, 71, has an acute ischaemic stroke; CT has excluded haemorrhage. He failed his swallow screen and has no enteral tube. He was not thrombolysed. How should his prescribed aspirin 300 mg be given?
o: Orally, dispersed in thickened water
Withheld until a speech and language assessment
Orally as a 75 mg dose with sips of water
Rectally, as he is not safe to swallow
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: he cannot take anything orally after failing the screen, and aspirin is due within 24 hours. NICE NG128 1.4.9: give aspirin 300 mg orally if no dysphagia, otherwise rectally or by enteral tube, and continue daily for 2 weeks.

n.0: He failed the screen, so nothing is given orally until assessed.
n.1: Delaying aspirin loses its early benefit; another route is used.
n.2: The dose is 300 mg and the oral route is unsafe.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Peggy, 77, is 10 hours into an acute stroke and needs help to move. Her condition is stable. A physiotherapy student plans an intensive walking session today. What is the best guidance?
o: Keep her flat in bed until her swallow is assessed
Sit her out but avoid high-intensity mobilising for 24 hours
Keep her on bed rest for 48 hours before any mobilising
Proceed, as intensive early walking improves recovery
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.7.2-1.7.3: help people with acute stroke to sit out of bed, stand or walk as soon as their clinical condition permits, but do not offer high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours to those who need help to move.

n.0: Swallow status does not dictate mobilisation; positioning is individual.
n.2: NICE supports sitting out and early help to move when her condition allows.
n.3: High-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours is not recommended.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Alan, 66, has a primary intracerebral haemorrhage that started 3 hours ago. His blood pressure is 196/104 mmHg. Rapid lowering is planned. Which target and rate are correct?
o: 185/110 mmHg or lower, the same as before thrombolysis
Systolic 140 or lower, falling no more than 60 mmHg in 1 hour
Systolic 120 mmHg or lower within the first hour
No lowering for the first 24 hours to protect cerebral perfusion
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: haemorrhage within 6 hours with systolic 150-220 qualifies for rapid lowering. NICE NG128 1.5: aim for systolic 140 mmHg or lower, without the fall exceeding 60 mmHg within 1 hour of starting treatment.

n.0: 185/110 applies to thrombolysis candidates, not haemorrhage.
n.2: Too low and too fast; NICE limits the fall to 60 mmHg in 1 hour.
n.3: NICE recommends rapid lowering within 6 hours of haemorrhage onset.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Lewis, 70, was admitted an hour ago with an acute stroke. He has not yet had a swallow screen. He asks for a cup of tea and says he feels fine. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Offer small sips of tea while you watch him closely for coughing
Explain he needs a swallow screen before anything to eat or drink
Offer the tea once he is sitting fully upright
Offer the tea thickened to reduce the choking risk
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.6.1: people with acute stroke should have their swallowing screened by a specially trained healthcare professional before being given any oral food, fluid or medication.

n.0: Even small sips are oral intake and can be aspirated silently.
n.2: Positioning does not replace a swallow screen.
n.3: Thickening is guided by a specialist assessment; nothing is given before the screen.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Iris, 74, has had a stroke and her swallow screen is not yet done. Her usual oral medicines, including atorvastatin and amlodipine, are due on the morning round. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the tablets with thickened fluid
Give the tablets with small sips of water
Crush the tablets and give them in a spoonful of yoghurt instead
Withhold oral doses, arrange the screen and ask about other routes
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.6.1: no oral food, fluid or medication before a swallow screen. Withhold, document the reason, arrange the screen promptly and discuss essential medicines and alternative routes with the prescriber.

n.0: Thickened fluids are not used before a screen and specialist advice.
n.1: No oral medication is given before the swallow screen.
n.2: Crushing changes the medicine and is still oral intake before the screen.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Ronald, 68, failed his swallow screen after an acute stroke. By when should he have a specialist swallowing assessment?
o: Within 24 hours of admission, and not more than 72 hours
Within 7 days of admission, once his condition is stable
At the next weekday speech and language clinic
Within 4 hours of admission
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.6.2: people with suspected swallowing difficulty after screening should have a specialist assessment, preferably within 24 hours of admission and not more than 72 hours afterwards.

n.1: 7 days is too long; NG128 sets 24 hours (72 at most).
n.2: The timeframe is fixed from admission, not from clinic days.
n.3: 4 hours is the swallow screen standard, not the specialist assessment.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Kathleen, 79, cannot take adequate nutrition by mouth after a stroke. She was admitted this morning. When should nasogastric tube feeding be started?
o: Within 24 hours of admission
After 7 days if oral intake has not improved
Within 72 hours of admission
Once a gastrostomy has been considered
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.6.4: people with acute stroke who are unable to take adequate nutrition and fluids orally should receive tube feeding with a nasogastric tube within 24 hours of admission.

n.1: NICE does not wait 7 days; feeding starts within 24 hours.
n.2: 72 hours is the outer limit for specialist swallow assessment, not feeding.
n.3: A gastrostomy is considered later if NG feeding is not tolerated.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: A healthcare assistant offers to carry out the swallow screen for Philip, 66, who has just been admitted with a stroke. She has not done the swallow screening training. Who should carry out the screen?
o: The healthcare assistant, supervised by a nurse
The admitting doctor as part of the admission clerking
A healthcare professional trained in swallow screening
Any registered nurse working on the stroke unit
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.6.1: swallowing should be screened by a specially trained healthcare professional before any oral intake.

n.0: Supervision does not replace the specific training required.
n.1: Clerking does not make the doctor trained in the screening tool.
n.3: Registration alone is not enough; the screener must be specially trained.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Doris, 71, passed her swallow screen after a stroke and is having a soft diet. During lunch she coughs after each mouthful and her voice sounds wet and gurgly. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage her to eat more slowly and to finish the rest of the meal
Record it and mention it at the next handover
Offer a drink of water to clear her throat
Stop the meal, sit her upright and refer for specialist assessment
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Assess then act: coughing and a wet voice when eating suggest aspiration. Stop oral intake, sit her upright and refer for specialist swallowing assessment (NICE NG128 1.6.2).

n.0: Continued feeding with signs of aspiration risks pneumonia.
n.1: Signs of aspiration need action now, not at handover.
n.2: Thin fluids can be aspirated more easily than food.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Albert, 73, has had an ischaemic stroke and is fed through a nasogastric tube that has been confirmed in position. Aspirin 300 mg is due. He is not safe to swallow. What is the most appropriate route?
o: Via the nasogastric tube, in dispersible form
By subcutaneous injection
Orally with a spoon of thickened yoghurt
Withheld until he passes a swallow screen
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG128 1.4.9: aspirin 300 mg is given orally if there is no dysphagia, or rectally or by enteral tube if there is. A confirmed NG tube allows a dispersible preparation.

n.1: Aspirin is not given subcutaneously.
n.2: He is not safe to swallow, so oral intake is unsuitable.
n.3: Aspirin should not be delayed when an enteral route is available.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Frank, 76, failed his swallow screen 8 hours ago after a stroke and is nil by mouth. He has no IV fluids or tube feeding prescribed. His mouth is dry and he has passed little urine. What should the nurse do?
o: Offer ice chips to suck to keep him hydrated
Wait for the speech and language therapy review tomorrow morning
Ask the medical team to prescribe hydration by another route
Give small sips of water to relieve his thirst
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Assess then act: dry mouth and low urine output show dehydration. Nil by mouth after a failed screen (NG128 1.6.1) means hydration must come from another route (IV or tube); the nurse escalates for a prescription.

n.0: Ice chips are oral intake and do not meet his fluid needs.
n.1: Delay risks dehydration and AKI; hydration is needed now.
n.3: He is nil by mouth after failing the screen; sips risk aspiration.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Derek, 54, has a clinic blood pressure of 152/94 mmHg, confirmed by a second reading in the same visit. He has no symptoms and no signs of target organ damage. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Diagnose stage 1 hypertension and start an antihypertensive
Recheck his clinic blood pressure again in 12 months
Offer ambulatory monitoring to confirm the diagnosis
Refer him for same-day specialist assessment
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG136 1.2: if clinic blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg or higher, offer ABPM (or HBPM if ABPM is unsuitable) to confirm the diagnosis.

n.0: NICE NG136 requires ABPM or HBPM confirmation before diagnosis at this level.
n.1: A clinic reading of 140/90 or higher needs prompt out-of-office confirmation, not a yearly recheck.
n.3: Same-day referral is for 180/120 or higher with red flags; his reading is below this.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Following a raised clinic reading, Hannah, 49, wears an ambulatory monitor. Her average daytime ABPM reading is 138/86 mmHg. How should this result be interpreted?
o: It is below the threshold, so hypertension is excluded
It shows severe hypertension needing urgent review
It confirms stage 2 hypertension
It confirms stage 1 hypertension
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG136: hypertension is confirmed if the ABPM daytime average (or HBPM average) is 135/85 mmHg or higher. Stage 1 = ABPM 135/85 to 149/94.

n.0: The ABPM diagnostic threshold is 135/85, which she exceeds.
n.1: Severe hypertension is a clinic reading of 180/120 or higher.
n.2: Stage 2 needs an ABPM average of 150/95 or higher.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Albert, 79, has had two falls and says he feels dizzy when he gets up. You are asked to check for postural hypotension. Which technique is correct?
o: Measure lying in each arm and compare the two readings
Measure sitting, then again immediately after he stands up
Measure lying, then again after standing for at least 1 minute
Measure standing, then again after lying for 5 minutes
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: NICE NG136 1.1.5-1.1.6: in people with symptoms such as falls or postural dizziness, measure blood pressure lying (or seated) and then after standing for at least 1 minute.

n.0: Comparing arms checks for an inter-arm difference, not postural change.
n.1: NICE asks for a reading after standing for at least 1 minute, not immediately.
n.3: The sequence is lying (or seated) first, then standing.

Cardiovascular & Stroke.q: Doris, 82, has postural dizziness. Her lying blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg. After standing for 1 minute it is 118/74 mmHg. How should this be interpreted?
o: Significant, because her standing systolic is below 120 mmHg
Not significant, because the diastolic fell by 6 mmHg
Not significant until she has stood for 10 minutes
Significant postural hypotension, with a systolic fall of 24 mmHg
Cardiovascular & Stroke.w: Two steps: systolic fall = 142 - 118 = 24 mmHg; diastolic fall = 80 - 74 = 6 mmHg. NICE NG136 1.1.7: a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, or a diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more, is significant postural hypotension.

n.0: The criterion is the size of the fall, not an absolute standing value.
n.1: A systolic fall of 20 or more is significant even if the diastolic fall is under 10.
n.2: NICE uses a reading after at least 1 minute of standing.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Tom, 30, has type 1 diabetes on a basal-bolus regimen and is admitted with leg cellulitis. He is alert, eating normally and has managed his insulin for 15 years. He asks to keep giving his own injections. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion while he is unwell
Explain that ward nurses must give all insulin while he is an inpatient
Withhold his mealtime insulin until the infection is controlled
Check he is willing, able and safe, then support self-administration
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG17 (1.13.6, 1.13.8) says inpatients with type 1 diabetes should be enabled to self-administer subcutaneous insulin if willing and able and it is safe, respecting their personal expertise. Because he is eating, subcutaneous insulin is appropriate (1.13.5).

n.0: IV insulin is for people unable to eat, missing more than one meal or with unpredictable glucose; Tom is eating.
n.1: This removes self-management from a capable adult, against NG17 recommendations on inpatient care.
n.2: Infection usually raises glucose; omitting mealtime insulin risks hyperglycaemia and ketosis.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Priya, 52, has type 1 diabetes and will be nil by mouth for at least 24 hours after emergency bowel surgery. She normally takes insulin glargine at night and insulin aspart with meals. Which insulin plan is most appropriate while she cannot eat?
o: Her usual aspart and glargine doses given subcutaneously
Intravenous insulin infusion, with her glargine continued
Intravenous insulin infusion, with her usual glargine stopped
Glargine continued, with aspart given if glucose exceeds 12 mmol/L
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: she will miss more than one meal, so NICE NG17 (1.13.3) advises intravenous insulin; NG17 (1.13.4) and JBDS advise continuing the person's basal insulin alongside it, which prevents ketosis if the infusion is interrupted.

n.0: Mealtime aspart given while nil by mouth would cause hypoglycaemia.
n.2: Stopping basal insulin risks rebound hyperglycaemia and DKA when the infusion stops or is interrupted.
n.3: Correction doses alone give unpredictable control when more than one meal will be missed; IV insulin is indicated.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Leah, 27, has type 1 diabetes. She phones the ward helpline saying she has had diarrhoea and vomiting since last night, is not eating and her glucose is 16 mmol/L. She plans to skip her insulin until she can eat. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop insulin until vomiting settles, sipping sugary drinks meanwhile
Keep taking insulin, check blood ketones and seek urgent help if raised
Omit long-acting insulin and continue mealtime doses with fluids
Halve all insulin doses and recheck glucose in 24 hours
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Insulin must not be stopped during illness: insulin deficiency drives ketone production. NICE NG17 (1.7.23, 1.10.1) recommends sick-day rules including ketone monitoring, and vomiting with raised ketones needs urgent assessment for DKA.

n.0: Stopping insulin while vomiting is a classic route into diabetic ketoacidosis.
n.2: Basal insulin is the dose that suppresses ketogenesis; omitting it is the most dangerous change.
n.3: Halving doses with a 24-hour wait ignores rising glucose and the need to check ketones now.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Martin, 61, has had type 1 diabetes for 35 years. At his annual review he says he no longer feels shaky or sweaty before a hypo and twice needed his wife's help this year. His Gold score indicates impaired awareness. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Repeat the Gold score at next year's annual review
Relax his glucose targets so that his readings run higher
Advise him to eat a carbohydrate snack before every insulin dose
Review his regimen and offer real-time continuous glucose monitoring
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG17 (1.9.4-1.9.8) advises reviewing insulin regimen and structured education and prioritising ways to avoid hypoglycaemia, including an insulin pump or real-time CGM, for impaired awareness. NG17 (1.9.6) says avoid relaxing individualised targets.

n.0: He has had two severe episodes needing help; waiting a year delays action on a significant risk.
n.1: NG17 1.9.6 specifically advises against relaxing individualised targets to address impaired awareness.
n.2: Routine extra snacks cause weight gain and erratic glucose without addressing the cause.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Rashid, 56, was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes last year. He manages it with diet and modified-release metformin and has had no hypoglycaemia. He asks the practice nurse what HbA1c he should aim for. Which target is recommended?
o: 58 mmol/mol (7.5%)
53 mmol/mol (7.0%)
48 mmol/mol (6.5%)
64 mmol/mol (8.0%)
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.5.7, amended 2026) supports adults managed by diet and healthy living, with or without medicines not associated with hypoglycaemia such as metformin, to aim for an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%).

n.0: 58 mmol/mol is the level at which NG28 advises intensifying treatment, not the target.
n.1: 53 mmol/mol applies to people taking a medicine associated with hypoglycaemia, such as a sulfonylurea or insulin.
n.3: 64 mmol/mol is not an NG28 target; it would leave Rashid at higher risk of complications.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Brenda, 63, has type 2 diabetes and takes gliclazide alongside metformin. She has had two mild hypos this year, both self-treated. She asks what HbA1c level she should now be aiming for. Which target should the nurse discuss with her?
o: 42 mmol/mol (6.0%)
48 mmol/mol (6.5%)
58 mmol/mol (7.5%)
53 mmol/mol (7.0%)
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.5.7) advises that adults taking a medicine associated with hypoglycaemia, such as a sulfonylurea like gliclazide, aim for an HbA1c of 53 mmol/mol (7.0%), agreed individually.

n.0: 42 mmol/mol is in the non-diabetic range and is not an NG28 target; it would increase hypoglycaemia.
n.1: 48 mmol/mol is for people on diet or medicines not associated with hypoglycaemia; it would raise Brenda's hypo risk.
n.2: 58 mmol/mol is the threshold for intensifying treatment, not her target.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Kofi, 49, has newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. His HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol on treatment started today. He asks how often his HbA1c will be checked. What should the nurse tell him?
o: Every 12 months, at his annual diabetes review appointment
Every month until his result falls below 48 mmol/mol
Every 3 to 6 months until stable, then every 6 months
Every 2 years once he is settled on medication
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.5.1) recommends measuring HbA1c every 3 to 6 months, tailored to need, until stable on unchanging therapy, then every 6 months.

n.0: Annual testing is too infrequent while treatment is being adjusted after diagnosis.
n.1: HbA1c reflects about 2 to 3 months of glycaemia, so monthly testing gives little new information.
n.3: Two-yearly testing would miss deterioration and is not an NG28 interval.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Jean, 58, has just been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. She is anxious about what changes she needs to make and asks how she can learn to manage the condition. According to NICE, what should the nurse offer first?
o: A printed leaflet, with education offered if HbA1c rises
Referral to a dietitian for a low-sugar meal plan
A group structured education programme, reinforced each year
Advice to buy foods marketed for people with diabetes
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.2.1, 1.2.4) says offer structured education at diagnosis with annual reinforcement and review, with group programmes as the preferred option and an equivalent alternative for those who cannot attend.

n.0: Education is an integral part of care from diagnosis, not something offered after deterioration.
n.1: Dietary advice is individualised and integrated, but it is not a substitute for structured education.
n.3: NG28 (1.3.8) discourages the use of foods marketed specifically for people with diabetes.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Marek, 52, has newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c of 61 mmol/mol. He has no heart failure, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease or frailty. Following the 2026 NICE update, which initial medicines plan is recommended?
o: Standard metformin alone, adding a second drug at 3 months
A DPP-4 inhibitor alone, adding metformin if needed
Metformin and a sulfonylurea started together
Modified-release metformin and an SGLT-2 inhibitor together
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.13.1, 2026) recommends offering modified-release metformin and an SGLT-2 inhibitor as initial therapy for adults with no relevant comorbidity, replacing the older metformin-first stepwise sequence.

n.0: This is the pre-2026 stepwise approach; NG28 now starts both medicines together.
n.1: DPP-4 inhibitors are reserved for situations such as low eGFR or frailty, not first-line in Marek.
n.2: Sulfonylureas carry hypoglycaemia risk and are not part of the recommended initial pair.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Colin, 64, had a myocardial infarction two years ago and is now diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 66 mmol/mol. He tolerates metformin. Which initial medicines plan does the 2026 NICE guideline recommend?
o: Metformin, a DPP-4 inhibitor and weekly semaglutide
Modified-release metformin, an SGLT-2 inhibitor and weekly semaglutide
Metformin and an SGLT-2 inhibitor, adding semaglutide if HbA1c stays above 58
Modified-release metformin with pioglitazone for cardiac protection
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.15.1, 2026) recommends that adults with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease are offered modified-release metformin, an SGLT-2 inhibitor and subcutaneous semaglutide up to 1 mg weekly for cardiovascular, renal and glycaemic benefit from the start.

n.0: NG28 1.24.6 advises against combining a GLP-1 receptor agonist with a DPP-4 inhibitor.
n.2: Semaglutide is offered at the outset for its cardiovascular benefit, not held back until HbA1c fails to fall.
n.3: Pioglitazone is not part of the recommended initial regimen in cardiovascular disease.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Edith, 84, has type 2 diabetes, moderate frailty, two falls this year and a lying-to-standing systolic drop of 22 mmHg. She takes modified-release metformin; HbA1c is 60 mmol/mol. The team considers adding an SGLT-2 inhibitor. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Add an SGLT-2 inhibitor and aim for an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol
Add an SGLT-2 inhibitor and aim for HbA1c 53 mmol/mol
Switch to gliclazide and aim for HbA1c 53 mmol/mol
Continue metformin and agree a relaxed individual HbA1c target
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: NG28 (1.19.1) offers an SGLT-2 inhibitor in frailty only if it will not cause adverse events such as volume depletion or hypotension, which Edith already has. NG28 (1.5.9) supports relaxing the HbA1c target in older, frailer people at risk of falls.

n.0: An SGLT-2 inhibitor risks volume depletion with her postural drop, and a tight target raises hypo and falls risk.
n.1: The SGLT-2 inhibitor remains unsafe given her postural hypotension and falls.
n.2: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia, which increases falls risk in frailty.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ahmed, 47, has type 2 diabetes managed with modified-release metformin and dapagliflozin. He does not drive for work and has never had a hypo. He asks for a glucose meter to test daily. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Advise testing once a week to track his response to treatment
Explain routine self-testing is not recommended on his medicines
Provide a meter and advise testing before each main meal
Provide a meter and advise testing each morning before breakfast
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.6.2) does not routinely recommend capillary self-monitoring in type 2 diabetes unless the person uses insulin, has hypoglycaemia, takes oral medicines that may cause hypos while driving or operating machinery, or is pregnant or planning pregnancy. HbA1c monitors his control.

n.0: Weekly snapshots do not reliably show response; HbA1c is the monitoring measure.
n.2: Pre-meal testing suits insulin dose adjustment, which Ahmed does not need.
n.3: Daily fasting checks are not routinely indicated on medicines that do not cause hypoglycaemia.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Joan, 70, has type 2 diabetes on insulin and is an inpatient on a medical ward. At 11:00 she feels sweaty and shaky; her capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. She is alert, cooperative and able to swallow. What should the nurse give first?
o: 1 mg glucagon intramuscularly
A 200 mL glass of semi-skimmed milk
Two plain biscuits
150 to 200 mL of pure fruit juice
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023) algorithm A: a conscious, cooperative adult below 4.0 mmol/L should have 15 to 20 g of rapid-acting carbohydrate, such as 150 to 200 mL pure fruit juice, 5 to 7 glucose tablets or a 60 mL glucose juice shot.

n.0: Glucagon is for people who cannot safely take oral treatment or who fail 3 oral cycles.
n.1: Milk is a follow-up long-acting carbohydrate; it raises glucose too slowly as first treatment.
n.2: Biscuits are the long-acting carbohydrate given after glucose is back above 4.0 mmol/L, not the initial treatment.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Sam, 58, with type 1 diabetes, has just been given glucose tablets for a capillary glucose of 3.4 mmol/L on the ward. He is alert and talking. When should the nurse recheck his capillary glucose?
o: After 60 minutes
After 10 to 15 minutes
After 30 to 45 minutes
At the next routine check before his meal
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023): recheck capillary glucose 10 to 15 minutes after rapid-acting carbohydrate; if still below 4.0 mmol/L repeat treatment, up to 3 cycles in total.

n.0: An hour delays repeat treatment if the first dose has not worked.
n.2: 30 to 45 minutes is the point at which medical help is called if glucose is still below 4.0 after repeated cycles.
n.3: Waiting for a routine check could leave hypoglycaemia untreated and worsening.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Arthur, 76, has type 2 diabetes on insulin and chronic kidney disease, with a low-potassium diet. His capillary glucose is 3.3 mmol/L; he is alert and able to swallow. The ward hypo box contains several options. Which is most appropriate?
o: 150 to 200 mL of pure orange juice
A 60 mL bottle of glucose juice shot
Two slices of toast with butter
A 200 mL glass of semi-skimmed milk
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023) advises 15 to 20 g rapid-acting carbohydrate, and says do not use fruit juice for people on a low-potassium diet because of its potassium content. A 60 mL glucose juice shot provides suitable rapid-acting glucose.

n.0: JBDS 01 advises against fruit juice for people on a low-potassium diet such as in CKD.
n.2: Toast is slow-release carbohydrate used after recovery, not to correct the hypo.
n.3: Milk is a follow-up long-acting carbohydrate and contains potassium.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Maureen, 67, has type 2 diabetes treated with insulin and acarbose. Her capillary glucose is 3.5 mmol/L and she is alert. Which first treatment is most appropriate?
o: 5 to 7 glucose tablets
A 300 mL glass of milk
Two digestive biscuits with a cup of tea
3 to 4 heaped teaspoons of sugar dissolved in water
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023): sugar dissolved in water is ineffective in people taking acarbose because acarbose blocks breakdown of sucrose to glucose. Glucose tablets supply glucose directly as the 15 to 20 g rapid-acting carbohydrate.

n.1: Milk is a follow-up long-acting carbohydrate, not first treatment.
n.2: Biscuits are slow-release carbohydrate for after recovery and also need digestion.
n.3: Acarbose prevents sucrose being broken down to glucose, so sugar in water is ineffective.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Frank, 81, has type 2 diabetes on insulin. He is found confused and pushing staff away; capillary glucose is 2.6 mmol/L. He is conscious and able to swallow but will not take a drink. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
o: 100 mL of 20% glucose intravenously by the nurse
Two plain biscuits placed within his reach
Two tubes of 40% glucose gel squeezed between teeth and gums
150 to 200 mL fruit juice given by the nurse from a beaker
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023) algorithm B: a conscious adult who is confused or uncooperative but able to swallow should be given 1.5 to 2 tubes of 40% glucose gel between the teeth and gums, or IM glucagon 1 mg if gel is not possible.

n.0: IV glucose is for unconscious people or failed oral treatment and needs medical prescription or PGD and access.
n.1: Slow-release carbohydrate does not treat a hypo and he is unlikely to eat it.
n.3: He is refusing drinks; forcing fluid risks aspiration and is unlikely to work.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Lorna, 55, is on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion after surgery and is eating small amounts. Her capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L and she is alert and able to swallow. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Halve the infusion rate and give 15 to 20 g rapid-acting carbohydrate
Stop the infusion until the medical team reviews her next morning
Stop the infusion, treat the hypo, then restart once above 4.0 mmol/L
Continue the infusion and give two tubes of glucose gel
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023): if an insulin infusion is in situ, stop it immediately, treat the hypoglycaemia, and restart once it has been treated (most VRIIIs restart once glucose is above 4.0 mmol/L), reviewing the rate with medical advice.

n.0: JBDS advises stopping, not reducing, the infusion while the hypo is treated.
n.1: Leaving the infusion off overnight risks hyperglycaemia and ketosis; it is restarted once treated.
n.3: Continuing the insulin infusion during a hypo drives glucose lower.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Kenneth, 72, has type 2 diabetes on twice-daily mixed insulin. At 16:00 he had a hypo of 3.0 mmol/L, treated with juice; at 16:15 his glucose is 5.6 mmol/L and he is well. His evening insulin and meal are due at 17:30. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Omit his evening insulin and recheck glucose at bedtime
Give half the evening insulin dose without a meal and recheck at 22:00
Give a snack now, give his evening insulin, and request a dose review
Start a variable rate infusion to stabilise his glucose overnight
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: after recovery JBDS 01 advises a 20 g long-acting carbohydrate snack (or the next meal), then states do not omit the next insulin injection if due, because it is unlikely to be the dose that caused the hypo; the active dose should be reviewed by the medical or diabetes team.

n.0: JBDS 01 specifically warns against omitting the next insulin dose, which risks hyperglycaemia and ketosis.
n.1: Insulin given without food after a hypo invites a further episode; dose changes are for the prescriber.
n.3: JBDS 01 advises against starting a VRIII to stabilise glucose after a treated hypo.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Hilda, 84, with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide and an eGFR of 28, had a hypo of 2.8 mmol/L on admission that was treated successfully. She is now eating. What is the most important ongoing nursing action?
o: Recheck glucose when she reports symptoms of a hypo
Recheck glucose once at 1 hour, then resume her usual checks
Give her usual gliclazide dose with breakfast tomorrow
Continue regular glucose monitoring for at least 24 to 48 hours
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 01 (2023): hypoglycaemia from a sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin may persist or recur for up to 24 to 36 hours, especially with renal impairment, so capillary monitoring should continue for at least 24 to 48 hours and the prescriber should review the dose.

n.0: Older people often have reduced warning symptoms, so waiting for symptoms is unsafe.
n.1: A single recheck misses recurrent hypoglycaemia from a long-acting sulfonylurea in renal impairment.
n.2: The dose active at the time of the hypo should be reviewed before it is given again.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Chloe, 19, has type 1 diabetes and presents with vomiting and abdominal pain. Four sets of venous results are reviewed during the shift. Which set meets the JBDS criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis?
o: Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 1.4 mmol/L, pH 7.34
Glucose 34 mmol/L, ketones 0.9 mmol/L, pH 7.36
Glucose 9 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, pH 7.29
Glucose 18 mmol/L, ketones 4.2 mmol/L, pH 7.21
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 02 (2023) requires all three: glucose above 11.0 mmol/L or known diabetes, blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L (or ketonuria 2+), and bicarbonate below 15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3.

n.0: Ketones of 1.4 mmol/L and a pH of 7.34 do not meet the ketonaemia or acidosis criteria.
n.1: Very high glucose with low ketones and normal pH suggests HHS, not DKA.
n.2: There is no ketonaemia; the low pH needs another explanation.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ben, 26, weighs 80 kg and is diagnosed with DKA. A fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion is prescribed using 50 units of soluble insulin in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride at the JBDS standard rate. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 0.8 mL/hour
8 mL/hour
4 mL/hour
10 mL/hour
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: JBDS 02 sets the FRIII at 0.1 units/kg/hour, so 80 kg x 0.1 = 8 units/hour. The syringe holds 1 unit per mL (50 units in 50 mL), so the rate is 8 mL/hour.

n.0: 0.8 mL/hour is a tenfold decimal error.
n.2: 4 mL/hour equals 0.05 units/kg/hour, the reduced rate considered once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L.
n.3: 10 mL/hour would deliver 0.125 units/kg/hour, above the JBDS fixed rate.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Rhys, 34, with type 1 diabetes, is on a fixed-rate insulin infusion for DKA. At 21:00 his usual subcutaneous insulin glargine is due. A colleague suggests leaving it as he is already receiving IV insulin. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give his usual glargine dose at the normal time
Withhold the glargine until the infusion is stopped
Withhold the glargine and increase the infusion rate
Give half the glargine dose and record the reason
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 02 (2023) and its nursing guide state that the person's usual long-acting basal insulin should continue alongside the FRIII. This prevents rebound ketosis when the infusion stops and smooths the transition back to subcutaneous insulin.

n.1: Stopping basal insulin causes rebound hyperglycaemia and ketosis when the IV infusion is discontinued.
n.2: The infusion rate is fixed by weight; withholding basal insulin to compensate is not the protocol.
n.3: JBDS advises continuing the usual basal dose; an unprescribed reduction is not appropriate.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Nadia, 23, is being treated for DKA. Her first litre of 0.9% sodium chloride has run in. The next litre is due and her serum potassium is now 4.2 mmol/L. According to the JBDS protocol, how much potassium chloride should the next litre contain?
o: 20 mmol
None
40 mmol
Senior review for additional potassium
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 02 (2023) potassium guide: above 5.5 mmol/L give none; 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L give 40 mmol per litre; below 3.5 mmol/L senior review because more is needed. Insulin drives potassium into cells, so levels fall during treatment.

n.0: 20 mmol per litre is not the JBDS replacement for a potassium of 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L.
n.1: No potassium is added when the level is above 5.5 mmol/L.
n.3: Senior review for extra potassium applies when the level falls below 3.5 mmol/L.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Aled, 41, has DKA and is on a fixed-rate insulin infusion with 0.9% sodium chloride. His glucose has fallen to 12.8 mmol/L; ketones are 2.1 mmol/L and falling. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Add 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour alongside the insulin infusion
Stop the sodium chloride and run 5% glucose at 125 mL/hour
Stop the insulin infusion and give his usual rapid-acting insulin
Switch to a variable rate infusion guided by the glucose level
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 02 (2023): when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour and consider reducing insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour. Insulin is still needed to clear ketones, which are still raised.

n.1: JBDS uses 10% glucose alongside continuing sodium chloride, not 5% glucose in place of it.
n.2: Ketones are 2.1 mmol/L; stopping insulin before resolution allows ketoacidosis to return.
n.3: A VRIII titrates to glucose and would cut insulin while ketones still need clearing.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ella, 30, has been treated for DKA for 14 hours. Her latest venous gas and capillary results are reviewed by the nurse before the next medical round. Which results show that the DKA has resolved?
o: Ketones 1.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.32
Bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 9.4 mmol/L
Glucose 7.8 mmol/L, eating and drinking
Ketones 0.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.35
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 02 (2023) defines resolution as blood ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH above 7.3. Bicarbonate alone and glucose are not used to judge resolution.

n.0: Ketones of 1.2 mmol/L are above the 0.6 mmol/L resolution threshold.
n.1: Bicarbonate can stay low from hyperchloraemia, and glucose does not reflect acidosis clearance.
n.2: Glucose and eating do not confirm that ketoacidosis has cleared.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Gareth, 37, is on a fixed-rate insulin infusion for DKA. Over the last hour his blood ketones have fallen from 4.6 to 4.4 mmol/L and glucose has barely changed. What should the nurse do first?
o: Check the pump and line, then inform the prescriber
Increase the infusion by 1 unit/hour and recheck in an hour
Give a subcutaneous bolus of rapid-acting insulin
Recheck ketones in 2 hours, as early falls are often slow
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: JBDS 02 targets a ketone fall of at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour. The nursing guide says if ketones and glucose are not falling as expected, first check the pump is working and connected, then call a prescribing clinician to increase the rate.

n.1: The rate is increased by the prescribing clinician after equipment problems are excluded.
n.2: Extra subcutaneous insulin is not part of the JBDS DKA protocol.
n.3: JBDS expects at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour; waiting 2 hours delays correcting a failing treatment.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Doris, 78, has type 2 diabetes and is drowsy and dehydrated. Glucose is 42 mmol/L, ketones 0.8 mmol/L, pH 7.36, calculated osmolality 345 mOsm/kg. HHS is diagnosed. Which initial treatment is most appropriate?
o: Fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour with 0.9% sodium chloride
0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour, insulin held while glucose falls
10% glucose at 125 mL/hour with a variable rate insulin infusion
0.45% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour, then insulin
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 06 (2022): HHS is treated with fluid first, using 0.9% sodium chloride (1 L over the first hour), aiming for gradual falls in osmolality (3.0 to 8.0 mOsm/kg/hour) and glucose (no more than 5 mmol/L/hour). Insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) starts once glucose stops falling with fluids alone, unless significantly ketonaemic.

n.0: Early insulin at the DKA rate causes rapid osmotic shifts; HHS uses fluid first and a lower insulin rate.
n.2: Glucose and VRIII are not initial HHS treatment; the priority is replacing lost fluid.
n.3: 0.45% sodium chloride is used only if osmolality is not falling despite adequate positive fluid balance.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Pauline, 62, has type 2 diabetes treated with modified-release metformin and empagliflozin. She phones the practice nurse with diarrhoea and vomiting since yesterday and is struggling to keep fluids down. What sick-day advice is most appropriate?
o: Pause both medicines until she is eating and drinking normally
Stop metformin but continue empagliflozin with extra fluids
Continue both medicines and double her usual fluid intake
Pause empagliflozin but continue metformin with extra fluids
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.10.1, 2026) says sick-day rules should state which medicines to stop when there is a risk of dehydration, vomiting and diarrhoea, naming metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors, and how to restart them after recovery.

n.1: SGLT-2 inhibitors raise the risk of DKA and volume depletion when dehydrated, so empagliflozin is paused too.
n.2: Continuing both while dehydrated risks AKI, lactic acidosis with metformin and DKA with the SGLT-2 inhibitor.
n.3: Metformin is also paused during dehydrating illness because of the risk with reduced kidney function.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Stuart, 55, has type 2 diabetes treated with dapagliflozin. He is admitted with two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. Capillary glucose is 11.2 mmol/L and blood ketones 3.9 mmol/L; he is breathing deeply. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage oral fluids and recheck his ketones in the morning
Give his next dapagliflozin dose and monitor as gastroenteritis
Escalate urgently as possible DKA and request a venous gas
Reassure him that his glucose is close to his usual range
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 03 and MHRA advice warn that DKA with an SGLT-2 inhibitor can present with only moderately raised glucose. Ketones above 3.0 mmol/L with vomiting and deep breathing need urgent escalation and a venous gas to confirm acidosis (JBDS 02 criteria).

n.0: Ketones of 3.9 mmol/L with symptoms need assessment now, not the next morning.
n.1: The SGLT-2 inhibitor should be stopped, not continued, during acute illness with ketosis.
n.3: Near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA in people taking SGLT-2 inhibitors.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ravi, 50, has type 2 diabetes and is about to start an SGLT-2 inhibitor. While discussing it, he mentions he began a very low carbohydrate ketogenic diet last week to lose weight. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start the medicine and check urine glucose weekly
Discuss delaying the medicine until he has changed his diet
Start the medicine and advise him to drink more water each day
Explain that the diet improves its effect on weight
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG28 (1.21.1-1.21.3) says check DKA risk before starting an SGLT-2 inhibitor, including a very low carbohydrate or ketogenic diet, and address modifiable risks first; such people may need to delay treatment until they have changed their diet.

n.0: SGLT-2 inhibitors cause glycosuria by design, so urine glucose gives no safety information.
n.2: Extra water does not remove the DKA risk created by combining ketosis with an SGLT-2 inhibitor.
n.3: The combination increases DKA risk; it is not a recommended weight strategy.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Irene, 68, has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and canagliflozin. She is listed for an elective hernia repair on Thursday morning. According to the JBDS perioperative guideline, when should she stop the canagliflozin?
o: Omit it for a full week before surgery
Omit it on Thursday morning, the day of surgery
Omit it on both Wednesday and Thursday
Take it as normal and omit it after surgery
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: JBDS 03 (CPOC, 2022) medicines table: omit SGLT-2 inhibitors on the day before surgery and on the day of surgery, and check ketones daily while in hospital, restarting once eating and drinking normally and ketones are normal.

n.0: A week is longer than standard advice; longer cessation applies to special cases such as reduced-calorie diets or bowel preparation.
n.1: Omitting it on the day of surgery is not enough; JBDS 03 omits it the day before as well.
n.3: SGLT-2 inhibitors are stopped before surgery because of the risk of perioperative DKA.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Walter, 74, has type 2 diabetes and is admitted to a medical ward with pneumonia. He says his feet are fine. What foot assessment should the admitting nurse ensure is completed?
o: Examine both feet with shoes, socks and dressings removed
Arrange foot screening at his next annual diabetes review
Record his report that he has no current foot problems
Examine the feet once he is well enough to mobilise
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG19 advises examining both feet of a person with diabetes on any admission to hospital, with shoes, socks, bandages and dressings removed, to identify risk and any active problem early.

n.1: Inpatients need examination on admission; deferring to primary care leaves risk unidentified.
n.2: Self-report misses neuropathic ulcers that the person may not feel.
n.3: Immobile and acutely unwell patients are at highest risk of heel ulceration, so examination cannot wait.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Doreen, 70, with type 2 diabetes, is an inpatient after a fall. On admission foot examination the nurse finds a small, clean, shallow ulcer on her left big toe. She is afebrile, with no spreading redness and warm feet with palpable pulses. What is the most appropriate referral?
o: Refer to the foot protection service for review within 2 to 4 weeks
Refer to the community podiatrist at discharge
Refer to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours
Refer to the vascular team as an emergency
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG19 (1.1.3) says refer an inpatient with a diabetic foot problem to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours of the initial examination of the feet.

n.0: 2 to 4 weeks is the NG19 referral time for people at high risk without an active problem.
n.1: An active ulcer needs specialist assessment during the admission, not after discharge.
n.3: There are no signs of limb-threatening ischaemia or infection needing emergency vascular input.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ken, 66, has type 2 diabetes and a foot ulcer managed by district nurses. Today the ulcer is malodorous, redness is spreading up the foot, and his temperature is 38.4 C with a pulse of 108. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to start oral antibiotics and review in a week
Refer to the foot care service for triage within 1 working day
Arrange immediate acute hospital assessment and inform the foot team
Take a wound swab and redress, reviewing again in 48 hours
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG19 (1.4.1): a limb- or life-threatening diabetic foot problem, such as ulceration with fever or signs of sepsis, needs immediate referral to acute services and the multidisciplinary foot care service informed.

n.0: Fever and tachycardia suggest sepsis; oral antibiotics in the community are not sufficient.
n.1: 1 working day is the NG19 timescale for active problems that are not limb- or life-threatening.
n.3: Swabbing and delaying review for 48 hours ignores systemic signs of a spreading infection.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Albert, 79, has type 2 diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and a healed ulcer from two years ago. He is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD and is spending most of the day in bed. Which preventive foot care is most appropriate?
o: Provide a pressure redistribution device to offload his heels
Raise his knees on pillows to keep his heels off the bed
Soak his feet in warm water each day to soften the skin
Fit anti-embolism stockings to protect his lower legs
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Neuropathy with a previous ulcer places Albert at high risk (NG19 risk classification). NG19 (1.3.12) says inpatients at moderate or high risk should be given a pressure redistribution device to offload heel pressure, with referral to the foot protection service at discharge.

n.1: Pillows under the knees increase heel pressure and do not offload the heels effectively.
n.2: Soaking macerates skin and risks scalds in a person who cannot feel heat.
n.3: NICE NG89 advises against anti-embolism stockings in people with peripheral neuropathy or sensory impairment.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Harold, 77, was admitted with a chest infection. His serum creatinine was 84 micromol/L on admission and is 118 micromol/L 36 hours later. His urine output has been adequate. How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: Not AKI until creatinine exceeds the reference range
Not AKI, because creatinine has not risen by 50% from baseline
Not AKI, because his urine output is adequate
AKI, because creatinine has risen by 34 micromol/L in 36 hours
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: 118 minus 84 = 34 micromol/L within 36 hours. NICE NG148 (1.3.1) defines AKI as a creatinine rise of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours, a 50% rise within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. Any one criterion is enough.

n.0: AKI is judged on change from baseline, not on exceeding the laboratory range.
n.1: The 50% rise is an alternative criterion over 7 days; the 48-hour absolute rise is already met.
n.2: Urine output is one of several criteria; a normal output does not exclude AKI by creatinine.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ivy, 69, weighs 70 kg and has a urinary catheter after a hip fracture. Over the last 7 hours her hourly urine output has been 20 to 30 mL. Using the NICE urine output criterion, how should this be interpreted?
o: It is acceptable because hourly output is above 20 mL
It is acceptable because output is above 0.25 mL/kg/hour
It meets the AKI criterion of below 35 mL/hour for more than 6 hours
It meets the AKI criterion once 12 hours at this rate have passed
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: 0.5 mL/kg/hour x 70 kg = 35 mL/hour. NICE NG148 (1.3.1) defines AKI in adults as urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours; she has been below 35 mL/hour for 7 hours.

n.0: 20 mL/hour is not a weight-adjusted threshold and is below her 35 mL/hour minimum.
n.1: 0.25 mL/kg/hour is not the NICE threshold; the criterion is 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
n.3: 12 hours is not the adult criterion; NG148 uses more than 6 hours.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Reg, 72, is admitted with three days of diarrhoea and vomiting and a creatinine rise from 90 to 150 micromol/L. His regular medicines are ramipril, omeprazole, atorvastatin and paracetamol. Which medicine should the nurse query with the prescriber first?
o: Atorvastatin
Ramipril
Omeprazole
Paracetamol
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG148 (1.1.1, 1.2.14) lists ACE inhibitors among drugs that can cause or worsen AKI and advises considering temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in people with diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis until stable. Pharmacist advice on dosing is also recommended (1.2.13).

n.0: Atorvastatin does not reduce renal perfusion and is not in the NG148 list.
n.2: Omeprazole is not among the nephrotoxic drugs NICE asks to be paused in acute dehydrating illness.
n.3: Paracetamol at normal doses is not among the nephrotoxic drugs listed in NG148.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Joyce, 81, has a rising creatinine and AKI is suspected by the medical team. She is able to pass urine. Which investigation should the nurse carry out as soon as AKI is suspected?
o: Send a midstream urine sample if she becomes febrile
Arrange a bladder scan in 24 hours
Start a 24-hour urine collection
Perform a urine dipstick test and document the result
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG148 (1.4.2) recommends urine dipstick testing for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose in everyone as soon as AKI is suspected or detected, documenting results and acting on abnormal findings.

n.0: Dipstick testing is done at once in all suspected AKI, not delayed until fever develops.
n.1: Waiting 24 hours delays the identification of retention, an obstructive cause.
n.2: A 24-hour collection delays information and is not the NG148 initial test.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Ali, 64, weighs 80 kg and has sepsis from a chest infection. He has a catheter, and his NEWS2 is 3 with no change in the last hour. His urine output has been 25, 22 and 20 mL in the last 3 hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Flush the catheter and recheck output in 4 hours
Escalate the falling urine output to the medical team now
Increase his oral fluid encouragement and recheck at handover
Wait until he has been below 40 mL/hour for 6 hours
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: his threshold is 0.5 x 80 = 40 mL/hour and output is well below it and falling. NICE NG148 (1.2.2) requires systems to recognise and respond to oliguria because NEWS2 does not score urine output, and sepsis is an AKI risk factor; prompt escalation allows treatment before AKI is established.

n.0: Checking for a blocked catheter is reasonable, but a 4-hour delay before escalation is unsafe.
n.2: Oral fluids may help but a falling output in sepsis needs medical review, not deferral to handover.
n.3: The 6-hour figure defines AKI; waiting for it delays treatment of a deteriorating septic patient.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Mavis, 70, has AKI. Despite medical treatment her potassium remains 6.9 mmol/L, she is breathless with bilateral crackles and her urine output is minimal. Which escalation is most appropriate?
o: Ask for referral to the renal outpatient clinic after discharge
Ask for a low-dose dopamine infusion to improve renal blood flow
Ask for immediate referral for renal replacement therapy assessment
Ask for a loop diuretic and recheck urea and electrolytes tomorrow
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG148 (1.5.8, 1.5.11): refer immediately for renal replacement therapy, to a nephrologist or critical care specialist, if hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema are not responding to medical management.

n.0: Outpatient referral ignores life-threatening complications needing urgent renal replacement therapy.
n.1: NG148 (1.5.5) says do not offer low-dose dopamine to treat AKI.
n.3: Refractory hyperkalaemia with pulmonary oedema needs immediate escalation, not a next-day recheck.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Eric, 58, has AKI from dehydration after gastroenteritis. He has dry mucous membranes and low urine output. A junior doctor plans IV furosemide to increase his urine output. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Suggest a low-dose dopamine infusion as a gentler alternative
Query the plan, as loop diuretics are not used to treat AKI routinely
Give the furosemide after a bladder scan confirms an empty bladder
Give the furosemide and start hourly urine output monitoring
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG148 (1.5.3) advises against routinely offering loop diuretics to treat AKI; they are considered for fluid overload while awaiting renal replacement therapy or during recovery (1.5.4). In a dehydrated patient a diuretic worsens hypovolaemia.

n.0: Low-dose dopamine is specifically not recommended for AKI (NG148 1.5.5).
n.2: A bladder scan excludes retention but does not make a diuretic appropriate in hypovolaemia.
n.3: Giving a diuretic to a dehydrated patient worsens hypovolaemia and kidney injury.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Lionel, 75, has CKD with an eGFR of 26 and takes ramipril. He is booked for a non-urgent contrast-enhanced CT as an inpatient tomorrow. Which preparation should the nurse discuss with the team?
o: Keep him nil by mouth for 6 hours before the scan
Cancel the scan because contrast is unsafe with an eGFR below 30
Encourage oral fluids and ask whether ramipril should be paused
Ask for a loop diuretic dose before the scan
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG148 (1.2.7-1.2.9) advises encouraging oral hydration before and after contrast in people at increased risk, considering IV volume expansion if eGFR is below 30, and considering temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs if eGFR is below 30.

n.0: Fluid restriction before contrast increases the risk of contrast-associated AKI.
n.1: Contrast is not prohibited; NG148 asks for risk discussion and preventive measures.
n.3: Diuretics cause volume depletion and increase the risk of kidney injury.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Gwen, 66, had an eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73 m2 on a blood test taken while she had a urinary infection. Previous results were above 60. She asks the practice nurse whether she now has chronic kidney disease. What is the most accurate reply?
o: Yes, because a single eGFR result below 60 confirms CKD
Yes, because CKD is diagnosed on any eGFR below 90
Not yet; CKD needs an eGFR below 30 on two separate occasions
Not yet; CKD needs results that persist for 3 months or more
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 defines CKD as abnormalities of kidney function or structure, such as eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or ACR 3 mg/mmol or more, present for 3 months or more. A single low result during acute illness needs repeating and may reflect AKI.

n.0: One result, especially during acute illness, cannot show the 3-month persistence that defines CKD.
n.1: An eGFR of 60 to 89 without markers of kidney damage is not CKD.
n.2: An eGFR below 30 is category G4; CKD is diagnosed at much higher eGFR levels.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Clive, 70, has CKD. His latest results are a stable eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 and a urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) of 12 mg/mmol. Using NICE classification, which category describes his CKD?
o: G3b A2
G3b A3
G4 A2
G3a A1
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 (1.2.1) classifies CKD by GFR and ACR category: G3b is eGFR 30 to 44 and A2 is ACR 3 to 30 mg/mmol. His eGFR of 38 is G3b and ACR of 12 is A2.

n.1: A3 is ACR above 30 mg/mmol.
n.2: G4 is eGFR 15 to 29.
n.3: G3a is eGFR 45 to 59, and A1 is ACR below 3 mg/mmol.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Eileen, 59, has type 2 diabetes. The practice nurse is arranging her annual kidney check, which includes a test to detect and quantify protein in the urine. Which urine test does NICE recommend?
o: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR)
Reagent strip for protein on a random sample
24-hour urine protein collection
Urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR)
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 (1.1.12-1.1.13) recommends urine ACR rather than PCR to detect and identify proteinuria, because it is more sensitive at low levels; an ACR of 3 mg/mmol or more is clinically important.

n.1: Reagent strips are not reliable for quantifying albuminuria.
n.2: 24-hour collections are impractical and are not the recommended test.
n.3: NICE recommends ACR rather than PCR for detecting and quantifying proteinuria.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Norman, 67, has CKD without diabetes and an ACR of 20 mg/mmol. His clinic blood pressure is 146/88 mmHg. Which blood pressure target applies to him under NICE guidance?
o: Systolic below 130 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg
Systolic below 150 mmHg and diastolic below 90 mmHg
Systolic below 140 mmHg and diastolic below 90 mmHg
Systolic below 120 mmHg and diastolic below 70 mmHg
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 (1.6.x) sets a target systolic below 140 mmHg (range 120 to 139) and diastolic below 90 mmHg for adults with CKD and an ACR below 70 mg/mmol.

n.0: Below 130/80 applies when ACR is 70 mg/mmol or more.
n.1: Below 150/90 is the NG136 clinic target for people aged 80 and over without CKD considerations.
n.3: Below 120/70 is lower than any NICE CKD target and risks hypotension.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Kamala, 54, has CKD with an ACR of 95 mg/mmol. Her clinic blood pressure is 136/84 mmHg on current treatment. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: It is within her target of below 150/90 for proteinuric CKD
It is above her target of below 130/80, so treatment review is needed
It is within her target of below 140/90, so no change is needed
It needs confirming by home readings above 145/85 first
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 sets a target systolic below 130 mmHg (range 120 to 129) and diastolic below 80 mmHg when ACR is 70 mg/mmol or more. At 136/84 she is above target.

n.0: Below 150/90 is not a CKD target.
n.2: Below 140/90 applies to people with an ACR below 70 mg/mmol.
n.3: Her clinic reading already exceeds her target; 145/85 is an ABPM figure for people aged 80 and over.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Douglas, 61, has CKD with an eGFR of 48 and an ACR of 40 mg/mmol. Ramipril is to be started. His potassium today is 4.6 mmol/L. Which monitoring plan should the nurse arrange?
o: Potassium and eGFR every 3 months for the first year
Potassium and eGFR 1 to 2 weeks after starting and after dose rises
Potassium and eGFR at the next annual CKD review
Blood pressure checks at 1 week, with bloods if he feels unwell
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 (1.6.14) says measure serum potassium and eGFR before starting renin-angiotensin system antagonists in CKD and repeat between 1 and 2 weeks after starting and after each dose increase.

n.0: 3-monthly checks miss the early changes that NG203 asks to be detected at 1 to 2 weeks.
n.2: Waiting a year could miss hyperkalaemia or a large fall in eGFR after starting the drug.
n.3: Hyperkalaemia and falling eGFR are often symptomless, so bloods are needed regardless of symptoms.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Hazel, 72, has CKD and started ramipril two weeks ago. Her eGFR has fallen from 50 to 43 mL/min/1.73 m2 and potassium is 5.0 mmol/L. She feels well. Which plan is consistent with NICE guidance?
o: Stop ramipril because potassium is above 4.5 mmol/L
Stop ramipril because eGFR has fallen
Halve the ramipril dose and recheck the bloods in 3 months
Continue the same dose and repeat the tests in 1 to 2 weeks
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: Two steps: the fall is 7 of 50, or 14%, below the 25% threshold. NICE NG203 (1.6.19-1.6.20) says do not modify the dose if eGFR falls by less than 25% (or creatinine rises less than 30%) and repeat the test in 1 to 2 weeks. Potassium of 5.0 is below the 6.0 mmol/L stopping threshold.

n.0: NG203 stops RAS antagonists at potassium 6.0 mmol/L or more, not 4.5.
n.1: A fall under 25% is expected with RAS blockade and is not a reason to stop.
n.2: NG203 advises no dose change for a fall under 25%, and a 3-month gap is too long for the recheck.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: A practice nurse is reviewing four adults with CKD. None has diabetes and all have stable results. Which person meets a NICE criterion for referral for specialist kidney assessment?
o: Lucy, 60, with eGFR 50 and ACR 15
Mo, 68, with a 5-year kidney failure risk of 2%
Jim, 82, with eGFR 55 and ACR 2 for five years
Ann, 57, with eGFR 46 and ACR 80 mg/mmol
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG203 (1.5.5) refers adults with an ACR of 70 mg/mmol or more (unless caused by diabetes and appropriately treated), a 5-year kidney failure risk above 5% on the 4-variable KFRE, ACR above 30 with haematuria, sustained eGFR decline, poorly controlled hypertension on 4 drugs, or suspected rare or genetic causes.

n.0: ACR 15 with a stable eGFR does not meet a referral criterion.
n.1: A 2% 5-year risk is below the 5% KFRE referral threshold.
