n.2: Stable G3a A1 CKD in an older person does not meet a referral criterion.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Aisha, 24, has type 1 diabetes and uses fingerprick capillary glucose testing. At a clinic review she asks what her blood glucose should be when she first wakes in the morning. Which target range should the nurse give her?
o: 4 to 7 mmol/L
6 to 10 mmol/L
5 to 9 mmol/L
5 to 7 mmol/L
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG17 (1.6.22) advises a capillary glucose target of 5 to 7 mmol/L on waking for adults with type 1 diabetes, individualised to the person.

n.0: 4 to 7 mmol/L is the NG17 target before meals at other times of day, not on waking.
n.1: 6 to 10 mmol/L is the JBDS perioperative capillary glucose target, not a self-management target on waking.
n.2: 5 to 9 mmol/L is the NG17 target at least 90 minutes after eating.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Owen, 38, has type 1 diabetes. At his annual review he asks what HbA1c level he should aim for to reduce his risk of long-term complications. He has no problems with hypoglycaemia. Which target should the nurse explain is recommended?
o: 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower
58 mmol/mol (7.5%) or lower
69 mmol/mol (8.5%) or lower
53 mmol/mol (7.0%) or lower
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG17 (1.6.6) supports adults with type 1 diabetes to aim for an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower, agreed individually, to minimise the risk of long-term vascular complications.

n.1: 58 mmol/mol is the NG28 level at which treatment is intensified in type 2 diabetes, not a type 1 target.
n.2: 69 mmol/mol (8.5%) is the JBDS 03 level above which diabetes control is optimised, with specialist referral, before elective surgery; it is not a type 1 target.
n.3: 53 mmol/mol is the NG28 target for adults with type 2 diabetes on a drug associated with hypoglycaemia.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Grace, 45, has type 1 diabetes and injects insulin into the same area of her abdomen because it hurts less. The nurse feels soft, rubbery swellings there, and Grace reports unpredictable glucose readings. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Massage the area firmly after each injection
Inject into the swellings to reduce discomfort
Rotate injection sites and avoid the swollen areas
Change to injecting into the deltoid muscle
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: These are signs of lipohypertrophy, which causes erratic insulin absorption. NICE NG17 (1.7.19-1.7.21) advises rotating sites within the same body area and avoiding repeated injection at the same point, with sites checked at least annually.

n.0: Massaging the site alters absorption and does nothing to resolve lipohypertrophy.
n.1: Injecting into lipohypertrophy is the cause of the unpredictable absorption and glucose readings.
n.3: Insulin is given subcutaneously; intramuscular injection speeds absorption and increases hypoglycaemia risk.

Diabetes & Kidney Care.q: Daniel, 22, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes three months ago and checks his capillary glucose with a meter. He asks how often he should test on an ordinary day. What should the nurse advise?
o: Before bed and 2 hours after each of the main meals
Once a day, rotating the time of the test each day
At least 4 times a day, including before each meal and bed
Twice a day, before breakfast and before the evening meal
Diabetes & Kidney Care.w: NICE NG17 (1.6.19) advises adults with type 1 diabetes using capillary monitoring to test at least 4 times a day, including before each meal and before bed, increasing up to 10 times a day in situations such as illness or before driving.

n.0: This misses the pre-meal readings on which mealtime insulin doses are based.
n.1: One test a day falls well below the NG17 minimum of 4 tests a day.
n.3: Twice-daily testing gives too little information to adjust mealtime insulin doses safely.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Brian, 54, has alcohol-related cirrhosis and is admitted vomiting large amounts of fresh blood. Pulse 118, BP 96/60. Variceal bleeding is suspected. Alongside resuscitation, which medicines should be given at presentation?
o: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics
Prophylactic antibiotics and propranolol
Terlipressin and vitamin K
Omeprazole and tranexamic acid
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.5.1-1.5.2): offer terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation to people with suspected variceal bleeding, followed by band ligation for oesophageal varices.

n.1: Propranolol lowers blood pressure in a shocked patient and is used later for prophylaxis, not at presentation.
n.2: Vitamin K is not the recommended presentation treatment; antibiotics are.
n.3: Pre-endoscopy acid suppression is not recommended and neither drug is the NICE treatment for variceal bleeding.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Ada, 76, has an upper GI bleed and continues to pass fresh melaena. Her platelet count is 42 x 10^9/L and her INR is 1.2. Which blood component is indicated now under NICE guidance?
o: Fresh frozen plasma
Cryoprecipitate
Prothrombin complex concentrate
Platelet transfusion
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: Two steps: she is actively bleeding, and her platelet count is below 50 x 10^9/L. NICE CG141 (1.2.4) says offer platelet transfusion to patients who are actively bleeding with platelets below 50 x 10^9/L. Her INR is not above 1.5 times normal, so FFP is not indicated.

n.0: FFP is for active bleeding with PT/INR or APTT above 1.5 times normal; her INR is 1.2.
n.1: Cryoprecipitate is added when fibrinogen stays below 1.5 g/L despite FFP.
n.2: Prothrombin complex concentrate is for actively bleeding patients taking warfarin.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Lillian, 81, takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation and is admitted with haematemesis and ongoing melaena. Her INR is 4.6 and she is actively bleeding. Which treatment does NICE recommend to reverse her anticoagulation?
o: Andexanet alfa
Recombinant activated factor VIIa infusion
Platelet transfusion
Prothrombin complex concentrate
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.2.5) recommends prothrombin complex concentrate for patients who are taking warfarin and actively bleeding.

n.0: Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban or rivaroxaban, not warfarin.
n.1: CG141 (1.2.7) says do not use recombinant factor VIIa unless all other methods have failed.
n.2: Platelets do not reverse warfarin, which acts on clotting factors.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Henry, 69, takes aspirin 75 mg after a previous heart attack and naproxen for knee pain. He has had a bleeding duodenal ulcer treated at endoscopy and haemostasis is achieved. Which medicines plan is consistent with NICE guidance?
o: Continue naproxen and stop aspirin until the ulcer heals
Continue both with added proton pump inhibitor cover
Stop both aspirin and naproxen for at least 3 months
Continue aspirin and stop naproxen during the acute phase
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.6.1-1.6.2): continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention of vascular events once haemostasis is achieved, and stop other NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors, during the acute phase.

n.0: Naproxen is the NSAID to stop; aspirin for secondary prevention continues.
n.1: Other NSAIDs are stopped in the acute phase, not continued under PPI cover.
n.2: Stopping secondary-prevention aspirin raises his risk of further cardiovascular events.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Yusuf, 29, is in the emergency department with 6 hours of right iliac fossa pain, scoring it 8/10. The surgical registrar will see him in about an hour. A junior doctor says analgesia should wait so the signs are not masked. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree, but give paracetamol in place of an opioid meanwhile
Ask for analgesia now, as early opioids do not mask the diagnosis
Ask the registrar to examine him before any analgesia is given
Agree and offer distraction until the registrar has examined him
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: A Cochrane review (Manterola et al, 2011) found opioid analgesia in acute abdominal pain does not increase errors in diagnosis or treatment decisions. Analgesia should not be withheld pending surgical review.

n.0: Paracetamol alone is unlikely to control 8/10 pain, and opioids need not be withheld.
n.2: Delaying analgesia until examination is the outdated practice the evidence does not support.
n.3: Leaving severe pain untreated for an hour is not justified by the evidence.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Stanley, 74, a smoker with hypertension, collapsed at home with sudden severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. In the emergency department his pulse is 122 and BP 86/52. Which condition should the nurse be most concerned about?
o: Acute mechanical low back pain
Renal colic from a ureteric stone
Acute uncomplicated cholecystitis
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG156 (1.1.7) says think about ruptured AAA in people with new abdominal and/or back pain, cardiovascular collapse or loss of consciousness, especially with an existing AAA, age over 60, current or past smoking, or hypertension.

n.0: Mechanical back pain does not cause hypotension, tachycardia and collapse.
n.1: Renal colic causes loin pain but does not usually cause shock and collapse.
n.2: Uncomplicated cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain, not sudden collapse with back pain.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Edna, 71, presents with new abdominal and back pain and a near faint. She has a known abdominal aortic aneurysm under surveillance. BP is 98/60. The team suspects rupture. Which action does NICE recommend?
o: Arrange a CT scan with contrast before contacting the vascular team
Arrange bedside aortic ultrasound now and discuss with vascular surgeons
Admit to the surgical ward for observation and repeat bloods
Refer to the AAA surveillance clinic for an urgent outpatient scan
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG156 (1.1.9): offer an immediate bedside aortic ultrasound when symptomatic or ruptured AAA is considered, and discuss immediately with a regional vascular service if it shows an AAA, or if ultrasound is unavailable or non-diagnostic and AAA is still suspected.

n.0: CT angiography may follow for people being evaluated for repair, but should not delay vascular discussion.
n.2: Ward observation delays definitive care for a possible rupture.
n.3: Outpatient surveillance is for asymptomatic aneurysms, not suspected rupture.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Tessa, 45, is admitted with mild acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. She is not vomiting and says she is hungry. Her care plan was written as nil by mouth by default. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Request parenteral nutrition while she is in hospital
Offer clear fluids for 48 hours before any food
Ask for review, as food is not withheld without a clear reason
Keep her nil by mouth until her amylase level has returned to normal
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.5) says ensure people with acute pancreatitis are not made nil by mouth and do not have food withheld unless there is a clear reason, such as vomiting.

n.0: Parenteral nutrition is for severe disease where enteral feeding has failed or is contraindicated.
n.1: Routine restriction to clear fluids is still withholding food without a clear reason.
n.3: NG104 advises against routine nil by mouth; normalising amylase is not a condition for eating.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Joseph, 52, is in a high-dependency unit on day 2 of severe acute pancreatitis. He has not eaten since admission and is not expected to manage oral intake soon. Which nutrition plan is consistent with NICE guidance?
o: Parenteral nutrition started as soon as possible after admission
Clear oral fluids for 7 days, then a light diet
Nil by mouth until his pain has settled
Enteral nutrition started within 72 hours of presentation
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.6-1.2.7): offer enteral nutrition to anyone with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis, starting within 72 hours of presentation; parenteral nutrition is for when enteral nutrition has failed or is contraindicated.

n.0: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for when enteral feeding fails or is contraindicated.
n.1: A week of clear fluids would leave a patient with severe illness malnourished.
n.2: Waiting for pain to settle risks malnutrition; NG104 sets a 72-hour start for enteral feeding.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Desmond, 60, has acute pancreatitis with a temperature of 37.8 C on day 1. A student nurse asks whether antibiotics should be started routinely to prevent infection of the pancreas. Which reply is consistent with NICE guidance?
o: Yes, prophylactic antibiotics are standard from admission
No, antibiotics are given after a CT scan confirms necrosis
Yes, prophylactic antibiotics are started once temperature exceeds 37.5 C
No, prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended in acute pancreatitis
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.3) says do not offer prophylactic antimicrobials to people with acute pancreatitis. Antibiotics are used to treat a confirmed or suspected infection, and sepsis is managed under NG253.

n.0: NG104 specifically advises against prophylactic antimicrobials.
n.1: Necrosis alone does not trigger prophylaxis; infected necrosis is treated when suspected.
n.2: A low-grade fever early in pancreatitis is usually inflammatory and does not justify prophylaxis.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Martin, 48, is admitted with acute pancreatitis and gallstones on ultrasound. He drinks about 8 units of alcohol a week. The admission note records the cause as alcohol. Which statement best reflects NICE guidance?
o: Gallstones are excluded as a cause if he drinks alcohol
His alcohol intake makes alcohol the presumed cause
The cause should not be assumed to be alcohol just because he drinks
The cause cannot be recorded until an abdominal CT scan has been done
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.1) says do not assume that acute pancreatitis is alcohol-related just because the person drinks alcohol. Gallstones and alcohol are the two main causes and other causes are investigated if both are excluded.

n.0: Gallstones are a leading cause and remain the likely cause here despite modest drinking.
n.1: Presuming alcohol because he drinks is the assumption NG104 warns against.
n.3: Ultrasound evidence of gallstones informs the likely cause; CT is not needed for that purpose.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Iris, 76, is awaiting emergency laparotomy for a perforated bowel. She is dehydrated, with a pulse of 110, and has diabetes and heart failure. Her chart includes regular ibuprofen for pain. What should the nurse do?
o: Swap the ibuprofen for a COX-2 inhibitor such as celecoxib
Give the ibuprofen, as NSAIDs reduce opioid requirements
Query the ibuprofen because NSAIDs raise her risk of AKI
Give the ibuprofen with food to protect her stomach
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG148 (1.1.13) lists emergency surgery with sepsis or hypovolaemia, intraperitoneal surgery, diabetes, heart failure, age 65 or over and NSAIDs among AKI risk factors in surgical patients. NSAIDs in a dehydrated patient should be queried with the prescriber.

n.0: COX-2 inhibitors carry the same renal risk, and substituting a medicine is for the prescriber.
n.1: The opioid-sparing benefit does not outweigh the AKI risk in a dehydrated high-risk patient.
n.3: Food does not reduce the effect of NSAIDs on renal blood flow, and she is nil by mouth for theatre.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Neil, 50, is listed for an elective inguinal hernia repair under general anaesthetic at 14:00. At his pre-admission appointment he asks until what time he can drink water on the day. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Until 12:00, 2 hours before his operation
Until 08:00, 6 hours before his operation
Until 06:00 on the morning of surgery
Until midnight the night before
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.4.1) advises telling people they may drink clear fluids until 2 hours before their operation, and that this can reduce postoperative headache, nausea and vomiting.

n.1: Six hours is the fasting interval for solid food; clear fluids such as water can continue until 2 hours before surgery.
n.2: Stopping at 06:00 means 8 hours without fluid, far longer than needed.
n.3: Fasting from midnight is outdated and causes unnecessary dehydration and discomfort.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Pam, 66, is waiting for an afternoon knee arthroscopy and it is now 3 hours before her operation. She asks which drink she may have from the ward trolley. Which drink fits the NICE description of a clear fluid?
o: A fruit smoothie
Black coffee without milk
Orange juice with pulp
A cup of milky hot chocolate
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.4.1) defines clear fluids as water, fruit juice without pulp, coffee or tea without milk, and ice lollies; these can be taken until 2 hours before the operation.

n.0: Smoothies contain fruit solids and are treated as food.
n.2: Juice containing pulp is not a clear fluid.
n.3: Hot chocolate is a milk-based drink, not a clear fluid.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Sunil, 41, is having elective laparoscopic surgery at 14:00 and has no diabetes or gastric emptying problems. He asks whether he can have two slices of toast for breakfast at 07:30. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: No, as solid food stops 12 hours before anaesthesia
Yes, as food can be taken until 2 hours before anaesthesia
No, as no food can be taken after midnight
Yes, as solid food can be taken until 6 hours before
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: The 2026 international consensus on perioperative fasting (Ruggeberg et al, Anaesthesia 2026) advises solid food until at least 6 hours before anaesthesia, with clear fluids until 2 hours before. Toast at 07:30 is six and a half hours before 14:00.

n.0: A 12-hour fast is not a recommended interval and causes avoidable harm.
n.1: The 2-hour limit applies to clear fluids, not solid food.
n.2: Fasting from midnight is longer than necessary and is no longer advised.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Ruth, 68, has type 2 diabetes and is being referred for an elective hip replacement. Her HbA1c measured last month is 74 mmol/mol. According to the JBDS perioperative guideline, what should happen?
o: Proceed with surgery and use a variable rate insulin infusion
Proceed with surgery, as HbA1c is not relevant to elective surgery
Optimise her diabetes before surgery, as HbA1c is above 69 mmol/mol
Cancel the referral until her HbA1c is below 48 mmol/mol
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: Two steps: JBDS 03 (CPOC, 2022) asks for an HbA1c within 3 months before referral and advises optimising diabetes before elective surgery if HbA1c is above 69 mmol/mol (8.5%), because poor control increases complications such as infection.

n.0: A VRIII manages glucose on the day but does not address the risk from poor preoperative control.
n.1: Raised HbA1c is linked with more postoperative complications, so it is relevant to elective surgery.
n.3: 48 mmol/mol is a long-term target, not the threshold for proceeding with surgery.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Graham, 63, has type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide twice daily and metformin twice daily. He is first on the morning theatre list tomorrow and will miss breakfast only. What does the JBDS perioperative guideline advise for tomorrow morning?
o: Take gliclazide as normal and omit metformin
Omit gliclazide and take metformin as normal
Take both gliclazide and metformin as normal
Omit both gliclazide and metformin
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: JBDS 03 (2022) medicines table: for a morning list, omit the sulfonylurea on the morning of surgery (hypoglycaemia risk while fasting) and take once- or twice-daily metformin as normal, provided eGFR is above 60 and no contrast is planned.

n.0: This reverses the advice: the sulfonylurea is the drug to omit.
n.2: Gliclazide while fasting risks hypoglycaemia, so it is omitted that morning.
n.3: Twice-daily metformin is taken as normal on the day of a morning list under JBDS 03.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Lorraine, 55, smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks about 30 units of alcohol a week. She is listed for major bowel surgery in 8 weeks. What should the preoperative nurse discuss with her?
o: Stopping smoking and reducing alcohol, with support
Postponing any lifestyle changes until she has recovered
Stopping smoking on the evening before her operation
Changing to e-cigarettes after the operation
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.3.2) recommends discussing lifestyle modifications such as stopping smoking and reducing alcohol with people having surgery, as part of prehabilitation within an enhanced recovery programme. Eight weeks gives time to benefit.

n.1: Prehabilitation is about changes before surgery, which NG180 encourages.
n.2: Stopping the night before gives little of the benefit that a longer quit period provides.
n.3: This delays any change until after surgery, losing the preoperative benefit.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Harriet, 79, is on the ward awaiting elective hip surgery. In the hour before transfer to theatre her temperature is 35.8 C. Her surgery is not urgent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck the temperature with a different thermometer in 4 hours
Transfer her and ask theatre staff to warm her during surgery
Warm her actively on the ward and transfer once 36.0 C or above
Give her an extra blanket and transfer her as planned
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG65 (1.2.3, 1.2.6): if preoperative temperature is below 36.0 C, start active warming on the ward unless surgery is urgent, and the patient should be 36.0 C or above before transfer to theatre.

n.0: A 4-hour wait delays treatment of hypothermia and her surgery.
n.1: CG65 advises against transfer below 36.0 C for non-urgent surgery.
n.3: A blanket is passive insulation, not active warming, and transfer below 36.0 C is not advised.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Molly, 34, takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and is booked for elective major knee surgery in 6 weeks. At her preoperative assessment, what advice about the pill should the nurse discuss?
o: Consider stopping it 4 weeks before, with other contraception
Stop it 2 weeks before surgery and use no contraception
Stop it on the morning of surgery and restart it on discharge
Continue it, as surgery does not change her VTE risk
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG89 (1.3.13) advises people to consider stopping oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives or HRT 4 weeks before elective surgery because of VTE risk, and to give advice on alternative contraception if stopped.

n.1: 2 weeks is shorter than NICE advises, and stopping without contraception risks pregnancy.
n.2: Stopping on the day does not reduce the oestrogen-related clotting risk in time.
n.3: Oestrogen-containing contraception adds to the VTE risk from surgery and immobility.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: A newly qualified nurse on a surgical ward asks which patients should be offered an enhanced recovery programme. According to NICE perioperative care guidance, which answer is correct?
o: People having elective major or complex surgery
People having emergency surgery out of hours
People having day-case surgery under local anaesthetic
People aged 65 and over having any operation
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.2.1-1.2.2) recommends offering an enhanced recovery programme to people having elective major or complex surgery, with preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative components.

n.1: NG180 recommends enhanced recovery for elective major or complex surgery, not by time of day.
n.2: Day-case local anaesthetic procedures are not the group NG180 targets for enhanced recovery.
n.3: Eligibility is based on the type of surgery, not age.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Wendy, 57, is on day 1 after a laparoscopic hysterectomy. Her pain score is 2/10 and she asks why she is still being offered regular oral paracetamol when her pain is mild. Which reply reflects NICE guidance?
o: It should stop now, as her pain is below 3 out of 10
It is offered before and after surgery whatever the pain level
It is given so that she can avoid opioids for the first week
It is given to reduce her temperature after the operation
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.5) recommends offering oral paracetamol before and after surgery irrespective of pain severity, as part of a multimodal approach (1.6.2).

n.0: NG180 advises offering oral paracetamol irrespective of pain severity, so a low score is not a reason to stop.
n.2: Paracetamol is part of multimodal analgesia; it does not mean opioids are avoided for a set period.
n.3: The indication here is analgesia within multimodal care, not fever control.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Clive, 62, is eating, drinking and taking tablets on day 1 after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His chart shows intravenous paracetamol 1 g four times daily. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
o: Ask the prescriber to review a switch to oral paracetamol
Give the IV dose, as it works faster than oral paracetamol
Omit paracetamol, as he can now take ibuprofen instead
Give the IV dose and add oral paracetamol for breakthrough pain
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.6) says do not offer intravenous paracetamol unless the person cannot take oral medicine. Clive can swallow, so the route should be reviewed with the prescriber.

n.1: Speed of onset does not justify IV use when oral medicines can be taken, per NG180.
n.2: NG180 uses paracetamol and an NSAID together in multimodal analgesia, not one in place of the other.
n.3: Combining IV and oral paracetamol risks exceeding the maximum daily dose.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Ethel, 86, is on day 1 after fixation of a fractured neck of femur. A colleague suggests adding regular oral ibuprofen, as NICE recommends it for postoperative pain. Which response is most accurate?
o: Agree, if she takes it with an oral proton pump inhibitor
Agree, as NICE recommends oral ibuprofen after orthopaedic surgery
Disagree, as NICE excludes hip fracture surgery from this advice
Disagree, as ibuprofen is used for mild pain and hers is severe
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.7) offers oral ibuprofen for immediate postoperative pain of all severities unless the person has had surgery for hip fracture, for whom the NICE hip fracture guideline on analgesia applies.

n.0: A PPI does not address the exclusion or the renal and bleeding risks in this group.
n.1: NG180 excludes people who have had hip fracture surgery from its ibuprofen recommendation.
n.3: NG180 offers oral ibuprofen for pain of all severities, so severity is not the reason.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Kevin, 48, is on day 1 after an open inguinal hernia repair. He is eating and drinking but cannot cough or walk to the bathroom because of pain, which he scores 7/10. He has taken regular paracetamol and ibuprofen. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give his prescribed oral opioid and reassess his pain
Encourage him to rest in bed until the pain settles
Wait for his next paracetamol dose, then reassess
Request an intravenous morphine bolus from the doctor
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.10): offer an oral immediate-release opioid for expected moderate to severe pain once the person can eat and drink, adjusting the dose so they can achieve functional recovery such as coughing and mobilising.

n.1: Bed rest delays recovery and raises VTE and chest complication risk; pain needs treating.
n.2: His pain is limiting coughing and walking now; waiting for the next dose leaves it uncontrolled.
n.3: IV opioids are not needed when he can take oral medicines.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Grace, 70, has had an open bowel resection and is nil by mouth with an ileus. She cannot take oral medicines and her pain is severe. According to NICE, what should she be offered for pain relief?
o: Regular intramuscular morphine every 4 hours
Oral immediate-release morphine as needed
A choice of PCA or a continuous epidural
Intravenous ibuprofen as the main analgesic
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.11): for people who cannot take oral opioids, offer a choice of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) or a continuous epidural, taking into account the benefits of an epidural after major open-torso surgery or with expected severe pain.

n.0: Intramuscular injections are painful, give erratic absorption and are not the NG180 option.
n.1: She cannot take oral medicines.
n.3: IV NSAIDs are adjuncts in multimodal analgesia and are not enough alone for severe pain.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Jamal, 59, does not have diabetes and is booked for an elective right hemicolectomy within an enhanced recovery programme. At pre-admission he asks about the carbohydrate drinks mentioned in his leaflet. Which reply reflects NICE guidance?
o: They replace the need for clear fluids on the day
They are considered before major abdominal surgery
They are used for people having day-case surgery
They are taken the evening before in place of a meal
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.4.2) recommends considering carbohydrate drinks before surgery for people having major or complex abdominal surgery, as part of an enhanced recovery programme.

n.0: They are used alongside clear fluids, which can still be taken until 2 hours before surgery.
n.2: NG180 recommends them for major or complex abdominal surgery, not day-case procedures.
n.3: They are an addition before surgery, not a substitute for an evening meal.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Maureen, 77, has CKD, mild cognitive impairment and frailty, and is booked for an elective hip replacement. At pre-assessment, which approach to planning her postoperative pain relief is most appropriate?
o: Use the standard ward protocol with no preoperative discussion
Plan to avoid opioids because of her cognitive impairment
Plan pain relief in recovery once the extent of surgery is known
Discuss options with her now, considering her kidneys and cognition
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.1) says discuss postoperative pain management options before surgery, taking into account comorbidities, age, frailty, renal and liver function, current medicines and cognitive function, as well as preferences and discharge plans.

n.0: NG180 asks for an individualised discussion, especially with comorbidities like hers.
n.1: Cognitive impairment calls for careful choice and dosing, not avoidance of effective analgesia.
n.2: Planning should start before surgery so that her preferences and risks are considered.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Sheila, 72, arrives in the recovery room after a 3-hour hip replacement. Her temperature is 35.6 C and she is shivering. The ward has called to collect her. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck her temperature in recovery in 1 hour
Transfer her with two warm blankets and recheck on the ward
Transfer her and start forced-air warming on the ward
Use forced-air warming and transfer once 36.0 C or above
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG65 (1.4.1): measure temperature on arrival in recovery and every 15 minutes; do not arrange ward transfer unless temperature is 36.0 C or above; if below 36.0 C, actively warm with forced-air warming until discharged from recovery or comfortably warm.

n.0: CG65 asks for temperature every 15 minutes in recovery and active warming now, not a 1-hour wait.
n.1: Blankets are passive warming, and CG65 advises against ward transfer below 36.0 C.
n.2: Warming should start in recovery, and transfer waits until she is 36.0 C or above.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Frank, 68, returned to the ward after bowel surgery 6 hours ago. On his 4-hourly observations his temperature has fallen to 35.8 C and he says he feels cold. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give paracetamol and recheck his temperature in 1 hour
Add a blanket and recheck at his next 4-hourly observations
Use forced-air warming, checking temperature every 30 minutes
Report it at handover as an expected effect of anaesthesia
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG65 (1.4.3): if a patient's temperature falls below 36.0 C on the ward, warm them with forced-air warming until comfortably warm (36.5 to 37.5 C), measuring and documenting temperature at least every 30 minutes during warming.

n.0: Paracetamol lowers temperature and does nothing to warm him.
n.1: A blanket is passive, and a 4-hour wait leaves hypothermia untreated.
n.3: Postoperative hypothermia increases complications and needs treating now, not reporting later.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Ahmed, 46, is on day 1 after an open appendicectomy. His wound dressing is soiled and needs changing, and the wound edges are closed and clean. Which solution should the nurse use to cleanse the wound?
o: Tap water from the ward sink
Sterile 0.9% sodium chloride
Povidone-iodine antiseptic solution
Eusol and gauze
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG125 (1.4.1-1.4.2): use an aseptic non-touch technique for dressing changes and sterile saline for wound cleansing up to 48 hours after surgery.

n.0: Tap water is used after 48 hours when a wound has separated or been opened, not on day 1.
n.2: NG125 (1.4.5) advises against topical antimicrobials for wounds healing by primary intention.
n.3: NG125 advises against Eusol and gauze for surgical wounds.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Brenda, 58, had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy yesterday and is going home today with dressings over her port sites. She asks when she can safely have a shower. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: After 24 hours, once the dressings are dry
After 48 hours from the end of surgery
After 7 days, once sutures are removed
After 10 days, once the wounds are fully healed
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG125 (1.4.3) advises telling patients that they may shower safely 48 hours after surgery.

n.0: 24 hours is earlier than the NG125 advice.
n.2: There is no need to wait for suture removal; showering is safe from 48 hours.
n.3: Waiting 10 days is unnecessary and affects hygiene and comfort.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Kenneth, 74, is on day 5 after a laparotomy. Part of his wound has separated and is now healing by secondary intention. He is well and afebrile. Which wound care plan is most appropriate?
o: Cleanse with tap water and ask tissue viability about dressings
Apply Eusol-soaked gauze twice daily to remove slough
Cleanse with sterile saline and pack with moist cotton gauze
Apply topical antibiotic cream and a dry dressing daily
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: Two steps: after 48 hours, NICE NG125 (1.4.4) supports tap water cleansing when a wound has separated, and (1.4.6-1.4.8) advises an appropriate interactive dressing chosen with tissue viability advice, avoiding Eusol and gauze or moist cotton gauze.

n.1: NG125 advises against Eusol and gauze for these wounds and for debridement.
n.2: NG125 advises against moist cotton gauze for secondary intention wounds.
n.3: There are no signs of infection, and routine topical antimicrobials are not recommended.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Doreen, 66, is on day 6 after a hysterectomy. Her wound is red, warm and swollen with spreading redness, and her temperature is 38.1 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remove alternate clips to let the wound drain and redress
Apply topical antiseptic and review the wound in 48 hours
Escalate for review and antibiotics for suspected infection
Apply a dry dressing and advise her to shower twice daily
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG125 (1.4.9): when surgical site infection is suspected by the presence of cellulitis, give an antibiotic that covers the likely causative organisms, guided by local resistance patterns and microbiology results. The nurse escalates for medical review and prescription.

n.0: Removing clips is a medical or surgical decision and does not treat the cellulitis.
n.1: Topical antiseptic does not treat cellulitis, and a 48-hour delay risks spreading infection.
n.3: Showering does not treat a spreading wound infection with fever.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Harold, 70, is being discharged after major abdominal surgery for colon cancer. He is surprised to be sent home with LMWH injections for nearly 4 weeks. Which explanation reflects NICE guidance?
o: The injections treat a clot found during his operation
LMWH is continued for 3 months after major abdominal surgery
LMWH is given at home because he cannot wear stockings
28-day prophylaxis is considered after abdominal cancer surgery
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE NG89 (1.14.3-1.14.4): pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 7 days after abdominal surgery when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, and consider extending it to 28 days after major cancer surgery in the abdomen.

n.0: This is prophylaxis; there is no information that a clot was found.
n.1: 3 months is the minimum treatment duration for confirmed DVT or PE, not prophylaxis after surgery.
n.2: Extended prophylaxis relates to his cancer surgery, not to stocking intolerance.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Winifred, 84, is on day 2 after surgery for a hip fracture. Yesterday she was chatty; today she is drowsy, slow to answer and cannot say the months backwards. Her family say this is not like her. What should the nurse do first?
o: Reassess her cognition at her follow-up clinic
Record that her dementia is progressing
Ask for a sedative to help her sleep tonight
Assess her with the 4AT and look for causes
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG103: people aged 65 or over with a hip fracture are at high risk of delirium. Recent changes, including hypoactive features such as drowsiness and slowed responses, should prompt assessment with the 4AT by a competent practitioner, then identification and treatment of underlying causes such as pain, infection, retention or hypoxia.

n.0: An acute change needs assessment now, not at a later clinic.
n.1: An acute change from yesterday suggests delirium; NICE advises treating for delirium first if unsure.
n.2: Sedatives can worsen delirium and are not first-line; causes need finding.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Victor, 63, arrives in the emergency department after vomiting blood twice at home. He is alert, pulse 98, BP 124/78. The team wants a formal risk score at first assessment to guide his management. Which score does NICE recommend at this stage?
o: Full Rockall score
Glasgow-Blatchford score
Two-level Wells score
Waterlow pressure ulcer score
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.1.1) recommends formal risk assessment for all acute upper GI bleeding: the Blatchford score at first assessment and the full Rockall score after endoscopy.

n.0: The full Rockall score needs endoscopic findings, so it is completed after endoscopy.
n.2: Wells scores estimate the probability of DVT or PE.
n.3: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk, not bleeding risk.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Shona, 34, had one small streak of blood in her vomit after a night of retching. She is well, with normal observations and blood results, and a pre-endoscopy Blatchford score of 0. According to NICE, what should the team consider?
o: Urgent endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
Intravenous proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy
Early discharge with outpatient follow-up
Admission for endoscopy within 24 hours
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.1.2) advises considering early discharge for people with a pre-endoscopy Blatchford score of 0, as they are at very low risk of needing intervention.

n.0: Immediate endoscopy after resuscitation is for unstable patients with severe bleeding.
n.1: CG141 (1.4.3) advises against acid suppression before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding.
n.3: Admission for inpatient endoscopy is for higher-risk patients; a score of 0 supports early discharge.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Ronald, 70, is admitted with melaena. He is now haemodynamically stable after an initial fluid bolus, with no further bleeding. His Blatchford score is 7. When should endoscopy be offered according to NICE?
o: Immediately, before any resuscitation
Within 24 hours of admission
At the next routine outpatient list
Within 72 hours of admission
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.3.1-1.3.2): offer endoscopy immediately after resuscitation to unstable patients with severe bleeding, and within 24 hours of admission to all other patients with upper GI bleeding.

n.0: Endoscopy follows resuscitation; it is not done before the patient is resuscitated.
n.2: An admitted patient with melaena and a Blatchford score of 7 needs inpatient endoscopy.
n.3: 72 hours exceeds the NICE standard for stable patients.

Acute & Perioperative Care.q: Frances, 58, is admitted with suspected bleeding from a peptic ulcer. Her prescription chart shows IV omeprazole to start now, before her endoscopy tomorrow morning. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: Give the omeprazole, as acid suppression stops ulcer bleeding
Give the omeprazole and arrange to give tranexamic acid with it
Give the omeprazole orally instead, as it is safer
Query it, as NICE advises against PPIs before endoscopy here
Acute & Perioperative Care.w: NICE CG141 (1.4.3) says do not offer proton pump inhibitors or H2-receptor antagonists before endoscopy to people with suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding. PPIs are offered after endoscopy if stigmata of recent haemorrhage are found (1.4.4).

n.0: NICE found no benefit from pre-endoscopy acid suppression in suspected non-variceal bleeding.
n.1: Adding an unprescribed drug is outside the nurse's role and does not resolve the query.
n.2: Changing the route does not address the recommendation against pre-endoscopy PPIs, and route changes are for the prescriber.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Albert, 86, has heart failure, COPD and osteoarthritis. He was admitted 6 hours ago with an acute exacerbation, is breathless at rest and drowsy. A student nurse wants to do a 4-metre gait speed test to complete his frailty assessment. What should the nurse advise?
o: Use a gait speed test now but halve the walking distance to 2 metres
Do the 4-metre gait test now while two staff are present to observe
Defer performance tests and gather his baseline history from family
Record him as CFS 8 based on how dependent he is today
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NICE NG56 1.4.2-1.4.3: be cautious about assessing frailty in a person who is acutely unwell and do not use a physical performance tool in that situation. The CFS is scored on baseline function, so history from Albert's family about the previous 2 weeks is the safer source.

n.0: Shortening the walk still uses a physical performance tool during acute illness and is not a validated measure.
n.1: NG56 1.4.3 advises against physical performance tools while acutely unwell, and testing a breathless drowsy man risks a fall.
n.3: CFS reflects baseline about 2 weeks before illness, not current dependency, so scoring today overstates frailty.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ivy, 79, has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and atrial fibrillation. On her baseline she is CFS 6. She takes 11 regular medicines and has attended the emergency department three times in four months. Which plan is most consistent with NICE NG56?
o: Repeat her frailty score in 12 months before changing any care
Refer each condition to its own specialist clinic for review
Offer an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity
Arrange a care home placement as frailty level 6 is advanced
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.2.1 suggests an approach that takes account of multimorbidity for people with frailty, frequent unplanned care or multiple regular medicines; 1.3.5 says consider it for those on 10 to 14 regular medicines. Ivy meets several criteria, so a coordinated, person-centred review is indicated.

n.0: Delay ignores current triggers (frailty, repeated emergency attendance, 11 medicines) that warrant action now.
n.1: Separate single-disease clinics increase treatment burden and fragment care, which NG56 aims to reduce.
n.3: CFS 6 (moderate frailty) does not by itself indicate care home placement; that decision depends on her needs and wishes.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ruth, 83, lives alone and is CFS 5 at baseline. She is being discharged after a fall-related admission. She sees a GP, a heart failure nurse, a diabetes clinic and a community physiotherapist. Her daughter is unsure who to contact. Which discharge action best supports safe coordination of care?
o: Give Ruth a list of every service telephone number to keep
Ask the daughter to phone each of the services weekly to check on her progress
Book Ruth into the ward follow-up clinic for all future concerns
Agree a care plan naming who coordinates care and share it with services
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.5.2 and 1.6.17 require an individualised management plan stating who is responsible for coordinating care, and that this is communicated to all professionals involved (with consent). This supports safe transitions between services (Platform 7).

n.0: A list of numbers leaves Ruth and her daughter to coordinate several services themselves.
n.1: Transferring coordination to the daughter is not a care plan and may not reflect Ruth's wishes.
n.2: A ward clinic cannot coordinate all community services and adds another appointment to her burden.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Frank, 88, is CFS 7 at baseline after a stroke two years ago and is fully dependent for personal care. He has a chest infection and is improving. A healthcare assistant says Frank 'must be dying' because CFS 7 is near the top of the scale. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: CFS 7 shows he is approaching the end of life and cannot recover
CFS 7 means dependency, but he appears stable and not likely dying soon
CFS 7 means life expectancy is usually under six months
CFS 7 should prompt a referral to the hospital end of life care team today
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CFS v2.0 level 7 (living with severe frailty) describes people completely dependent for personal care who seem stable and not at high risk of dying within about 6 months. Levels 8 (very severe frailty, approaching end of life) and 9 (terminally ill, life expectancy under 6 months) describe approaching death.

n.0: Approaching end of life and unable to recover from minor illness describes level 8.
n.2: Life expectancy under 6 months describes level 9, terminally ill.
n.3: An end of life referral is not indicated by CFS 7 when he is stable and improving.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Walter, 81, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He slipped in the ward bathroom 20 minutes ago and hit his forehead. He is alert with a GCS of 15, has not vomited and has no other indication for imaging. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue routine observations and scan if his GCS falls
Request a CT head scan within 1 hour of the fall
Escalate so a CT head scan can be considered within 8 hours
Arrange a CT head scan within 24 hours if he develops a headache
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NICE NG232 1.5.13: for people on anticoagulants (including DOACs such as apixaban) with no other indication for CT, consider a CT head scan within 8 hours of the injury, or within 1 hour if they present more than 8 hours after it. NG249 links inpatient falls care to this guidance.

n.0: Relying on a GCS drop misses bleeding that can be detected earlier on CT in people taking anticoagulants.
n.1: The 1-hour timing applies to people on anticoagulants presenting more than 8 hours after the injury, or those with other high-risk features.
n.3: Waiting for a headache and a 24-hour window is too late for someone on an anticoagulant.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Hilda, 77, has been admitted to a medical ward with a urinary tract infection. The nurse begins the NICE NG249 comprehensive falls assessment. Which assessment does NG249 include for hospital inpatients that it does not list for people in community settings?
o: Assessment for delirium
A structured medication review
Examination of footwear and feet
Assessment of visual impairment
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG249 1.2.2 lists delirium assessment for hospital inpatient and residential care settings only. Vision, medication review and footwear and foot condition are part of the comprehensive assessment in every setting.

n.1: Medication review is part of the comprehensive falls assessment in all settings.
n.2: Footwear and foot condition are assessed in all settings.
n.3: Visual impairment is assessed in all settings, not inpatients alone.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ken, 72, tells the practice nurse at his annual review that he tripped on a kerb once last spring. He was not injured and got up unaided. His gait and balance assessment today is normal and he takes no regular medicines. Under NICE NG249, what should the nurse offer?
o: A referral to a community falls prevention exercise programme
A comprehensive falls assessment and falls management
A home hazard assessment and intervention using a validated tool
Health and wellbeing information and physical activity advice
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG249 1.1.6: for people who have had a single fall in the last year and do not have a gait or balance impairment, offer health and wellbeing information and advice on physical activity in line with the Chief Medical Officer's guidelines.

n.0: A falls prevention exercise programme is offered when a single fall is accompanied by a gait or balance impairment (1.1.5).
n.1: Comprehensive assessment is for people meeting 1.1.3 criteria (for example frailty, injury, 2 or more falls, unable to get up); Ken meets none.
n.2: A home hazard assessment is considered for people with gait or balance impairment or needing comprehensive management.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Nora, 74, fell once in her garden 4 months ago with no injury and got up herself. She has no frailty. On assessment today she has an unsteady tandem walk and poor single-leg balance. According to NICE NG249, which plan is most appropriate?
o: Arrange a comprehensive falls assessment with a CT brain scan
Offer a falls prevention exercise programme and consider home hazards
Give written advice on physical activity and review her again in a year
Start daily vitamin D supplements to lower her risk of falling
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG249 1.1.5: for people who have fallen in the last year and have a gait or balance impairment, offer a falls prevention exercise programme and consider a home hazard assessment.

n.0: She does not meet the 1.1.3 criteria for comprehensive assessment, and brain imaging is not part of it.
n.2: Advice alone is for people with a single fall and no gait or balance impairment; Nora has an impairment.
n.3: NG249 states there is insufficient evidence for vitamin D specifically to lower falls risk.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Mavis, 82, is an inpatient who has fallen twice at night. Her regular medicines include zopiclone and amitriptyline, both taken for several years. As part of her falls management, what is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Continue both medicines unchanged because they are long-standing
Request that zopiclone is replaced with a short-acting benzodiazepine
Ask for a review of both medicines and a discussion of their falls risk with her
Withhold both medicines from tonight and inform the ward doctor in the morning
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG249 1.3.17 (hospital inpatients): as part of a structured medication review, consider adjusting medicines to reduce the risk of falls. For psychotropic medicines NG249 (1.3.3, 1.3.22) adds: review them, discuss the increased falls risk with the person and plan withdrawal as appropriate. Long-term hypnotics and tricyclics should not be stopped abruptly by the nurse.

n.0: Long duration does not remove the falls risk; NG249 asks for review and discussion.
n.1: Benzodiazepines are also psychotropics that increase falls risk, so this swap does not reduce it.
n.3: Abruptly withholding long-term psychotropics risks withdrawal effects and is not a nurse's prescribing decision.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Patrick, 79, is on day 3 of an admission for cellulitis. He has started staying in bed all day because he is worried he will fall, though he walked independently with a stick before admission. Which approach best reflects NICE NG249?
o: Keep him on bed rest until the physiotherapist has assessed him
Fit a chair sensor alarm and ask him to stay seated during the day
Provide a bedside commode so that he does not need to walk to the toilet
Reassure him he can get up, and encourage dressing and regular walking
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG249 1.3.19: encourage people to remain active in hospital by reassuring them they can still get up and do not need to restrict activity (unless advised not to), and help them get out of bed, get dressed and regularly stand and walk around.

n.0: Bed rest increases deconditioning and falls risk; he was independently mobile and has no restriction.
n.1: Restricting him to a chair is the sedentary behaviour NG249 asks staff to reduce.
n.2: A commode reduces walking further when the aim is to keep him active.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Walter, 81, who takes apixaban, had a CT head scan after an inpatient fall. It shows no injury and his GCS remains 15. The doctor asks for head injury observations. According to NICE NG232, what is the minimum frequency once his GCS is 15?
o: Hourly for 4 hours, then 4-hourly
Half-hourly for 1 hour, then hourly for 2 hours, then 4-hourly
Every 15 minutes for 1 hour, then hourly until the next day
Half-hourly for 2 hours, then hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG232 1.9.11: for people with a GCS of 15, minimum observation frequency is half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1-hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly. If the GCS drops after the first 2 hours, revert to half-hourly (1.9.12).

n.0: This omits the initial half-hourly period after the injury.
n.1: These periods are too short; NG232 sets 2 hours then 4 hours.
n.2: 15-minute observations are not the NG232 schedule, and it omits the later 2-hourly stage.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Gwen, 80, is being discharged after a fall. Her daughter asks whether she should buy vitamin D tablets because she heard they stop older people falling. Which response is most accurate according to NICE NG249?
o: Vitamin D is recommended for all older people who have had a fall
Falls evidence is lacking, but follow NHS vitamin D advice for bones and muscles
Vitamin D prevents falls when it is taken together with a calcium supplement
Vitamin D should be avoided because it can raise calcium levels and cause dizziness
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG249 1.3.18: although there is insufficient evidence to support vitamin D specifically to reduce falls, encourage people to follow NHS advice on taking vitamin D to maintain bone and muscle health.

n.0: NG249 does not recommend vitamin D to prevent falls; evidence for that purpose is insufficient.
n.2: NG249 makes no recommendation that vitamin D with calcium prevents falls.
n.3: NG249 encourages following NHS vitamin D advice; it does not advise avoiding it.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Arthur, 85, is screened with the 4AT. He is fully alert. He gives his age, date of birth and the hospital correctly but says the year is 2019. Asked for the months backwards, he says December to August, then stops. His wife reports no change from his usual state. What is his score and its meaning?
o: Score 6, suggesting delirium is likely
Score 0, suggesting no delirium or cognitive impairment
Score 2, suggesting delirium is likely
Score 2, suggesting cognitive impairment without delirium
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: 4AT: alertness normal 0; AMT4 one mistake 1; months backwards fewer than 7 correct (December to August is 5) 1; no acute change 0. Total 2. A score of 1 to 3 suggests cognitive impairment but not delirium; 4 or more suggests delirium (4AT user guide; NICE CG103 1.6.1).

n.0: A total of 6 would need the acute change item (4 points), which his wife does not report.
n.1: He made one AMT4 mistake and recited fewer than 7 months, so he scores 2, not 0.
n.2: The total is 2, but delirium is suggested by a score of 4 or more, not 2.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Frederick, 87, was living independently last week. Today he is very drowsy, keeps falling asleep mid-sentence and cannot attempt the orientation questions or the months backwards. A colleague says the 4AT 'cannot be done' and should be left blank. What should the nurse do?
o: Use the Abbreviated Mental Test 10 instead of the 4AT today
Leave the 4AT blank and repeat it once he is more awake
Record a 4AT of 4 for drowsiness and leave the other items blank
Score each untestable item 2 and complete the 4AT
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: The 4AT can always be scored: untestable AMT4 and attention items score 2 each, clearly abnormal alertness scores 4, and acute change from his independent baseline scores 4 (total 12). A score of 4 or more suggests delirium, which should prompt urgent clinical assessment (4AT user guide; CG103 1.6.1).

n.0: CG103 1.6.1 names the 4AT for assessment outside critical care, and he cannot attempt an AMT10 either.
n.1: Leaving it blank delays recognising delirium, a medical emergency; the 4AT is designed to score drowsy patients.
n.2: The remaining items must also be scored; untestable items score 2 and acute change scores 4.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Leonard, 80, has dementia with Lewy bodies and has developed delirium with a chest infection. He is frightened and hitting out. Verbal and non-verbal de-escalation has not worked. The junior doctor plans to prescribe haloperidol. What should the nurse do first?
o: Apply bed rails and mittens to stop him hitting out at staff
Suggest regular lorazepam instead, as it is safer in delirium in older people
Alert the prescriber to his Lewy body dementia before any dose
Give the first dose and observe him for drowsiness afterwards
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NICE CG103 1.7.4: if de-escalation fails, consider short-term haloperidol at the lowest dose, taking account of MHRA advice on cardiac and neurological risks, especially in Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. NG97 1.7.4 warns of severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions in Lewy body dementia, so the prescriber must weigh this first.

n.0: Mechanical restraint is not a CG103 intervention and increases distress and injury risk.
n.1: CG103 does not recommend benzodiazepines as first-line for delirium distress, and they can worsen confusion.
n.3: Giving it without raising the Lewy body risk exposes him to a possible severe sensitivity reaction.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Elsie, 88, is admitted with a hip fracture and has no confusion yet. Her hearing aids are in her handbag and she says the right ear 'feels blocked'. Which action best reflects the NICE CG103 delirium prevention package?
o: Ask for night sedation so that she sleeps through the noise
Move her to a side room by the nurses' station each night
Check her ears for wax, then make sure working hearing aids are used
Insert a urinary catheter so that her fluid balance can be monitored closely
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG103 1.4.12: address sensory impairment by resolving reversible causes such as impacted ear wax and making sure hearing and visual aids are available, used and in working order. Hip fracture and age 65+ put Elsie at risk (CG103 1.2).

n.0: Sedatives increase delirium risk; CG103 promotes sleep hygiene such as reducing noise.
n.1: CG103 1.4.1 advises avoiding moving people between rooms unless absolutely necessary.
n.3: CG103 1.4.7 lists avoiding unnecessary catheterisation as part of infection prevention.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Bert, 83, is at risk of delirium after bowel surgery. He is woken at 02:00 for a routine weight and at 06:00 for the ward medicine round, and the bay is noisy overnight. His NEWS2 is 0. Which change best reflects NICE CG103?
o: Give a hypnotic at 22:00 so that he sleeps through the night
Keep the timings but provide earplugs and an eye mask
Move his medicines to the 06:00 round on the next ward
Reschedule routine checks and medicines outside his sleep hours
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG103 1.4.13: promote good sleep by avoiding nursing or medical procedures during sleeping hours where possible, scheduling medication rounds to avoid disturbing sleep, and reducing noise during sleep periods.

n.0: Hypnotics increase delirium and falls risk and do not remove the avoidable disturbances.
n.1: Earplugs help with noise but leave the avoidable 02:00 and 06:00 disturbances in place.
n.2: Moving wards is discouraged (CG103 1.4.1) and keeps the early round that disturbs his sleep.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ada, 84, developed delirium with a urinary tract infection. The infection has been treated, but three weeks later she remains confused and forgetful, though calmer. Her family ask what happens next. Which plan best follows NICE CG103?
o: Discharge without follow-up as delirium usually settles by itself
Start a regular antipsychotic to help her settle at home
Re-evaluate for other causes and arrange a dementia assessment
Record a diagnosis of dementia and refer her for a care home
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG103 1.7.5: for people in whom delirium does not resolve, re-evaluate for underlying causes and follow up and assess for possible dementia (in line with NG97).

n.0: Persisting symptoms need follow-up; CG103 asks for re-evaluation and dementia assessment.
n.1: There is no indication for an antipsychotic; she is calmer and not at risk of harm.
n.3: Dementia cannot be diagnosed without assessment, and persisting confusion may still have another cause.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Cyril, 79, is admitted for elective knee replacement surgery tomorrow. He is orientated and well, but is over 65 and has mild cognitive impairment. When should a tailored delirium prevention package begin, according to NICE CG103?
o: After a 4AT score of 4 or more has been recorded on the surgical ward
Within 24 hours of admission, after assessing contributing factors
When the first signs of confusion appear on the ward
After surgery, once he has returned to the orthopaedic ward
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG103 1.4.2: within 24 hours of admission, assess people at risk for clinical factors contributing to delirium and provide a tailored multicomponent intervention package. Age 65+ and cognitive impairment are risk factors (1.2).

n.0: A 4AT of 4 or more indicates possible delirium; prevention should start before this.
n.2: Prevention begins before delirium appears; waiting for confusion means it has already developed.
n.3: Delaying until after surgery loses the pre-operative window for prevention.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Winifred, 90, has hyperactive delirium. Her daughter is upset and asks, 'Has Mum gone mad? Will she be like this for ever?' Which response by the nurse best reflects NICE CG103?
o: It will clear within 24 hours now her antibiotics have started
It would help her settle if visits stopped until she is calmer
It is common and usually temporary; please tell us about sudden changes
It is probably the start of dementia, so you should plan for more care at home
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG103 1.8.1: inform people and families that delirium is common and usually temporary, describe the experience, and encourage them to tell staff about any sudden changes or fluctuations. CG103 1.4.4 and 1.7.2 also support family visits to help reorientation.

n.0: Promising resolution within 24 hours is inaccurate; recovery time varies.
n.1: Family visits help reorientation; CG103 encourages involving family and friends.
n.3: Delirium is not dementia; suggesting this without assessment causes alarm and is inaccurate.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Dorothy, 86, has Alzheimer's disease and lives in a care home. For three afternoons she has been shouting, pacing and pushing staff away during personal care. She cannot explain what is wrong. According to NICE NG97, what should the nurse do first?
o: Move her to a quieter unit within the home for the afternoons
Increase checks to every 15 minutes and record each episode
Assess for causes such as pain, delirium or unsuitable care
Ask the GP for as-required risperidone to use in the afternoons
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.7.1: before any non-drug or drug treatment for distress, carry out a structured assessment to explore reasons for distress and check for clinical or environmental causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care. Psychosocial and environmental interventions come next (1.7.2).

n.0: Moving her may add disorientation and does not identify the cause of her distress.
n.1: Recording episodes without looking for the cause leaves pain or delirium untreated.
n.3: Antipsychotics are for risk of harm or severe distress after causes are explored (NG97 1.7.3).

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: George, 81, has Alzheimer's disease. Six weeks ago he started low-dose risperidone because hallucinations were causing him severe distress. Staff report he has been calm for a month. His daughter asks what happens next. Which response follows NICE NG97?
o: It must be stopped today, as six weeks is the maximum course allowed
He should now be reviewed to see if he still needs it, with you involved
The dose should be increased slightly to stop the hallucinations returning
It continues for 12 weeks in total before any review takes place
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.7.6-1.7.7: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, reassess at least every 6 weeks whether the medicine is still needed, and stop it if there is no clear ongoing benefit after discussion with the person and family.

n.0: NG97 sets a reassessment interval, not a fixed maximum course; stopping follows review and discussion.
n.2: Increasing the dose contradicts the lowest-effective-dose principle when he is settled.
n.3: Review is needed at least every 6 weeks, not after 12.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Mr Okafor, 79, has vascular dementia and is admitted to an acute ward. His daughter brings a completed 'This is Me' leaflet describing his preferred name, his routine, his love of hymns and that he becomes upset if rushed. What is the most appropriate use of this document?
o: Keep it at the nurses' station and refer to it if he becomes distressed
File it in his notes for the social worker to review before discharge
Use it to shape his care plan and share it with staff caring for him
Return it, as the ward admission assessment replaces this information
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: 'This is Me' (Alzheimer's Society and RCN) records personal preferences so staff can give person-centred care and communicate effectively. Using it in the care plan supports Code 1.1 and 2.1 (treat people as individuals, work in partnership) and NG97's emphasis on continuity and sharing information (1.3.5).

n.0: Waiting for distress before reading it loses the chance to prevent it.
n.1: Filing it for discharge wastes information that helps day-to-day communication now.
n.3: Standard assessments do not capture his personal routines and triggers, so it should not be returned.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Margaret, 83, has mixed dementia and no history of epilepsy or bipolar disorder. She has become verbally aggressive in the evenings. A locum doctor suggests starting sodium valproate to calm her. What should the nurse do?
o: Query it, as NICE advises against valproate for agitation in dementia
Give it, as valproate is safer than antipsychotics in older people
Give it, then check her valproate blood level after the first week
Give it, as mood stabilisers are first-line for agitation in dementia
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.7.10: do not offer valproate to manage agitation or aggression in people living with dementia, unless it is indicated for another condition. Code 18 and 19 require nurses to question medicines that may cause harm.

n.1: NICE does not recommend valproate as an alternative to antipsychotics for this purpose.
n.2: Monitoring levels does not address that valproate should not be started for this indication.
n.3: First-line management is a structured assessment and psychosocial interventions, not mood stabilisers.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Jean, 78, has Alzheimer's disease and lives with her husband. She is awake for much of the night and sleeps in her chair during the day. Her husband asks the community nurse whether melatonin would help. Which advice follows NICE NG97?
o: Melatonin at bedtime to restore her natural sleep pattern
Encourage longer daytime naps so that she is less tired
Daytime daylight, exercise and activities with a sleep routine
A short course of zopiclone to reset her sleep and wake pattern
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.7.13-1.7.14: do not offer melatonin to manage insomnia in people living with Alzheimer's disease; consider a personalised multicomponent approach with sleep hygiene education, daylight exposure, exercise and personalised activities.

n.0: NG97 1.7.13 says do not offer melatonin for insomnia in Alzheimer's disease.
n.1: More daytime sleep worsens night waking; NG97 suggests daytime activity and daylight.
n.3: Hypnotics raise falls and confusion risk and are not the NG97 approach.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Harold, 76, has mild Alzheimer's disease. Over two months he has become low in mood, tearful and anxious, and his GP assesses this as mild to moderate depression. He has no previous mental health history. What does NICE NG97 suggest?
o: Start an SSRI antidepressant as first-line treatment
Consider a psychological treatment for his low mood
Increase his donepezil dose to improve mood and memory
Refer for a care home placement to reduce his isolation
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.7.11-1.7.12: for people with mild to moderate dementia and mild to moderate depression or anxiety, consider psychological treatments; do not routinely offer antidepressants unless indicated for a pre-existing severe mental health problem.

n.0: NG97 1.7.12 says do not routinely offer antidepressants in this situation.
n.2: Donepezil is for cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, not a treatment for depression.
n.3: Mild dementia with low mood is not an indication for care home placement.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ted, 82, has dementia and is going home after an admission. He sees the memory clinic, a district nurse, a social worker and his GP. His wife says she never knows who to ask about his care. Which arrangement is recommended by NICE NG97?
o: A single named professional responsible for coordinating his care
A weekly GP review until his needs have become stable again
A carers' helpline number for her to use whenever she has any concerns
A care plan held by the memory clinic and reviewed every year
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.3.1-1.3.2: provide people living with dementia with a single named health or social care professional responsible for coordinating their care, who develops and reviews a care and support plan with the person and family.

n.1: Frequent GP reviews add burden without providing coordination across services.
n.2: A helpline is useful support but does not coordinate care across services.
n.3: NG97 asks the named coordinator to agree the plan and specify review timing, not an annual default by one service.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Mary, 84, has moderate dementia and cannot reliably describe pain. Using the Abbey pain scale, the nurse finds signs of pain linked to her arthritic knee and gives her prescribed paracetamol. What should happen next, according to NICE NG97?
o: Repeat the observational pain assessment after the analgesia
Reassess her pain at the next weekly multidisciplinary review
Use her verbal self-report from now on as she seems calmer
Record the pain as resolved once she stops calling out
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.8.3-1.8.5: use a structured observational pain tool alongside standard assessment, and repeat pain assessments after any pain management intervention and when behaviour changes may be caused by pain.

n.1: Waiting a week fails to evaluate the intervention promptly.
n.2: In moderate dementia an observational tool is used alongside self-report, which is unreliable for her.
n.3: Quietness is not proof of pain relief; the assessment should be repeated with the tool.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Bill, 70, has diabetes, heart failure, COPD and gout. At his annual review the practice nurse counts 16 regular prescribed medicines. He manages them himself and has had no recent admissions. What does NICE NG56 advise?
o: Use it, because 15 or more regular medicines puts him at higher risk
Consider it, because 10 to 14 medicines is the trigger range
Defer it until he has an adverse event from a medicine
Use it, because the NG56 threshold is 12 or more regular medicines
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.3.4: use an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity for adults of any age prescribed 15 or more regular medicines, because they are likely to be at higher risk of adverse events and interactions. For 10 to 14 it is 'consider' (1.3.5).

n.1: 10 to 14 medicines leads to 'consider'; at 16 NG56 says 'use' the approach.
n.2: NG56 is proactive; waiting for harm defeats the purpose.
n.3: There is no 12-medicine threshold; the bands are 15 or more, and 10 to 14.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Sally, 68, has chronic kidney disease and two recent episodes of acute kidney injury. She takes 7 regular medicines, including ibuprofen, furosemide and ramipril. Her nurse wonders whether a multimorbidity-focused review is appropriate. Which statement is correct under NICE NG56?
o: It is indicated when she reaches 10 or more regular medicines
Consider it, as fewer than 10 medicines can qualify when risk is high
It is not indicated, because she takes fewer than 10 regular medicines
It is not indicated, as kidney disease is a single condition
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.3.5: consider an approach that takes account of multimorbidity for adults prescribed fewer than 10 regular medicines but at particular risk of adverse events. NG56 1.6.2 names acute kidney injury among higher-risk adverse events.

n.0: Waiting for 10 medicines ignores her current high risk of further AKI.
n.2: NG56 includes people on fewer than 10 medicines who are at particular risk of adverse events.
n.3: She has several conditions and recurrent adverse events, so the approach can apply.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: A pharmacist and nurse are reviewing the medicines of Peggy, 84, using the STOPP/START criteria. A student nurse asks what the tool is designed to do. Which answer is most accurate?
o: Identify medicines to stop and beneficial medicines that are missing
Check that each dose is within the licensed range for her age
Calculate the total anticholinergic score of all her medicines
Predict her risk of falling from the number of medicines she takes
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.10 suggests a screening tool such as STOPP/START in older people to identify medicine-related safety concerns and medicines the person might benefit from but is not taking. Version 3 (2023) has 190 criteria: 133 STOPP and 57 START.

n.1: Dose-range checking is a prescribing check, not the purpose of STOPP/START.
n.2: Anticholinergic burden is scored with separate scales, such as the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden scale.
n.3: STOPP/START is not a falls prediction tool, and NG249 advises against falls prediction tools.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Lily, 85, has Alzheimer's disease. Her medicines include immediate-release oxybutynin for urgency, amitriptyline at night and chlorphenamine for itch. Her family say her memory and confusion have worsened over two months. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Stop the oxybutynin today and tell the GP at the next routine visit
Request a memory clinic appointment to repeat cognitive testing
Record the decline as progression of her Alzheimer's disease
Raise her combined anticholinergic burden for a medication review
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG97 1.6.2-1.6.3: be aware that some medicines increase anticholinergic burden and can worsen cognition; minimise this during medication reviews. NG123 1.4.29 advises against immediate-release oxybutynin in older women at higher risk of sudden deterioration.

n.0: Nurses do not stop prescribed medicines unilaterally; the prescriber must review all three together.
n.1: Cognitive testing without addressing the likely medicine cause delays the fix.
n.2: Assuming progression misses a reversible medicine-related cause.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Arthur, 79, has taken regular co-codamol 30/500 for back pain for two years. At a medication review he says he is unsure it helps and has been badly constipated. Which next step reflects NICE NG56?
o: Continue it and add a regular laxative to treat the constipation
Discuss reducing or stopping it and plan a review of the effects
Switch to an equivalent dose of tramadol to reduce constipation
Stop it today because he is unsure whether it is helping him
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.12: ask whether symptom-relieving treatments give benefit or harm. If the person is unsure of benefit or is experiencing harm, discuss reducing or stopping the treatment and plan a review of any changes, including whether to restart.

n.0: Adding a laxative adds to his treatment burden without addressing doubtful benefit.
n.2: Tramadol is also an opioid with constipation and other risks, and does not address the lack of benefit.
n.3: Stopping abruptly without discussion or a planned review risks withdrawal and loses shared decision making.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Edith, 91, is CFS 7 at baseline and lives in a care home. She takes atorvastatin for primary prevention and says, 'I'm on so many tablets, do I still need them all?' Which nursing response best reflects NICE NG56?
o: Advise her to stop taking the atorvastatin and tell the GP at the next visit
Explain that statins are lifelong once started and should continue
Arrange for her to discuss whether treatments of limited benefit continue
Explain that her GP will decide and arrange no further discussion
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.13-1.6.14: take into account the lower overall benefit of treatments that offer prognostic benefit in people with frailty or limited life expectancy, and discuss whether they wish to continue them.

n.0: A nurse should not advise stopping a prescribed medicine without prescriber review and shared decision.
n.1: NG56 specifically asks clinicians to reconsider preventive treatments in frailty.
n.3: NG56 requires discussion with the person about her goals and priorities.
