Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: During a medication review, the nurse notes that Rose, 84, who has osteoarthritis and had a recent fall, takes naproxen, low-dose aspirin, paracetamol, amlodipine and senna, with no gastroprotection. Which medicine combination should be highlighted first for its risk of serious harm?
o: Naproxen with low-dose aspirin
Paracetamol taken with amlodipine
Senna with paracetamol
Amlodipine with senna
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.2 lists medicines with a higher risk of adverse events, such as gastrointestinal bleeding and acute kidney injury, as a review priority. An NSAID with aspirin and no gastroprotection in an 84-year-old carries a high risk of GI bleeding.

n.1: This combination has no significant interaction or bleeding risk.
n.2: Senna and paracetamol do not combine to cause serious harm.
n.3: Senna and amlodipine do not combine to cause serious harm.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: A nurse is preparing for a structured multimorbidity review with Ahmed, 77, who takes 13 regular medicines. Following the NICE NG56 sequence, which step should come before reviewing his medicines?
o: Deciding who will coordinate his ongoing care
Arranging the timing of his follow-up review
Agreeing his individualised management plan
Establishing his goals, values and priorities
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.5.2 order: discuss the purpose of the approach, establish disease and treatment burden, establish goals, values and priorities, review medicines and other treatments, then agree an individualised plan (including coordination and follow-up).

n.0: Coordination of care is set within the final management plan.
n.1: Follow-up timing is part of the plan agreed at the end.
n.2: The management plan is agreed after the medicines review.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: A community nurse is identifying people on her caseload who meet the NICE NG56 definition of multimorbidity. Which person meets the definition?
o: Carol, 58, who has well-controlled type 1 diabetes
Derek, 71, recovering from a wrist fracture and a chest infection
Elaine, 63, who has hypertension treated with three medicines
Brian, 66, who has hearing loss and chronic back pain
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.1.1: multimorbidity is 2 or more long-term health conditions, which can include sensory impairment such as hearing loss and symptom complexes such as chronic pain. Brian has two long-term conditions.

n.0: Carol has one long-term condition.
n.1: A healing fracture and a chest infection are acute problems, not long-term conditions.
n.2: Several medicines for one condition is still a single long-term condition.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Gladys, 80, has heart failure, glaucoma, CKD and rheumatoid arthritis. She attends nine hospital appointments a month across five clinics and says the travel leaves her exhausted. Which action best reflects NICE NG56?
o: Explain that each specialty must see her separately for safety
Explore combining or reducing appointments within an agreed plan
Suggest that she misses the appointments she feels are less useful
Ask her family to take turns driving her to each appointment
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.2 and 1.6.4: establish treatment burden, including the number and type of appointments, and identify alternative follow-up arrangements to coordinate or optimise the number of appointments, with an agreed plan (1.6.17).

n.0: Separate specialty follow-up is the burden NG56 asks clinicians to reduce through coordination.
n.2: Missing appointments without a plan risks unsafe gaps in monitoring.
n.3: Transport help does not reduce the treatment burden itself.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Tom, 74, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis. During a multimorbidity review he says he has 'given up', rarely leaves the house and has stopped seeing friends. What should the nurse do next?
o: Refer him to a pulmonary rehabilitation programme straight away
Focus the review on his inhaler technique and blood glucose
Assess him for depression and anxiety and act on the findings
Reassure him that low mood is normal with long-term conditions
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.5: be alert to the possibility of depression and anxiety and consider identifying, assessing and managing these in line with NICE guidance on common mental health problems; 1.6.3 includes mental health when establishing disease burden.

n.0: Rehabilitation may help later, but his mood needs assessing first.
n.1: Concentrating on physical measures misses possible depression, which affects all his self-management.
n.3: Normalising low mood risks missing treatable depression.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Joan, 79, has taken alendronic acid for osteoporosis for 3 years. She has multimorbidity and asks the practice nurse whether she must keep taking it. What should the nurse explain, in line with NICE NG56?
o: It must continue lifelong to keep protecting her bones from fracture
Further benefit after 3 years is unproven, so discuss stopping
It should stop now, because 3 years is the maximum licensed course
It should continue for 10 years before any review is considered
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.16: tell people who have taken a bisphosphonate for at least 3 years that there is no consistent evidence of further benefit from continuing for another 3 years, or of harm from stopping; discuss stopping, including patient choice, fracture risk and life expectancy.

n.0: NG56 specifically suggests discussing stopping after 3 years.
n.2: Stopping is a shared decision based on fracture risk and choice, not a fixed maximum.
n.3: NG56 sets the discussion at 3 years, not 10.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: After a multimorbidity review, Harold, 82, agrees a management plan that changes two medicines and names his practice nurse as care coordinator. He consents to information sharing. Who should receive a copy of the plan?
o: Harold, in an accessible format, and those involved in his care
The practice nurse, who keeps it safely in the GP record
Harold's family, who can then tell the other professionals
Harold's GP, who then passes on any changes to the other services involved
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.17: share copies of the individualised management plan in an accessible format with the person and, with their permission, other people involved in care, including professionals, services and family or carers.

n.1: Keeping it in the GP record does not give Harold his own copy or inform other services.
n.2: Families should not be the channel for informing professionals; the plan goes to services directly.
n.3: Relying on the GP to pass on changes fragments communication between services.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Mr Patel, 76, has heart failure, diabetes and macular degeneration. At the start of his multimorbidity review his wife is present. He has capacity. What should the nurse clarify first about involving his family, according to NICE NG56?
o: Whether his wife will sign the management plan with him
Whether and how he wants his wife involved in key decisions
Whether his wife can take responsibility for his medicines
Whether his wife holds a lasting power of attorney for health
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.6.6: clarify with the patient whether and how they would like partner, family or carers involved in key decisions, review this regularly, and share information if the patient agrees.

n.0: NG56 does not require family signatures; the plan is agreed with the person.
n.2: Handing over medicines responsibility assumes involvement he may not want.
n.3: He has capacity, so an attorney's role is not the question; his own wishes are.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Violet, 87, lives alone with frailty, Parkinson's disease and recurrent falls. She is admitted through the emergency department with a urinary infection and new confusion. According to NICE NG56, when should a comprehensive assessment of her complex needs begin?
o: At her first outpatient appointment after she has gone home
Once her infection has been treated and her confusion has fully settled
At the point of admission, preferably in a unit for older people
When the discharge team is contacted to arrange her care
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.7.1 (from NG27): start a comprehensive assessment of older people with complex needs at the point of admission and preferably in a specialist unit for older people.

n.0: Outpatient assessment after discharge is too late to inform her inpatient care.
n.1: Delaying assessment until recovery loses information needed to plan care.
n.3: Waiting for discharge planning delays assessment that should start on admission.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: A student nurse asks why a person with five long-term conditions should not simply be treated according to each condition's NICE guideline. Which explanation is consistent with NICE NG56?
o: Their evidence often comes from people without multimorbidity
Single-condition guidelines apply to people under 65 years
Their evidence is drawn from studies in primary care
Single-condition guidelines have been replaced by NG56
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.1.3-1.1.4: evidence for single-condition guidance is regularly drawn from people without multimorbidity and taking fewer medicines, so think carefully about risks and benefits of each recommendation for the individual.

n.1: Single-condition guidelines are not restricted to people under 65.
n.2: The concern is the population studied, not whether trials were in primary care.
n.3: NG56 does not replace single-condition guidance; it informs how to apply it.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Brenda, 58, tells the continence nurse that she leaks small amounts of urine when she coughs, sneezes or lifts shopping. She has no urgency and her urine dipstick is clear. A digital assessment confirms she can contract her pelvic floor. Which first-line treatment does NICE NG123 recommend?
o: Bladder training for at least 6 weeks with a voiding schedule
Duloxetine for 3 months before considering surgery
An anticholinergic medicine with a low acquisition cost
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.4.4: offer a trial of supervised pelvic floor muscle training of at least 3 months as first-line treatment for stress or mixed urinary incontinence. 1.3.4 asks for digital assessment of contraction first. Brenda's symptoms are typical of stress incontinence.

n.0: Bladder training is first-line for urgency or mixed incontinence (1.4.11), not pure stress.
n.1: NG123 1.4.35 says do not use duloxetine as first-line for stress incontinence.
n.2: Anticholinergics treat overactive bladder, which she does not have.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Sheila, 66, attends for initial assessment of urinary incontinence. The nurse gives her a bladder diary to complete at home. Which instruction is consistent with NICE NG123?
o: Wear pads, weigh them and record the total leaked for 24 hours
Record every drink and void for 24 hours on a typical weekday
Complete it for at least 3 days, including work and leisure days
Record the number of times you wake to pass urine over 7 nights in a row
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.3.13: use bladder diaries in the initial assessment and encourage women to complete a minimum of 3 days, covering variations in usual activities such as working and leisure days.

n.0: This is a pad test, which NG123 1.3.14 says not to use routinely.
n.1: 24 hours is shorter than the minimum 3 days and misses day-to-day variation.
n.3: Night-time voids miss daytime frequency, urgency and intake, which a full diary captures.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Pauline, 72, has a sudden urge to pass urine and often leaks before reaching the toilet. She passes urine every hour and drinks six cups of strong coffee a day. Infection has been excluded. Which plan follows NICE NG123?
o: An indwelling urinary catheter while waiting for urodynamic studies
Immediate-release oxybutynin with a review at 6 months
Supervised pelvic floor training for 3 months, with pads
Bladder training for at least 6 weeks, with caffeine reduction
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.4.11: offer bladder training lasting a minimum of 6 weeks as first-line treatment for urgency or mixed incontinence; 1.4.1 recommends a trial of caffeine reduction in overactive bladder.

n.0: Catheterisation is not a treatment for overactive bladder, and urodynamics are not routine before conservative treatment.
n.1: Drug treatment follows conservative measures, review is due at 4 weeks (1.4.38), and IR oxybutynin is cautioned in older women.
n.2: Pelvic floor training is first-line for stress or mixed incontinence; her picture is urgency.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Marjorie, 81, has recently become incontinent of urine at home. Her daughter phones the district nurse asking for a supply of incontinence pads 'to sort the problem out'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Assess the type and cause of incontinence; use pads short term
Arrange an indwelling catheter so that she stays dry at night
Advise Marjorie to limit her fluids to about 1 litre a day
Order a 12-month supply of pads and review her at the end of it
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.4.16: do not offer absorbent containment products to treat incontinence; use them as a coping strategy pending treatment, as an adjunct, or long term once treatment options have been explored. New incontinence needs assessment (1.3.1-1.3.5).

n.1: Catheterisation is not a first-line response and brings infection risk.
n.2: Restricting fluids concentrates urine and risks dehydration; NG123 advises modifying intake only if high or low.
n.3: Supplying pads without assessment treats them as the treatment and delays diagnosis.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Gail, 69, attends with urinary incontinence. She has no dysuria, frequency change, fever or other symptoms of infection. Her urine dipstick is positive for both leucocytes and nitrites. What should the nurse do, in line with NICE NG123?
o: Start antibiotics now while the culture result is awaited
Send a midstream urine sample and await culture first
Repeat the dipstick in one week before taking any action
Treat the dipstick as normal because she has no symptoms
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.3.8: if women do not have symptoms of UTI but test positive for both leucocytes and nitrites, do not offer antibiotics without the results of midstream urine culture.

n.0: Antibiotics pending culture apply when there are UTI symptoms with a positive dipstick (1.3.6).
n.2: Repeating the dipstick delays the culture that NG123 asks for.
n.3: A positive result for both markers needs a culture, not dismissal.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Doreen, 70, started an anticholinergic medicine for overactive bladder a week ago. She tells the nurse her mouth is dry and her symptoms are no better yet, so she wants to stop it. Which response is consistent with NICE NG123?
o: Stop it now, as a dry mouth shows the medicine is unsuitable for her
Ask her GP to double the dose so that it works more quickly
Benefits can take 4 weeks, and dry mouth may show it is working
Ask her GP to switch her to immediate-release oxybutynin
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.4.25: explain that dry mouth and constipation may indicate the medicine is starting to work and that substantial benefit may take at least 4 weeks; review at 4 weeks (1.4.38), or sooner if adverse effects are intolerable (1.4.39).

n.0: Dry mouth is an expected effect; stopping at one week abandons treatment before benefit can appear.
n.1: Increasing the dose early increases side effects before the 4-week review.
n.3: Switching after a week is premature, and NG123 cautions against IR oxybutynin in older women at risk.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ivy, 72, has overactive bladder, hypertension and ischaemic heart disease. Nocturia is troubling her and a locum prescribes desmopressin. Before giving the first dose, what should the nurse do?
o: Give it at bedtime and restrict fluids for 1 hour beforehand
Give it in the morning instead, to reduce her night-time urine production
Query it, as NICE advises avoiding it over 65 with heart disease
Give it at bedtime and check her blood pressure next morning
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.4.34: desmopressin may be considered for troublesome nocturia, but avoid it in women over 65 years with cardiovascular disease or hypertension. Ivy has both, so the prescription should be questioned (Code 18).

n.0: Fluid timing advice does not address the contraindication in her case.
n.1: Changing the time does not remove the contraindication and would not target nocturia.
n.3: Monitoring after the dose does not prevent the harm the guidance warns about.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Betty, 84, has used absorbent pads for long-term management of urinary incontinence for two years after other treatments were tried. How often should her continence product use be reviewed, according to NICE NG123?
o: When she or her carers ask for a change in product
Every 3 years, as part of her general health check with the GP
At least once a year, including continence and skin integrity
Every 5 years, unless her symptoms change before that time
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG123 1.4.17-1.4.18: offer a review at least once a year to women using absorbent containment products long term, covering continence, skin integrity, changes in symptoms and circumstances, alternative treatments and product efficacy and quantity.

n.0: Waiting for a request is reactive; NG123 requires a scheduled annual review.
n.1: 3 years is longer than the annual review NG123 sets.
n.3: 5 years is far longer than the annual minimum.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Lisa, 45, has had widespread pain for 8 months with poor sleep and low mood. Blood tests and imaging are normal and no injury or disease explains the pain or its impact. Using NICE NG193 terms, how is her pain best classified?
o: Neuropathic pain, as it is widespread and has no visible cause or injury
Chronic primary pain, as no condition adequately accounts for it
Chronic secondary pain, as it has lasted more than 3 months
Acute pain, as it began less than 12 months ago
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193: chronic pain persists or recurs for more than 3 months. Chronic primary pain is where no underlying condition adequately accounts for the pain or its impact; chronic secondary pain is where one does. The two can coexist.

n.0: Neuropathic pain arises from nerve damage or disease, which has not been identified here.
n.2: Secondary pain requires an underlying condition that accounts for it, which has not been found.
n.3: Pain lasting more than 3 months is chronic, not acute.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Lisa, 45, has chronic primary pain. She asks the nurse what treatment might help her manage day to day. Which non-drug option does NICE NG193 recommend offering?
o: A course of therapeutic ultrasound sessions
A supervised group exercise programme
A course of TENS to use at home during flare-ups
Biofeedback sessions with a physiotherapist
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.2.1: offer a supervised group exercise programme to people aged 16 and over with chronic primary pain, taking needs and preferences into account.

n.0: NG193 1.2.6 says do not offer ultrasound for chronic primary pain.
n.2: NG193 1.2.6 says do not offer TENS for chronic primary pain, as there is no evidence of benefit.
n.3: NG193 1.2.4 says do not offer biofeedback for chronic primary pain.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Lisa, 45, has chronic primary pain that is affecting her sleep and quality of life. After a full discussion, her GP plans to prescribe a medicine. Which option is consistent with NICE NG193?
o: Duloxetine, after discussing its benefits and harms
Naproxen, taken with a proton pump inhibitor
Regular paracetamol, 1 g four times a day by mouth
Pregabalin, starting at a low dose taken at night
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.2.7: consider an antidepressant (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline) for people aged 18 and over with chronic primary pain after a full discussion. 1.2.10 lists medicines not to initiate.

n.1: NSAIDs are on the 'do not initiate' list for chronic primary pain.
n.2: Paracetamol is on the 'do not initiate' list for chronic primary pain.
n.3: Gabapentinoids are on the NG193 'do not initiate' list for chronic primary pain.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Lisa, 45, is offered amitriptyline for chronic primary pain. She becomes upset and says, 'So you think it's all in my head and I'm just depressed.' Which response is most appropriate?
o: It is a low dose of a strong painkiller that works on the nerves
It is mainly prescribed because chronic pain usually causes depression
It is used first because exercise and therapy have not worked for you
It can ease pain, sleep and distress even when there is no depression
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.2.9: if an antidepressant is offered for chronic primary pain, explain that it may help quality of life, pain, sleep and psychological distress, even in the absence of a diagnosis of depression. 1.1.16 also asks clinicians not to invalidate the person's experience.

n.0: Amitriptyline is not an opioid or a strong painkiller; this misinforms her.
n.1: This implies her pain is psychological and does not match the NG193 explanation.
n.2: NG193 does not make antidepressants conditional on failed exercise or therapy, and she has not tried them.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Mark, 52, has chronic primary pain and has taken codeine 60 mg four times a day for two years. He says it helps very little and makes him drowsy at work. What is the most appropriate approach, in line with NICE NG193?
o: Advise him to stop the codeine today as it has no evidence
Ask the GP to change to modified-release morphine for better effect
Explain the risks and support a plan to reduce and stop it
Continue the current dose because he has taken it for two years
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.2.11-1.2.12: if a person is already taking a medicine on the 'do not initiate' list and reports little benefit or significant harm, explain the risks of continuing and encourage and support them to reduce and stop, discussing withdrawal problems.

n.0: Abrupt cessation after two years risks withdrawal; NG193 asks for a supported, shared plan.
n.1: Switching to a stronger opioid adds risk without evidence of benefit for chronic primary pain.
n.3: Long use does not justify continuing a medicine giving little benefit and significant harm.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Rachel, 39, has had low back pain for 6 months. Her MRI is reported as normal. She looks anxious as the nurse prepares to share the result. Which statement best reflects NICE NG193?
o: The scan is normal, but that does not mean your pain is not real
The normal scan suggests the pain may be stress-related
Good news, the scan shows that your back is healthy and undamaged
We will repeat the scan in 6 months to find the cause
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.1.16: when communicating normal or negative test results, be sensitive to the risk of invalidating the person's experience of chronic pain. 1.1.15 also explains that a cause may not be found.

n.1: Attributing pain to stress without assessment dismisses her experience.
n.2: Calling her back healthy and undamaged implies the pain has no basis, which invalidates her ongoing pain and undermines trust.
n.3: Repeat imaging is not indicated by a normal result and reinforces a search for a cause.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Joyce, 61, has chronic primary pain managed with exercise and CBT. She contacts the nurse with a flare-up over the past week. She has no new neurological or other red-flag symptoms. Which response follows NICE NG193?
o: Arrange a short course of oral morphine for the flare-up
Refer her for an urgent MRI scan of the whole spine
Tell her that a flare-up means her underlying condition is getting worse
Reassess her, review her care plan and explore possible triggers
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.1.22-1.1.23: offer reassessment for a flare-up, review the care and support plan, consider investigating any new symptoms, and discuss what might have contributed. 1.1.15 explains flare-ups are expected and a cause may not be found.

n.0: NG193 1.2.10 says do not initiate opioids for chronic primary pain.
n.1: Without new or red-flag symptoms, urgent imaging is not indicated.
n.2: Flare-ups are an expected fluctuation (1.1.15), not proof of deterioration.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Dev, 48, is seen for the first time with chronic pain in his neck and shoulders. The nurse wants to understand how the pain and his life affect each other, as NICE NG193 recommends. Which question best does this?
o: How does the pain affect your sleep, mood, work and relationships?
Can you rate your pain on a scale of 0 to 10 at the moment?
Which of the painkillers have you found to work best for you so far?
Where exactly is the pain and does it spread anywhere else?
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG193 1.1.8: ask the person to describe how chronic pain affects their life (activities, work, sleep, wellbeing, relationships, social concerns) and how aspects of life may affect the pain.

n.1: A numerical rating measures intensity but not the effect of pain on his life.
n.2: Medicine history is part of assessment but does not explore life impact.
n.3: Location and radiation describe the pain, not its effect on his life.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Pat, 64, had chemotherapy for breast cancer 9 days ago. She arrives at the acute oncology unit feeling shivery and generally unwell. Her temperature is 37.9 C and heart rate 108. Bloods, including a full blood count, have just been sent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait for the neutrophil count before starting any antibiotics
Give paracetamol and repeat her observations in 30 minutes
Recheck her temperature in 1 hour, as it is below 38 C
Give the prescribed empiric antibiotics immediately
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NICE CG151 1.4.1.1: treat suspected neutropenic sepsis as an acute medical emergency and offer empiric antibiotic therapy immediately. Suspicion is based on being unwell after recent anticancer treatment, not on waiting for the count or a temperature threshold.

n.0: Waiting for the count delays treatment; antibiotics are given on suspicion.
n.1: Paracetamol can mask fever and delays the emergency treatment she needs.
n.2: A temperature below 38 C does not exclude neutropenic sepsis in someone unwell after chemotherapy.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Kathleen, 70, is at home 12 days after chemotherapy. She phones the district nurse saying she feels shivery, weak and 'not right', but her temperature is 37.6 C. What should the nurse advise?
o: Take paracetamol and phone back if her temperature goes above 38 C
Rest at home and drink plenty of fluids for the next 24 hours
Go to hospital now for urgent assessment for neutropenic sepsis
Book a GP home visit for tomorrow morning to check her over
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG151 1.3.1.1-1.3.1.2 (and NG253 1.1.10-1.1.11): suspect neutropenic sepsis in people having anticancer treatment who become unwell, and refer immediately for assessment in secondary or tertiary care. A fever threshold is not needed.

n.0: Paracetamol can mask fever and waiting for 38 C delays emergency treatment.
n.1: Staying home for 24 hours risks rapid deterioration.
n.3: A next-day visit delays emergency assessment and antibiotics.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Sean, 55, with lymphoma, is admitted with suspected neutropenic sepsis 8 days after chemotherapy. He has no allergies and no specific microbiology concerns. Which initial empiric antibiotic regimen does NICE CG151 recommend?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav with a review after 48 hours
Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam plus gentamicin
Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam as monotherapy
Intravenous vancomycin as he has a central venous line
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG151 1.4.3.1: offer beta-lactam monotherapy with piperacillin with tazobactam as initial empiric therapy for those needing IV treatment, unless patient-specific or local microbiological contraindications.

n.0: Initial empiric therapy is intravenous; oral switching is considered later in low-risk patients.
n.1: CG151 1.4.3.2 says do not offer an aminoglycoside in initial empiric dual therapy without a specific indication.
n.3: CG151 1.4.3.3 says do not offer empiric glycopeptides because of a central line.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Amira, 47, has a PICC line for chemotherapy and is admitted with suspected neutropenic sepsis. The nurse is preparing to start treatment. Which action is correct according to NICE CG151?
o: Avoid using the PICC line until blood cultures are back
Arrange a chest X-ray before starting the antibiotics
Remove the PICC line and send the tip for culture
Take blood cultures from the PICC and a peripheral vein
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG151 1.4.2.1: take an additional peripheral blood culture in patients with a central venous access device if feasible. CG151 1.4.3.4 says do not remove the device as part of initial empiric management.

n.0: The line can be used; avoiding it delays treatment for no benefit.
n.1: CG151 1.4.2.2 says do not perform a chest X-ray unless clinically indicated, and antibiotics must not wait.
n.2: CG151 1.4.3.4 advises against removing the device as part of initial management.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Four people who are receiving chemotherapy have blood results and temperatures recorded. None has other signs of sepsis. Which result confirms a diagnosis of neutropenic sepsis under NICE CG151?
o: Neutrophils 1.2 x 10^9/L, temperature 38.6 C
Neutrophils 0.8 x 10^9/L, temperature 38.2 C
Neutrophils 0.4 x 10^9/L, temperature 37.6 C
Neutrophils 0.4 x 10^9/L, temperature 38.4 C
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG151 1.4.4.1: diagnose neutropenic sepsis when the neutrophil count is 0.5 x 10^9/L or lower and there is a temperature higher than 38 C or other signs of clinically significant sepsis.

n.0: A neutrophil count of 1.2 is above the 0.5 threshold.
n.1: A neutrophil count of 0.8 is above the 0.5 threshold.
n.2: The count qualifies, but 37.6 C is not above 38 C and there are no other sepsis signs.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Grace, 66, attends the emergency department feeling unwell with rigors. Her last dose of chemotherapy was 3 weeks ago. The triage healthcare assistant says neutropenic sepsis is unlikely because treatment 'was too long ago'. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: Suspect it, as treatment within the last 48 hours counts
Suspect it, as treatment within the last 7 days counts
Suspect it, as treatment within the last 14 days counts
Suspect it, as treatment within the last 30 days counts
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NICE NG253 1.1.10: suspect neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell and are having or have had systemic anticancer treatment within the last 30 days. Grace's chemotherapy was 21 days ago.

n.0: 48 hours is far shorter than the 30-day window.
n.1: 7 days is not the NG253 window, and Grace's treatment would wrongly fall outside it.
n.2: 14 days is not the NG253 window, and her treatment would wrongly fall outside it.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ben, 58, is about to start his first cycle of chemotherapy. The chemotherapy nurse is preparing him for possible neutropenic sepsis. Which information is most important to give him, in line with NICE CG151?
o: Take paracetamol for a fever and call if it lasts beyond 24 hours
How and when to use the 24-hour oncology line and emergency care
Check your temperature weekly and record it in your treatment diary
Contact your GP surgery on the next working day if you feel unwell
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG151 1.1.1.1: provide written and oral information, before and throughout treatment, on neutropenic sepsis, how and when to contact 24-hour specialist oncology advice and how and when to seek emergency care.

n.0: Paracetamol can mask fever and a 24-hour delay is dangerous.
n.2: Weekly checks would miss rapid onset; the priority is knowing when to seek urgent help.
n.3: Waiting for the next working day delays emergency treatment.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Moira, 60, is on day 3 of IV piperacillin with tazobactam for confirmed neutropenic sepsis. She still has a fever of 38.3 C but her NEWS2 is stable and blood cultures show no growth. The junior doctor asks whether antibiotics should change. What does NICE CG151 advise?
o: Continue the current regimen while she remains stable
Add vancomycin to cover resistant skin organisms
Stop antibiotics because the blood cultures are negative
Switch to meropenem because the fever has not settled
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CG151 1.5.3.2: do not switch initial empiric antibiotics in patients with unresponsive fever unless there is clinical deterioration or a microbiological indication. 1.5.4.1: continue inpatient empiric therapy in patients with unresponsive fever unless another cause is likely.

n.1: There is no microbiological indication for adding a glycopeptide.
n.2: Negative cultures do not justify stopping while fever persists.
n.3: Persistent fever alone, without deterioration or microbiology, is not a reason to switch.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Derek, 68, has metastatic prostate cancer. He tells the ward nurse he has had worsening mid-back pain for a week, his legs feel heavy and he has had difficulty passing urine since yesterday. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Contact the MSCC coordinator immediately as an emergency
Seek advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours
Request a plain X-ray of his thoracic spine today
Give analgesia and refer him to the ward physiotherapist
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NICE NG234 1.3.2: if a person with a past or current cancer diagnosis has symptoms or signs of cord compression (limb weakness, bladder or bowel dysfunction, gait disturbance), immediately contact the MSCC coordinator and treat it as an oncological emergency.

n.1: The 24-hour advice route (1.3.3) is for pain suggesting spinal metastases without cord compression signs.
n.2: NG234 1.5.9 says do not use plain X-ray to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases or MSCC.
n.3: Leg weakness and urinary difficulty indicate cord compression, which needs emergency action, not routine physiotherapy.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Linda, 59, had breast cancer treated 4 years ago. At a clinic visit she reports 3 weeks of progressive back pain that wakes her at night and worsens when she coughs. Her strength, sensation, bladder and bowel function are normal. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours
Reassure her that this sounds like mechanical back pain
Request a plain spinal X-ray before any specialist referral
Refer her for a routine outpatient MRI within 6 weeks
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG234 1.3.3: seek advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours if a person with a past or current cancer diagnosis has pain with characteristics suggesting spinal metastases (progressive, night pain, pain on straining), without cord compression signs.

n.1: Night pain and pain on straining in someone with previous cancer are red flags for spinal metastases.
n.2: NG234 1.5.9 says do not use plain X-ray to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases.
n.3: A 6-week routine wait is too slow for pain suggesting spinal metastases.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Arthur, 72, has suspected MSCC with leg weakness and is being nursed flat while awaiting MRI. He becomes breathless and says he cannot tolerate lying flat. His oxygen saturation is stable. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Help him stand briefly to open up his chest
Sit him upright in the bedside chair to help his breathing settle
Raise the bed head partly while keeping his spine supported
Keep him completely flat and increase his oxygen
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG234 1.4.3: nurse people who are immobilised in a supine position (lying flat or with partial elevation) to minimise spinal weight bearing; if they cannot tolerate this because of pain or breathlessness, adjust their position to reduce these symptoms.

n.0: Standing loads the spine before stability is assessed.
n.1: Sitting fully upright in a chair puts full weight through a possibly unstable spine.
n.3: NG234 allows partial elevation; keeping him flat ignores his intolerance, and his saturation is stable.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Derek, 68, has metastatic prostate cancer and new leg weakness from suspected MSCC. The doctor asks the nurse about corticosteroids before his MRI. Which plan follows NICE NG234?
o: Dexamethasone 8 mg once the MRI has confirmed MSCC
Prednisolone 5 mg daily, starting after radiotherapy is planned
Dexamethasone 16 mg orally now, with blood glucose monitoring
Dexamethasone 16 mg after the oncologist has reviewed the MRI
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG234 1.8.1: for neurological symptoms or signs of MSCC, offer 16 mg oral dexamethasone (or parenteral equivalent) as soon as possible. 1.8.8: monitor blood glucose and offer a proton pump inhibitor. If MSCC is later ruled out, stop it (1.8.2).

n.0: The dose is 16 mg and it should not wait for MRI confirmation.
n.1: Low-dose prednisolone after radiotherapy planning is the wrong drug, dose and timing.
n.3: The dose is right but delaying until MRI review loses time; give it as soon as possible.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Ruth, 64, has lung cancer and has developed new numbness in both legs and a band of pain around her chest. The MSCC coordinator has been contacted. Within what time frame should her MRI be performed, according to NICE NG234?
o: Within 48 hours, at the regional spinal surgery centre
Within 1 week, as an urgent outpatient
As soon as possible, and always within 24 hours
Within 72 hours, once she is pain controlled
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG234 1.5.2: offer MRI to people with suspected MSCC as soon as possible and always within 24 hours, at the local hospital or appropriate centre with direct access to imaging.

n.0: 48 hours is too long, and transfer is used if local MRI is not possible.
n.1: A week's delay risks permanent neurological loss.
n.3: Imaging should not wait for pain control, and 72 hours exceeds the limit.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Following radiotherapy, the team judges that Joe's spine, affected by metastases, is likely to be stable. He starts graded sitting. When the bed head is raised to 60 degrees his back pain increases sharply and his legs feel weaker. What should the nurse do?
o: Stand him with a frame, as standing can relieve back pain
Give breakthrough analgesia and continue sitting him upright
Continue to 90 degrees, as pain is expected when sitting up
Lower him until the changes reverse, then seek reassessment
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG234 1.6.2-1.6.4: monitor neurological symptoms and pain continuously during mobilisation; if pain or neurological symptoms significantly increase, return the person to a position where these changes reverse and reassess spinal stability.

n.0: Standing increases spinal loading when there are signs of instability.
n.1: Analgesia may mask warning signs; the new weakness needs reassessment.
n.2: Progressing despite increasing pain and weakness risks further cord damage.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Maureen, 70, has multiple myeloma and takes no opioids. Over three days she has become very thirsty, is passing large volumes of urine, is constipated and is now newly confused. Her blood glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. What is the nurse's most appropriate interpretation and action?
o: Possible hyperkalaemia; arrange an urgent 12-lead ECG
Possible hyponatraemia; restrict her fluid intake today
Possible hypercalcaemia; escalate for an urgent calcium level
Possible dehydration from poor intake; encourage more oral fluids
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: Thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion in a person with myeloma or bone metastases suggest hypercalcaemia of malignancy, an oncological emergency that needs urgent blood calcium measurement and medical review (Cancer Research UK guidance on high calcium in cancer; recognition-level).

n.0: Hyperkalaemia does not explain thirst, polyuria and constipation.
n.1: Fluid restriction would worsen dehydration caused by polyuria.
n.3: Poor intake does not explain large urine volumes; this cluster points to high calcium.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Colin, 66, had bowel cancer treated 2 years ago. He has had mild low back pain for a month. Recent imaging showed no spinal metastases and his examination is normal. What should the nurse explain before he goes home, in line with NICE NG234?
o: Which symptoms to watch for, and to seek urgent help if they occur
Take regular anti-inflammatory painkillers and rest in bed
Ask your GP for a repeat spinal scan every 6 months while the pain lasts
Back pain after bowel cancer is expected and needs no review
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG234 1.3.6: for people with a cancer history and low back pain but no clinical evidence of spinal metastases or MSCC, explain what changes in symptoms to look out for (box 1, such as leg weakness or bladder problems) and to contact a professional urgently if symptoms change or worsen.

n.1: Bed rest and NSAID advice do not provide the safety-net information NG234 requires.
n.2: Routine repeat scanning is not what NG234 recommends; safety-netting is.
n.3: Dismissing review leaves him unaware of red flags that need urgent action.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Edna, 84, is admitted with pneumonia and currently needs two staff to help her wash and move in bed. The nurse is asked to record her Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score on the admission document. Which information should the score be based on?
o: Her usual function about two weeks before this illness began
Her function today while she is acutely unwell with pneumonia
Her Timed Up and Go result measured on the ward today
Her expected function on the day she is discharged home
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: The CFS is scored on the person's baseline, their usual state about 2 weeks before the acute illness, using clinical judgement (CFS v2.0 guidance). NICE NG56 1.4.2-1.4.3 also advises caution assessing frailty during acute illness and no physical performance tools when acutely unwell.

n.1: Scoring her current dependency would overstate frailty because acute illness temporarily worsens function.
n.2: NG56 1.4.3 says do not use a physical performance tool such as TUG in a person who is acutely unwell.
n.3: A predicted discharge state is speculation; the CFS records the established baseline.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Before her recent admission, Margaret, 80, washed and dressed herself and made simple meals, but her son managed her finances, drove her to appointments and did the heavy housework. Using the Clinical Frailty Scale v2.0, which level best describes her baseline?
o: Level 7, living with severe frailty
Level 5, living with mild frailty
Level 6, living with moderate frailty
Level 4, living with very mild frailty
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: CFS v2.0 level 5 (living with mild frailty) describes people who need help with high order instrumental activities of daily living such as finances, transportation and heavy housework, while personal care remains independent.

n.0: Level 7 means completely dependent for personal care, which she is not.
n.2: Level 6 means help with all outside activities and keeping house, plus help with bathing; Margaret washes herself.
n.3: Level 4 describes people not dependent on others for daily help whose symptoms limit activities; Margaret already needs help with finances and transport.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: Joseph, 78, attends a practice nurse clinic for a long-term condition review. He is well today. The practice uses the PRISMA-7 questionnaire to identify frailty, as suggested in NICE NG56. Joseph scores 4. How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: It indicates frailty, as the threshold is 4 or more
It indicates frailty, as the threshold is 3 or more
It is borderline and needs a repeat score in a year
It is below the threshold, so no frailty is indicated
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.4.4-1.4.5 lists the PRISMA-7 questionnaire with scores of 3 and above indicating frailty. A score of 4 is above that threshold, so frailty is indicated and a multimorbidity-aware approach should be considered.

n.0: The threshold is 3, not 4; a person scoring 3 would be missed by this rule.
n.2: A score of 4 is clearly above the threshold, not borderline, so it needs acting on now.
n.3: The NG56 threshold is 3 or more, so 4 indicates frailty.

Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.q: In a hospital outpatient clinic, Doris, 82, is well and is asked to stand from a chair, walk 3 metres, turn, walk back and sit down. She takes 15 seconds. According to NICE NG56, what does this result indicate?
o: Normal mobility, as the frailty cut-off is above 15 seconds
Normal mobility, as the frailty cut-off is above 20 seconds
Frailty, as more than 12 seconds indicates frailty
Frailty, as more than 5 seconds indicates frailty
Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer.w: NG56 1.4.5 lists the Timed Up and Go test, with times of more than 12 seconds indicating frailty. Doris took 15 seconds, so the result indicates frailty.

n.0: 15 seconds is not the threshold; anything over 12 seconds indicates frailty.
n.1: 20 seconds is not the NG56 cut-off; it is 12 seconds.
n.3: More than 5 seconds is the NG56 cut-off for walking 4 metres in a gait speed test, not for TUG.
